talks.title: Eugene Lim- You Have 1 New Appwntment
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Eugene Lim- You Have 1 New Appwntment - Hacking Proprietary iCalendar Properties.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DEF CON presentation, Eugene Lim (known online as 'space raccoon') investigates the security risks surrounding the iCalendar (ICS) format across modern email and calendar clients. While red teams frequently use calendar invites for phishing, Lim focuses on exploit scenarios stemming from parser discrepancies, legacy features, and proprietary client extensions. His research surveyed diverse targets across mobile, web, desktop, and IoT ecosystems—including VMware Boxer, Synology Calendar, Apple Calendar, Microsoft Outlook, Google Calendar, and NextCloud Calendar.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of the iCalendar Format**: Tracing the standard from RFC 2445 (1998) to RFC 5545 (2009), which aimed to ensure interoperability across competing office suites.
- **Insecure Standard Implementations**: How modern software unsafely implements default RFC properties, including automatic calendar additions that trigger zero-interaction issues.
- **Proprietary Extensions (X-Properties)**: How vendors add custom 'X-' properties for non-standard functionality, creating unexpected parsing behaviors and zombie features due to legacy code.
- **Protocol Interactions**: Vulnerabilities introduced at the boundaries between iCalendar and adjacent protocols like SMTP and CalDAV.

### Technical Details
- **Dangerous Standard RFC Properties**:
  - `VALARM`: Historically allowed sending local system files via email attachments or loading audio from remote FTP/HTTP servers.
  - `DESCRIPTION`: Intended as raw text, but Google and VMware interpreted it as HTML. In VMware Boxer (specifically the iOS client), lack of sanitization enabled script execution. Because many clients automatically ingest ICS files into calendars before user acceptance, payloads can trigger without user interaction.
  - `ATTENDEE` / `ORGANIZER`: Defined as a `mailto:` URI, RFC-compliant email formats support double quotes and special characters. In Synology Calendar, this allowed payload injection upon importing or receiving invites.
  - `ATTACH`: Apple Calendar checks if an attachment URL ends with `.icloud.com`. Because it automatically downloads such attachments and follows HTTP redirects, attackers can abuse this for zero-click remote file downloads.
- **Proprietary 'X-' Extensions**:
  - Microsoft historically introduced `X-MICROSOFT-CDO-AUTOSTARTCHECK` and `X-MICROSOFT-CDO-COLLABORATEDOC` (tested on Windows XP and Office 2003), which automatically launched video apps or opened remote files. Legacy properties like `MWSURL` (Meeting Workspaces URL) caused Outlook to send SOAP messages to arbitrary URLs and exposed clickable buttons that bypassed standard custom URI checks.
  - Google's `X-GOOGLE-CALENDAR-CONTENT` allowed embedding images and unsandboxed iframes within calendar entries (still functional in components like Google embedded calendar), leaking tracking data or executing dynamic scripts.
  - Apple's `X-APPLE-STRUCTURED-DATA` embeds Base64-encoded binary property lists, which decode to XML containing reservation details—creating four layers of abstraction and parsing.
- **Protocol Boundary Exploits**:
  - **SMTP Injection**: When replying to an event, the client inserts the `ORGANIZER` email into the SMTP `RCPT TO` command. By injecting newlines into RFC-valid quoted email strings, an attacker can append arbitrary SMTP commands, altering recipients, forged senders, or message bodies.
  - **CalDAV**: Because CalDAV is an older HTTP/WebDAV-based sync protocol that remains supported across Apple, Microsoft, and Google, it often lacks the strict input validation and API sanitization found on modern HTTP REST/Graph APIs, providing an alternate vector for injecting malicious ICS properties.

### Takeaways
Developers and vendors must be cautious with non-standard properties, as backward compatibility ensures that legacy features persist as long-term liabilities. Vendors should contribute to unified parsing standards, similar to Microsoft's internal iCalendar to Appointment Object Conversion Algorithm. Researchers are encouraged to explore the largely undocumented, multi-layered parsing behaviors across email and calendar applications.

talks.title: LiveCTF
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate LiveCTF and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This transcript captures the live commentary and gameplay during the kickoff of the LiveCTF tournament at DEF CON 30 CTF Finals. LiveCTF is organized alongside the main Nautilus Institute DEF CON CTF as a spectator-friendly, single-elimination knockout side tournament. Hosted by Jordan (ciphertext) and Carl (zeta-two), with assistance from Glenn behind the scenes, the tournament features 16 qualifying teams competing head-to-head in 1-on-1 matches on identical, rapid-fire exploitation challenges lasting roughly 30 to 45 minutes.

### Key Topics
- **Tournament Structure & Scoring**: Sixteen qualified teams compete across four rounds (15 matches total over three days). Each match pits one player from each team against the other with a dedicated laptop, earmuffs to block commentary, and no outside team assistance (though internet searching is allowed). Results award points that contribute to the overall DEF CON CTF attack-defense scoreboard. If matches run over ~45 minutes, sudden-death backup challenges (designed for ~5-minute solves) are prepared to keep the schedule on track.
- **Challenge Characteristics & Tooling**: Unlike lengthy, multi-hour defense/attack services in the main contest, LiveCTF challenges are focused, fast-paced pwnables and reverse engineering problems (predominantly x86 and x64 Linux binaries). Competitors rely on binary analysis frameworks (IDA Pro, Ghidra, Binary Ninja), decompilers, debuggers with extensions (GDB with GEF, pwndbg, PEDA), and exploit frameworks (pwntools, custom ptrlib, ropper, rp++).

### Technical Details
- **Match 1: "Just Call Me Maybe" (Pwnable)**:
  - **Teams**: PTB WTL (PwnTheBytes / WreckTheLine) vs. Shellfish.
  - **Mechanics**: The binary acts as an interactive syscall runner, allowing players to supply arbitrary syscall numbers and arguments repeatedly, returning the syscall's return value. The challenge is effectively shellcode/primitive construction rather than memory corruption discovery.
  - **Exploitation**: The primary barrier to spawning a shell via `execve` is getting the program path string (`/bin/sh` or `/bin/bash`) into readable memory. Shellfish explored `vsyscall` mapping, local C harness testing, and setting up an `mmap` syscall. PTB WTL implemented a Python wrapper leveraging `mmap` (using `MAP_FIXED` to place memory at a predetermined address), `read` (to write `/bin/sh` into memory), and `execve`. Shellfish narrowly edged out PTB WTL by seconds to secure the first win.
- **Match 2: "Open to Interpretation" (Pwnable)**:
  - **Teams**: Slashers (`/v/home/r/.bin/tw`) vs. Starbug.
  - **Mechanics**: A custom interpreter/VM implementing a switch statement over various command characters (including comparisons checking boundaries like 0 and 128).
  - **Exploitation**: Competitors analyzed sign mismatches in comparisons, leaked libc base addresses by reading function pointers (such as `putchar`), subtracted offsets, and identified paths to redirect execution (either via ROP gadgets found using `ropper` or jumping to libc `one_gadget` / `system`). Slashers won the match.
- **Match 3: "Knop Coding" (Source Provided Pwnable)**:
  - **Teams**: Maple Mallard Magistrates (MMM / "Mighty Ducks") vs. OSUSEC (Oregon State University Beavers).
  - **Mechanics**: Players are tasked with running code verified via the Capstone disassembly engine to contain only NOPs. The fundamental vulnerability is an architecture decoding mismatch: instructions are validated by Capstone under 64-bit disassembly mode but executed in a 32-bit execution context.
  - **Exploitation**: MMM brute-forced byte values to discover bytes that decode as multi-byte NOPs under x86-64 while executing as active instructions under 32-bit mode (such as stack modifications like `inc esp`). This allowed stack pivoting, corrupting return addresses, and aiming control flow at an internal `win` function present in the source.

### Takeaways
LiveCTF emphasizes speed, composure, and rapid tool fluency over exhaustive research. The transcript highlights how minor tactical decisions—such as whether to build clean abstractions versus hardcoding offsets, testing syscall sequences locally in C, or spotting subtle architecture mismatches in source code—dictate outcomes decided by mere seconds under intense stage pressure.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DEF CON talk, Sam Bent shares his firsthand experiences and operational security (OpSec) practices as a former darknet vendor and darknet market administrator. Drawing parallels between the hacking scene and darknet culture—such as shared paranoia, high valuation of anonymity, and intellectual challenge—Bent explains how he approached illegal vending with a structured security mindset. He highlights his research methodologies, physical and digital hygiene, shipping tactics, laundering practices, and the eventual legal fallout that led to his arrest and subsequent release from federal custody.

### Key Topics
- **Hacker Mindset vs. Darknet Operations:** Bent notes that transitioning from hacking to darknet operations was seamless because both rely heavily on security awareness, operational hygiene, and counter-adversarial thinking. However, darknet subculture is far more insular and lacks open-source educational resources.
- **Adversary Modeling and Manuals:** Drawing inspiration from Kevin Mitnick's approach in *Ghost in the Wires*, Bent studied law enforcement manuals—specifically the United States Postal Inspection Service guidelines on suspicious packages—to reverse-engineer what postal inspectors look for.
- **Logistics and Shipping OpSec:** Analyzing package volume and postal regulations, Bent preferred the United States Postal Service (USPS) over private carriers (UPS, DHL) because USPS requires a federal search warrant to open mail. To evade package screening, he avoided excessive tape, handwritten labels, and fake-looking recipient or return details, instead sourcing real addresses from public registries.
- **Digital Persona and Community Standing:** Building credibility on darknet markets (such as Hansa) and forums (such as Dread, created by Hugbunter after Reddit banned darknet market subreddits) by actively contributing thousands of helpful posts. Bent maintained strict PGP key hygiene, occasionally burning keys and resetting personas to shed scrutiny.
- **Countering Interceptions and Deliveries:** Managing controlled deliveries and postal interception "love letters" by ignoring drop-offs, keeping packages untouched to let potential tracking device batteries drain, and never signing for packages.
- **Financial Hygiene:** Avoiding custodial Bitcoin tumblers in favor of converting Bitcoin to Monero and back to break transaction chains, utilizing platforms like Changelly over ShapeShift.

### Technical Details
- **Physical & RF OpSec:** Bent maintained no home internet under his own name. Instead, he utilized a directional Yagi antenna to connect to an unsuspicious neighbor's Wi-Fi within direct line of sight, allowing him visual notice if law enforcement staged a raid on that IP location.
- **Package Integrity:** Utilizing multiple vacuum-sealed layers and visual barriers for shipments delivered within a 2- to 3-day window to prevent odor permeation before canine screening.
- **Legal & Case Research:** Leveraging PACER to examine Department of Justice filings and federal indictments against former vendors to identify specific OpSec failures and technical indicators.
- **Arrest and Sentencing:** Caught in connection with Operation Dark Gold (a federal sting targeting Bitcoin-to-cash laundering), Bent faced a 10-count federal indictment. After pursuing a Franks hearing on grounds of an unlawful warrant-free package inspection by a postal inspector, a co-conspirator's statement established conspiracy, prompting a plea deal resulting in a 60-month sentence. In prison, Bent studied federal law for 18 months and successfully petitioned for compassionate release with a 200-page motion.

### Takeaways
Bent emphasizes that even meticulous OpSec cannot guarantee absolute safety, as external factors, human error, complacency, and co-conspirators can compromise an operation. He strongly advises against entering the darknet vending trade due to high stress, extreme legal risks, and poor return on investment compared to legitimate security careers.

talks.title: Sam Quinn, Steve Povolny - Perimeter Breached Hacking an Access Control System
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Sam Quinn, Steve Povolny - Perimeter Breached Hacking an Access Control System.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At DEFCON, Steve Povolny and Sam Quinn from Trellix presented their vulnerability research on access control systems, specifically focusing on the HID Mercury access control panel family and the Lenel-4420 controller. Despite marketing materials claiming government-level physical security vetting, the researchers demonstrated that these controllers—widely used across critical infrastructure and Fortune 100 companies—suffered from severe cybersecurity flaws. Their research resulted in eight reported and patched CVEs, including four unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) zero-day vulnerabilities affecting millions of controllers across more than 20 partner brands.

### Key Topics
- **Target & Architecture**: Analysis of the HID Mercury / Lenel-4420 controller, its network-accessible embedded web interface (ports 80/443), its communication with the OnGuard management server (port 3001), and physical door relay control via GPIO.
- **Authentication Bypass & Command Injection**: Exploiting broken session cookie handling on HTTP POST requests and bypassing input filtering in the hostname configuration to execute arbitrary root commands at boot.
- **Reboot Primitives & Fuzzing**: Employing IDA Python automation and the Radamsa fuzzer inside an ARM QEMU emulated chroot environment to identify memory corruption bugs that trigger automated system reboots via a custom core dump script.
- **Firmware Upload Heap Overflow & ROP**: Exploiting an unauthenticated firmware update endpoint (`view_firmware_update.cgi`) suffering from a heap overflow due to dynamic signature size parsing into a static malloc buffer, generating a single-gadget ROP chain in ARM emulation.
- **Physical Impact**: Writing cross-compiled C code interacting with `/dev/` GPIO interfaces using `ioctl` calls to continuously toggle electrical door relays and force open physical doors.

### Technical Details
1. **Unauthenticated Hostname Command Injection (CVSS 9.0)**: The researchers identified that the controller's web server validated session IDs on GET requests but failed to perform any validation on POST requests, accepting arbitrary session cookies (e.g., `13371337`). While client-side JavaScript and the server-side `xss_string_test` function filtered special characters (such as spaces, slashes, and semicolons), tabs could be used as separators to evade string tokenization. Injecting into the hostname parameter in the network configuration allowed injecting commands into a root-level DHCP client execution (`-H` flag). To ensure network access before executing the payload, researchers nested an additional DHCP call to fetch a reverse shell script via `wget`.
2. **Reboot Trigger via Crash Handler (Unauthenticated DoS)**: Because the DHCP command executed only during device boot, the researchers required an on-demand reboot primitive. System crashes on the device invoked `CustomMSC_CoreDump_handler`, a bash script configured in `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` that ends in a system reboot. Using IDA Python and Radamsa within an ARM QEMU environment, they identified an out-of-bounds read in `advanced_network.cgi` (`strcpy`), forcing a segmentation fault and triggering a reboot.
3. **Firmware Upload Heap Overflow (CVSS 10.0)**: Upon upgrading to newer firmware with an official test setup from Convergint, the core dump handler was scoped to specific binaries, breaking the previous crash vector. However, a new diagnostics feature exposed an unauthenticated endpoint (`view_firmware_update.cgi`). The firmware parser allocated a static buffer (`0x190` bytes) with `malloc`, sought to the end of the uploaded file minus three bytes (`fseek`), read three ASCII bytes (`fread`), and converted them with `strtol` to determine the signature read length. Supplying a signature size exceeding the buffer (e.g., `999`) triggered a heap overflow. In ARM QEMU, the researchers leveraged register control over `r0`, `r1`, `r3`, `r4`, and `r6` to construct a 5-instruction ROP gadget calling `system()` with a `socat` reverse shell.
4. **Exploitation & Hardware Control**: On physical hardware, the heap overflow was used directly as a reliable reboot trigger to execute the staged hostname injection. Once root access was established, the researchers interacted with the door lock relays via a kernel module through `ioctl` calls targeting the GPIO device, running a tight `while` loop to continuously override the panel's automatic relock mechanism and keep the physical door unlocked.

### Takeaways
The presentation highlighted how physical security appliances often lag behind in software security hygiene. High-privilege access control controllers deployed directly on enterprise networks must be strictly isolated and subjected to rigorous cybersecurity audits, as flaws in administrative web interfaces can completely bypass physical perimeter security controls.

talks.title: Bill Graydon - Defeating Moving Elements in High Security Keys
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Bill Graydon - Defeating Moving Elements in High Security Keys.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Bill Graydon examines the security mechanics of moving elements in high-security physical keys—such as those found in Mul-T-Lock Interactive and MT5, ABLOY PROTEC2, and Medeco M4. Lock manufacturers incorporate moving elements (e.g., sliding pins, springs, and captive ball bearings) primarily to prevent casting, restrict standard 3D printing, and enforce patent protections over key blanks. Graydon explores naive bypass approaches before revealing a simpler method: creating a static surrogate key by removing material from the blank, enabling the entire key to shift within the keyway and actuate the required internal lock components.

### Key Topics
- **Purpose of Moving Elements**: Designed to stop unauthorized duplication via static casting or simple 3D printing, while serving as a legal mechanism to maintain 20-year utility patent control over blanks.
- **Naive 3D Printing & Compliant Mechanisms**: Challenges encountered when printing captive elements due to printer resin tolerances, and how flexible compliant mechanisms (spring tongues) can work around tolerance limits.
- **The Static Key Bypass Technique**: Removing material from the reverse side of a key to allow whole-key displacement, positioning a fixed protrusion at the required height without binding upon insertion or extraction.
- **Targeted Lock Platforms**: Testing and implementations across Mul-T-Lock Interactive, Mul-T-Lock MT5/MT5+, ABLOY PROTEC2, and the Medeco M4.
- **Coordinated Disclosure & NDA Dynamics**: Interacting with lock vendors (ASSA ABLOY group brands), navigating problematic intellectual property clauses in NDAs, and production mitigation strategies.
- **Broader Facility Security Defenses**: Addressing fundamental physical vulnerabilities (supply chain theft, modified code cards, installation flaws) before focusing on advanced key duplication attacks.

### Technical Details
- **ABLOY PROTEC2**: A naive approach used a modified PROTEC1 blank with a slot to manipulate the internal disc detainer mechanism using a pick. 3D printing a captive sphere failed because tight tolerances fused the ball while loose tolerances let it fall out. A functional design was achieved using a compliant mechanism with a flexible resin tongue. Graydon also demonstrated a completely static bypass using OpenSCAD to take the geometric intersection of two key profiles rotated relative to each other by two degrees on the y-axis, removing rear material so the static protrusion could enter the keyway and actuate the lock.
- **Mul-T-Lock Interactive & MT5/MT5+**: The Interactive model requires a moving component to lift a short pin above the normal shear plane. By shaving off the back of an inexpensive surrogate blank (sourced via AliExpress) and leaving a protrusion only at the interactive position, the whole key tilts inside the plug to reach the shear line. For the MT5/MT5+, a similar protrusion was modeled in OpenSCAD and 3D printed with a slider track on the reverse side; tilting the key successfully actuated the offset secondary pin.
- **Medeco M4**: The M4 uses a moving "shuttle pin" that interacts with an internal sidebar "lift pin." Initial attempts with a modified Schlage SC9 blank encountered binding because spring-loaded finger pins acted like a ratchet against key movement, and rotational tensioning caused the sidebar to bind against the finger pins. A subsequent bypass attempted a bent J-shaped overhang with a peak to depress the internal element below the core milling line, achieving sporadic operation (approximately 2 out of 10 attempts).

### Takeaways
- **Vendor Response & Disclosure**: Mul-T-Lock and ABLOY did not respond to vulnerability disclosures. In contrast, Medeco (via Clyde Roberson) engaged immediately, prompting extensive testing under an NDA after striking an overreaching intellectual property ownership clause. Medeco evaluated tooling modifications, such as deepening the cut or introducing a concave shape, to mitigate the J-hook bypass.
- **Defensive Mitigations**: Designers can counter full-key motion attacks by using opposing dual moving elements that widen the key profile, or by adding springs behind secondary locking elements (e.g., finger pins in MT5) to prevent sequential manipulation.
- **Holistic Security Perspective**: High-security key control can be completely bypassed by lower-tech avenues, including altered code authorization cards, stolen key blank supply chains, or gross installation errors such as loose retaining screws that allow an entire cylinder to spin in a door.

talks.title: CTF
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CTF.
talks.summary:
This talk features a detailed conversation with Nautilus organizers about designing DEFCON 30's Attack-and-Defense CTF, their first year running the competition. The CTF features 16 teams, each defending identical vulnerable servers while attacking others' systems. Teams reverse engineer services, find vulnerabilities, write exploits, and submit flags to a scoreboard.

Key design philosophy centers on creating fresh challenges that force elite hackers to iterate rapidly. The speaker emphasizes that successful teams distinguish themselves through fast iteration—trying multiple approaches quickly rather than getting stuck on single ideas. One highlighted challenge, "Web4Factory" by team member Itzen, features deeply nested Java class hierarchies designed as both technically challenging and humorous.

Infrastructure proved rougher than expected for their first year; the organizers had to retire one challenge early and reconfigured hardware overnight to manage server loads. The speaker compares this to previous DEFCON CTF runs with Legitimate Business Syndicate in 2017, noting that first-year CTFs typically face unexpected challenges.

Critical design decisions include multiple vulnerabilities per challenge to sustain engagement, careful scoring balance to prevent one challenge from dominating gameplay, and Service Level Agreement (SLA) penalties that make patching vulnerabilities more valuable than denial-of-service attacks. King of the Hill challenges were calibrated (win: 3 points, tie: 1, loss: 0) to encourage direct competition.

The organizers address the fundamental tension in hack competitions: designing sufficiently vulnerable systems for world-class hackers while maintaining solvability in finite time. They discuss preventing 'gaming the game' through transparent scoring and enforcing game spirit rules—permitting targeted attacks on patched services while prohibiting fork bombs that crash shared infrastructure.

Observations show strong on-site participation with most physical seating occupied. The speakers reflect on unintended bugs discovered by teams (such as the Mambo heap vulnerability) as design successes. The philosophical stance favors visible scoring over hidden scores, comparing transparent competition to standard sports models.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Hak5 interview at DEF CON 30, hosts Darren Kitchen and Shannon Morris sit down with DEF CON founder Jeff Moss (The Dark Tangent). The conversation explores the 30-year evolution of DEF CON from an unplanned gathering into one of the world's most influential hacker conferences. The group discusses the post-pandemic return to in-person events, the philosophical divergence between corporate information security and hacker culture, and the operational logistics required to manage an event with tens of thousands of attendees.

### Key Topics
- **Origins of DEF CON:** Moss recounts the accidental inception of the conference. While acting as a US hub for BBS networks, a planned farewell party in Las Vegas for a shutting Canadian network (Platinum Net) fell apart when the organizer vanished. Moss proceeded anyway, inviting people across IRC (`#hack`, `#freak`), EFnet, Usenet, and faxes, establishing an open, non-gatekept alternative to exclusive invite-only events like Summercon and HoHoCon.
- **Hacker Culture vs. Infosec Industry:** The speakers contrast the transactional, career-advancement focus of corporate infosec with the genuine curiosity and joy of discovery inherent to hacking culture. Moss notes that while conferences often cater to vendor sponsors, DEF CON established itself before corporate sponsorships were prevalent, allowing it to preserve its grassroots ethos.
- **Scale and Logistics:** Running DEF CON 30 relies on roughly 1,500 people, including about 1,000 community creators and 500 "Goons." To prevent tens of thousands of attendees from feeling lost, DEF CON utilizes over 30 specialized villages (such as Hardware Hacking and Voting Machine Hacking) to create micro-communities where people can find their tribe.
- **Preserving Hacker History:** The group addresses the difficulty the community faces in preserving its own past. Moss highlights his initiative, `infocon.org`, which archives hacking conference media, and mentions community-built projects like `infocondb.org`, created by a community member as an open database linking speakers and talks.
- **Conference Policies and Governance:** DEF CON adopted early transparency reports and codes of conduct, setting standards that Moss hoped other conferences would copy to elevate community norms.

### Technical Details
- **Logistical Constraints:** Moss explains venue selection hurdles in Las Vegas, noting why giant venues like the Las Vegas Convention Center (LVCC) are unsuitable: they lack movable air walls to divide spaces, which would be cost-prohibitive to install. DEF CON instead spans properties like Caesars Forum, Flamingo, The Linq, and Harrah's, organizing specific functions (such as workshops) into dedicated properties.
- **Hardware & Badge Tampering:** Moss recounts discovering attendees who created sophisticated counterfeit badges by heating vinyl records in ovens to precise temperatures and applying reflective films to replicate holograms, turning the forgery into a practical lesson in physical security and tamper evidence.
- **Security and Operational Precautions:** Practical aspects of attending DEF CON are touched upon, including turning off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on mobile devices to prevent unwanted interactions with custom hardware tools (such as Bluetooth Duckies).

### Takeaways
- DEF CON serves as an open learning environment where curiosity precedes corporate objectives: infosec teaches tool proficiency, while hacking teaches creative problem-solving.
- The village model provides critical "off-ramps" for attendees to engage directly with peers across specialized domains, regardless of background.
- Preserving history through community archives and documentation remains vital to maintaining the hacker community's foundational knowledge.

talks.summary:
### Overview
At DEF CON 30, host Shannon sits down with Eric and Justin from the Ham Radio Village to discuss the weekend lineup, hands-on activities, contests, and accessibility of amateur radio for convention attendees. The interview highlights how the village bridges the gap between traditional amateur radio culture and DEF CON's hacker mindset.

### Key Topics
- **Presentation Lineup**: Talks range from introductory guidance for newly licensed operators to technical presentations aligned with the DEF CON spirit, such as hacking ham radio software and exploring legacy protocols like 1200 baud over packet radio.
- **Software Security Realities**: Much of the existing amateur radio software was originally authored for legacy operating systems like Windows XP and remains unpatched despite ongoing usage.
- **Contests and Challenges**: The village hosts a beginner-friendly fox hunt contest requiring attendees to locate a hidden transmitter using handheld gear, along with offering special patches or badges as rewards.
- **Licensing Exams**: Free amateur radio license exams are administered throughout the weekend for both the United States and Canada, featuring unlimited retakes during operating hours.
- **Community and Mentorship**: The organizers highlight the value of mentorship (traditionally called "Elmers") and describe their ongoing community presence through hamvillage.org and Discord.

### Technical Details
- **Operating Frequencies**: The primary convention ham frequency noted for active DEF CON monitoring is 146.58 MHz (referred to as 14658 megahertz in transcript dialogue).
- **RF Challenges**: Operating on-site within conference hotels presents physical signal challenges due to venue structures functioning like massive Faraday cages. To counter this, organizers coordinate live operating from the outdoor patio at the Flamingo alongside remote station setups operating over the internet.
- **Packet Radio**: A featured talk covers 1200 baud over packet radio, a classic protocol not widely highlighted at DEF CON since its earliest iterations.

### Takeaways
The Ham Radio Village encourages attendees of all skill levels to visit, try out hardware, and attempt the free licensing exam regardless of prior preparation. With active mentor support and immediate retake policies, the village aims to broaden participation in amateur radio beyond traditional demographics.

talks.summary:
## Overview

Jon Marler (callsign K4CHN) provides an introductory overview of digital communication modes used by amateur radio operators, spanning voice transmission, data modes, and practical DIY hardware solutions. The presentation begins with his amateur radio background—receiving his first radio (Lafayette KT-200) from his grandfather and earning his technician and general licenses, including an attempt at DEF CON 27. He emphasizes that digital modes offer significant advantages in weak-signal scenarios while acknowledging their steep performance falloff compared to analog modes.

## Digital Voice Modes

Marler explains the fundamental difference between analog and digital voice: applying an encoded digital signal rather than analog audio to a carrier wave. He discusses bandwidth division methods (FDMA and TDMA) and introduces the AMBE/AMBE+ 2 voice encoder standard used by most commercial systems. He notes AMBE's controversial status: while the specification is open, it is patented by Digital Voice Systems Inc., requiring manufacturers to license and pay fees. In response, open-source alternatives like FreeDV and M17 exist without patent encumbrance.

Commercial systems covered include D-STAR (Icom), Yaesu System Fusion (YSF), DMR (Digital Mobile Radio), and P25—all incompatible with each other. Marler emphasizes this incompatibility as critical: operators must choose equipment matching their local network. He recommends the Yaesu FT-991 as an accessible entry point and discusses hotspots (including Open Spot and DIY Raspberry Pi solutions) as lower-cost alternatives for accessing digital networks over the internet.

## Digital Data Modes

**RTTY** (radioteletype): The first widely adopted digital mode using Murray/Baudot code at 45.5 baud (up to 75 baud), employing frequency shift keying. Lacks error correction and is highly interference-prone; requires clear signals for reliable QSOs. Used historically by the US Navy.

**PSK (Phase Shift Keying)**: Includes PSK31 (created by Peter Martinez at 31 baud), PSK63, and PSK125. PSK31 was designed for typing speed (~50 words per minute). More resistant to crowding and interference than RTTY; some modes include error correction. Software like FL Digi enables operation.

**Packet Radio (AX.25)**: Pioneered by Canadian amateurs in 1978 and authorized by the FCC in 1980. Requires a terminal node controller (TNC)—either hardware or software-based (Direwolf). **APRS** (Automated Packet Reporting System) enables location sharing via GPS coordinates, message store-and-forward, and telemetry reporting. Networks like TARPN and TexNet operate regionally.

**SSTV (Slow Scan Television)**: Developed in the 1950s, officially approved by the FCC in 1968, and famously transmitted images from the Apollo missions to the Moon. Supports both black-and-white and color modes (Scottie One, Robot, and others). Requires no license to receive; numerous free apps exist for phones, computers, and the International Space Station regularly transmits SSTV images.

**MFSK (Multi-Frequency Shift Keying)**: Excellent for weak-signal propagation via tropospheric scatter. Includes modes like FT8 and WSPR, popularized by WSJT-X software. FT8 allows rapid QSOs with signal reports; WSPR is a one-way mode for testing propagation and antenna performance via an internet database. Marler notes Raytheon uses military MFSK capable of 100 Mbps over extremely long distances.

## Hardware and DIY Solutions

Marler presents a simple, practical DIY circuit for Raspberry Pi integration using:
- GPIO pin connected to an opto-isolator (optical relay)
- A 3.5mm jack for push-to-talk control
- A $10 USB sound card for audio in/out (Raspberry Pi lacks native audio input)
- Direwolf software TNC requiring only one line of configuration

He demonstrates this with a $15 Kenwood 2-meter radio acquired without programming cables or microphone. After removing the proprietary connector and rewiring, he programmed it via TTL serial for APRS use. The circuit isolates the radio electrically and enables toggling GPIO pins to trigger push-to-talk. He suggests using ground-loop isolators ($8 each) for audio isolation if concerned about voltage spikes.

## Live SSTV Demonstration

Marler concludes with a recorded QSO using SSTV on an iPad app over 145.500 MHz (simplex). He calls CQ, his father-in-law responds, and they exchange images. He emphasizes that no license is required to receive SSTV—anyone can monitor and decode images from the ISS or other operators using iPhones, Androids, or computers.

## Takeaways

- Digital modes excel in weak-signal scenarios but require stronger discipline in frequency selection and timing
- Voice mode incompatibility necessitates community research before purchasing hardware
- Packet radio and APRS provide practical emergency communication and location-sharing capabilities
- SSTV is highly accessible and engaging for all skill levels
- Simple Raspberry Pi circuits enable integration of legacy radio hardware into modern digital networks
- Open-source software (Direwolf, WSJT-X, FL Digi) lowers barriers to entry

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DEF CON Recon Village presentation, Rae Baker explores how Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) techniques can be utilized to assist law enforcement in investigating human trafficking and smuggling cases. Drawing on experience as a senior recon analyst and volunteer for organizations like The OSINT Curious Project, Innocent Lives Foundation, and Operation Safe Escape, the speaker addresses the pervasive nature of trafficking, highlights key statistics, and deconstructs a comprehensive fictional investigation to demonstrate end-to-end OSINT tracking methodologies.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Human Trafficking Dynamics:** Trafficking affects diverse demographics regardless of age, race, sex, gender, or education level, though vulnerable groups include undocumented workers, LGBTQ+ individuals, abuse victims, asylum seekers, and ethnic minorities. Motivations span sex trafficking, forced child soldiery, criminal coercion, forced labor, forced marriage, and organ removal. Recruitment typically hinges on identifying a target's vulnerability or need—such as debt, substance abuse, unstable housing, or mental health concerns—and creating dependency.
- **Trafficking Realities and Cultural Context:** During 2020–2021, pandemic conditions spurred an increase in commercial exploitation and child sexual exploitation material (CSEM). Baker emphasizes that spreading viral social media misinformation (such as unverified rumors about children smuggled in furniture) diverts critical investigative resources away from actual victims. In 2020, U.S. records showed 109,216 victims identified, but only 9,876 prosecutions and 5,271 convictions. The speaker compares modern recruitment cycles—isolation, coercion, abuse, and deprivation—to cultural narratives like *Pinocchio*.
- **The Role of Misinformation and Public Engagement:** Well-intentioned users recirculating material or misinformation often inadvertently revictimize individuals or tie up law enforcement resources.

### Technical Details
A detailed fictional scenario demonstrates how analysts track traffickers across platforms:
- **Grooming Analysis & Selector Enumeration:** A victim named Naomi is groomed on Instagram by an operative named Crystal using compliments, displays of luxury goods, and an introduction to an accomplice named Jay under the guise of modeling work. Analysts use tools like `whatsmyname.app` and `Namechk` to enumerate usernames across platforms, surfacing related accounts on Cash App, Facebook, Kik, and adult sites.
- **Geolocation & Reflection Analysis:** While Instagram strips EXIF metadata from uploaded images, analysts examine Naomi's last posted photo in Las Vegas. By zooming in and reversing the reflection in her sunglasses, they identify the South Point Hotel, Casino & Spa and verify the location via Google Maps. Baker notes real-world precedents where online stalkers identified victims' train stations through eye reflections in photos.
- **Infrastructure & Whois Pivoting:** Analysts discover an escort website (`fake.net`) hosting the victim's photo, extracting the registrant name (Tabiru Bulat) and organization (Escorts International). Corporate records link the registrant to Bulat Trucking, operated by Pieter Bulat.
- **Dark Web Intelligence & Username Reuse:** Cross-referencing an associated Kik account username (`smalls_vic`, linked to Victor Small) reveals dark web forum activity where the user boasts about smuggling people in shipping containers aboard a vessel named *Iron Spire*.
- **EXIF Extraction & Image Verification:** Photos uploaded directly to the escort site retain embedded GPS coordinates pointing to an address on West 4th Street in Los Angeles (the All-Star Inn). Analysts correlate room photos with Google hotel listings and note its proximity to the Port of Los Angeles / Terminal Island.
- **Maritime Tracking & Remote Surveillance:** Public port cameras, shipping schedules, and terminal webcams are used to monitor the *Iron Spire* departing Los Angeles for Rotterdam. Upon arrival, terminal cameras capture a Bulat Trucking vehicle loading the container, providing actionable intelligence to alert Dutch authorities.
- **Real-World Parallels:** Baker notes the simulated scenario simplifies real-world tracking, contrasting the rescue with the tragic 2019 Essex case where 39 Vietnamese migrants died inside a refrigerated container.

### Takeaways
- **Actionable Law Enforcement Support:** OSINT analysts can uncover digital touchpoints—such as server records, IP addresses, subdomains, EXIF data, and physical vehicle identifiers—to supply actionable leads to law enforcement.
- **Combating Trafficking:** Individuals can report suspicious activity in trafficking hubs, practice ethical consumerism regarding supply chains, volunteer or donate to anti-trafficking groups, advocate for legislation, and offer employment or skills training to survivors.

talks.title: Crypto and Privacy Village
talks.teaser: Day 2 examines Crypto and Privacy Village.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session from the Crypto and Privacy Village comprises two complete presentations and a portion of an opening talk. The first portion explores modern and quantum cryptography concepts as well as historical cipher mysteries. The second presentation, titled "Breaking Historical Ciphers with Modern Algorithms" by Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh, investigates computational methods—specifically hill climbing and frequency analysis—to crack classical encryption schemes. The third presentation, "Cryptanalysis in the Time of Ransomware" by Mark Mager, outlines how malware reverse engineering and cryptanalysis uncover flaws in ransomware implementations, enabling the creation of free decryption tools.

### Key Topics
- **Modern & Quantum Cryptography Basics**: Discussions of elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) as a trapdoor function, threats posed by Shor's algorithm on classical factoring, and quantum key distribution (QKD) using polarized photons.
- **Historical Codebreaking vs. Modern Cryptanalysis**: Why modern cryptanalytic techniques (e.g., differential or linear cryptanalysis) fail on historical texts where algorithms, plaintexts, and keys are unknown, and ciphertext volumes are strictly limited.
- **Algorithmic Solutions for Classical Ciphers**: Applying hill climbing algorithms, scoring functions, simulated annealing, and frequency analysis to break monoalphabetic substitutions, turning grills, nomenclators, and Enigma messages.
- **Notable Historical Unsolved Ciphers**: Examination of the Phaistos Disc, Voynich Manuscript, Tamam Shud (Somerton Man), Ricky McCormick cipher, Blitz ciphers, Zodiac ciphers (Z408, Z340, Z32, Z13), Kryptos, and the Dorabella cipher.
- **Ransomware Cryptanalysis Methodology**: Combining dynamic analysis in sandbox environments with static reverse engineering to audit key generation, storage, and algorithm implementations.
- **Ransomware Implementation Pitfalls**: Case studies showing how ransomware authors introduce critical flaws such as hard-coded keys, static initialization vectors (IVs), flawed AES-CTR modes, and simple repeated XOR operations.

### Technical Details
- **Elliptic Curves & Trapdoor Functions**: An elliptic curve equation creates a trapdoor where drawing a line through two points intersects a third point, which is then reflected across the x-axis. The private key represents the secret number of iterations a point is looped.
- **Quantum Key Distribution**: Alice transmits photons with random polarizations (horizontal, vertical, diagonal). Bob uses random filters to detect them. Alice and Bob publicly share filter choices to derive a shared secret key from matching measurements. Any eavesdropping attempt collapses the wave function due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
- **Hill Climbing Optimization**: Used on classical ciphers (such as the 1896 Baring-Gould cryptogram and a 20x20 turning grill challenge). It starts with a random key candidate, scores decrypted plaintext using letter or n-gram frequencies, applies slight key mutations, and climbs toward higher scores while running multiple iterations to avoid local maxima.
- **Enigma Decryption via Modern Compute**: Jim Gillogly's 1995 algorithm breaks Enigma without requiring a known crib by independently attacking the first three key components (rotor choice, order, and start position) using letter frequencies, followed by attacking the plugboard (steckerbrett).
- **Ransomware Vulnerability Analysis**:
  - *PowerWare*: Claims to use RSA-2048 and AES-128, but decompiled PowerShell reveals AES-CBC using `RijndaelManaged` with a hard-coded 256-bit key, static IV, and zero padding, encrypting only the first 2048 bytes.
  - *Nemucod*: Claims RSA-1024, but merely executes a byte-wise XOR against a hard-coded 255-byte key on the first 2048 bytes; running the encryptor twice restores the plaintext.
  - *TorrentLocker*: Employs LibTomCrypt for AES in counter mode (CTR). By encrypting a file filled with null bytes, an analyst isolates the keystream and decrypts target files by XORing the keystream against ciphertext blocks.
  - *Apocalypse*: Discards advertised military-grade crypto for a simple custom loop combining two XOR operations with a static key and a four-byte magic header.

### Takeaways
Historical codebreaking and ransomware defense both benefit heavily from algorithmic cryptanalysis. While classical ciphers yield to modern heuristic search methods like hill climbing, ransomware schemes frequently collapse under basic cryptanalysis due to severe developer implementation errors, hard-coded secrets, and cryptographic misuse. Public disclosure of decrypters and collaborative research forums (such as Bleeping Computer) remain vital counter-measures against ransomware campaigns.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Cloud Village, Mazin Ahmed discusses the inherent security risks associated with Terraform environments and Infrastructure as Code (IaC). While Terraform provides major advantages for infrastructure automation, scalability, peer review, and compliance scanning, it by default requires extensive permissions and careful configuration to remain secure. Ahmed highlights that Terraform's default setup is not inherently safe, emphasizing that a single mistake or compromise in a Terraform environment can result in full cloud infrastructure takeover, data exfiltration, or cloud ransomware.

### Key Topics
- **Infrastructure as Code (IaC) & Terraform Basics**: Overview of how Terraform manages state using HCL and applies configurations across cloud providers with elevated permissions.
- **Terraform State File Risks**: How state files act as databases storing plain-text secrets, including database credentials, IAM keys, and SSL certificates, both in S3 remote backends and self-hosted Terraform Enterprise instances.
- **Attack Persistence & Exposure**: Why Terraform Enterprise instances make ideal targets for attackers due to high cloud permissions, lack of regular patching/auditing, and accidental public internet exposure.
- **Remote Code Execution via Terraform Plan**: Exploiting external data sources and malicious providers during `terraform plan` execution via unapproved pull requests.
- **The Evil Provider Attack & Live Demonstration**: Registering backdoored custom providers on the official Terraform registry and popping a reverse shell inside HashiCorp's Terraform Cloud (`app.terraform.io`).

### Technical Details
Ahmed outlines multiple attack scenarios and proof-of-concept vectors:
- **State File Access**: S3 buckets configured as remote backends often permit `GetObject` calls that leak sensitive deployment outputs in cleartext. Similarly, Terraform Enterprise or Terraform Cloud's `state_version_output` API can be queried by a compromised developer account to download state files directly.
- **Plan-Stage Remote Code Execution**: Referencing work by Alex K, Ahmed explains that running `terraform plan` on untrusted branches can trigger code execution via malicious external data sources or providers before code is merged. He notes that a 2018 proposed restriction by Eric Ostermann in Atlantis was rejected, leaving platforms executing `terraform plan` susceptible.
- **Registry Backdoor Demo**: Ahmed created a GitHub account (`evilterraform`) and uploaded a provider (`terraform-provider-evil`) containing reverse shell code. Because HashiCorp's provider publishing is automated, the provider was accepted into the official Terraform registry under the "cloud automations" category. VirusTotal showed zero detections. By referencing this provider in a configuration run on HashiCorp's Terraform Cloud (`app.terraform.io`), Ahmed obtained a reverse shell inside HashiCorp's infrastructure. HashiCorp's security team detected the activity within hours, contacted Ahmed, and engaged in discussions regarding mitigations.

### Takeaways & Recommendations
- **Secure Remote Backends**: Implement strict S3 bucket access policies to restrict state access specifically to the Terraform execution identity.
- **Isolate Management Instances**: Deploy Terraform Enterprise within isolated VPCs rather than exposing them directly to the public internet.
- **Restrict Repository Access**: Treat pull requests and feature branch write access as high-risk, since even unmerged code can execute commands during plan workflows.
- **Inspect Providers & Add CI Checks**: Implement CI checks to monitor for rogue or unverified Terraform providers, and continually audit state storage and Terraform host instances.
- **Review Security Models**: Consult resources like the Terraform Cloud Security Model for formal threat modeling.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk celebrating the one-year milestone of Blue Team Village's (BTV) "Meet a Mentor" program, host matechi provides an update on the program's operations, design principles, and community impact. Launched around DEF CON the prior year, the initiative pairs mentors and mentees for three to six months to help participants achieve professional goals, broaden perspectives, and foster connections across the information security community. The presentation features operational statistics, core lessons learned, and three interviews highlighting experiences from active mentor-mentee pairs.

### Key Topics
- **Program Structure and Matching**: Matches run for 3–6 months and are generated using an intake form and a custom Python script that pairs participants based on selected options and interests, complemented by human review. The program operates through Discord (using both public and private channels) and offers monthly meetups, panel discussions, lightning talks, and happy hours.
- **Definition of Mentorship**: The organizers emphasize that mentoring focuses on guidance, perspective-sharing, career navigation, and learning strategies rather than purely technical tutoring. It is designed as a reciprocal, bi-directional relationship requiring active participation and effort from both sides.
- **Demographics and Demand**: Most individuals seeking mentorship are early in their careers or university students, while mentors predominantly occupy mid-to-late-career infosec positions. There is significant demand for mentees that outpaces available mentors, particularly in shared interest areas such as DFIR, SIEM/logging, and threat hunting/intelligence.
- **Pair Case Studies**:
  - *Nico (Mentor) & Selenia (Mentee)*: Discussed moving from an unstructured approach to structured goal-setting. Mentorship helped Selenia transition out of a "lurker" mindset to take on public speaking and volunteer roles with BTV and The Diana Initiative, while Nico gained reinforced security knowledge and community engagement.
  - *Scooby (Mentor) & Danny Dev (Mentee)*: Highlighted cross-cultural communication and transitioning career levels. When Danny Dev was promoted from analyst to manager during the program, Scooby provided guidance on people management and stakeholder relations rather than purely technical resolution. Scooby noted that mentoring across different countries (Canada, US, Europe) helped him understand diverse workplace dynamics.
  - *Ali (Mentor) & serial_killer (Mentee)*: Showcased how non-traditional, business-oriented backgrounds contribute effectively to security mentorship. Ali created a structured goals-and-tasks worksheet and scheduled regular weekly meetings. serial_killer shared how the experience helped overcome imposter syndrome, build confidence, and become more communicative within the community.

### Technical Details
- **Matching Tooling**: Python-based script for matching candidates according to questionnaire intake selections.
- **Communication Infrastructure**: Dedicated private text and voice channels alongside a public channel hosted on the Blue Team Village Discord server.
- **Common Domain Interests**: Frequently declared technical focus areas during matching included DFIR (Digital Forensics and Incident Response), SIEM and logging, and threat hunting and threat intelligence.

### Takeaways
- **Mentorship is Bi-Directional**: Both experienced professionals and newcomers gain valuable insights; mentees gain guidance and confidence, while mentors gain fresh perspectives, leadership skills, and opportunities for self-reflection.
- **It Takes a Village**: Sustaining community initiatives requires both big-picture planners and reliable task executors, supported by collaborative community question-and-answer interactions.
- **Ask for Help**: Both mentors and mentees emphasized the necessity of overcoming hesitation to ask for help, stepping out of comfort zones, and actively driving one's own goals.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Byeongcheol Yoo presents quantitative research evaluating whether embedding a Secure Element (SE) genuinely strengthens cryptocurrency wallet security. Motivated by rising cryptocurrency theft and real-world incidents where hardware wallet users still lost their funds, the study conducts a formal threat modeling and risk assessment comparing cold (hardware) and hot (software) wallets, as well as hardware wallets with and without a Secure Element.

### Threat Modeling & Attack Trees
The research uses Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs) across multiple abstraction levels (Level 0 to Level 2) for both cold and hot wallet architectures. Known attack vectors were gathered into an attack library referencing 39 distinct attack factors. Using Microsoft's STRIDE methodology, the authors systematically evaluated the DFDs, identifying 103 threats for cold wallets and 112 threats for hot wallets. Following the STRIDE analysis, attack trees (proposed by Bruce Schneier) were constructed targeting three primary attacker goals: stealing cryptocurrency (187 threat nodes), denial of service (62 threat nodes), and privacy breach (86 threat nodes).

### Bayesian Network Risk Measurement Methodology
To evaluate risk quantitatively, the attack trees were converted into Bayesian networks by reversing parent-child relationships into directed acyclic graphs representing conditional dependencies with Bernoulli random variables. Prior probabilities for root nodes were derived by combining CVSS exploitability metrics with three additional factors drawn from selected risk assessment standards and Common Criteria (CC) attack potential: attack vector, access complexity, privileges required, user interaction, time complexity, expertise, and equipment. The chain rule was applied to compute joint probabilities and marginal probabilities for each attack goal. Overall risk was calculated as likelihood multiplied by impact, incorporating financial and reputation factors.

### Risk Assessment Results
The methodology was applied across six market wallets: two hardware cold wallets (Ledger Nano S with a Secure Element and Trezor One with a general-purpose MCU) and four hot software wallets (Bread and Trust Wallet on Android; Copay and Electrum on Windows). Key findings include:
- Software wallets exhibited an average overall risk 1.22 times greater than hardware wallets, confirming hardware wallets are generally safer.
- The Ledger Nano S had the lowest overall risk score (17.50), while Trezor One had the second lowest (19.47), making Trezor One's overall risk 1.11 times higher than Ledger Nano S.
- However, Trezor One's higher overall risk was largely driven by denial-of-service risks resulting from its lack of a recovery phrase backup feature. For the specific goal of stealing cryptocurrency—where a Secure Element's role is critical—Trezor One's risk was only 1.05 times higher than Ledger's.
- The speaker explains that threats mitigated by a Secure Element already possess very low prior probabilities of occurrence, meaning the addition of an SE provides only marginal overall risk reduction.

### Usable Security and Takeaways
Attackers preferentially exploit simple, efficient avenues rather than complex physical or chip-level vulnerabilities. Common attacks include clipboard-hijacking malware replacing copied addresses, malicious photo apps scanning for screenshots of recovery phrases, and users storing unencrypted recovery phrases in compromised email accounts. The speaker advocates adopting "usable security" and security-by-design through early threat modeling and Bayesian risk assessment. Wallet developers should prioritize mitigating straightforward vectors—such as preventing screenshots, blocking clipboard copying, deploying virtual keyboards, and detecting rooted/jailbroken devices—before treating Secure Elements as a primary defense.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DEF CON presentation from the IoT Village, Ken Pyle (Partner and exploit developer at CYBIR and graduate professor at Chestnut Hill College) presents his "BLUEMONDAY" series. The talk examines how appliance and IoT self-registration features, dynamic DNS regimes, and cloud management ecosystems can be passively farmed and abused to map, track, and compromise internal networks and critical infrastructure at scale.

### Key Topics
- **Architectural Gaps Between Devs and Engineers:** Application and IoT developers typically view the stack down to Layer 7, treating the lower network layers as a simple transport exit ramp. Conversely, infrastructure engineers focus on Layer 3 and Layer 4 connectivity without evaluating higher-layer implications. This disconnect results in systemic design oversights and metadata leakage.
- **The "DENNIS System" of IoT and Self-Registration:** Vendors build automated ecosystems designed for convenience and mass deployment where the DNS regime and fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are unknown or unreliable. To remove configuration overhead, devices implement default Dynamic DNS (DDNS) services, automated external PKI/SSL certificate enrollment, and discovery tools ("find me" features). These mechanisms nurture vendor dependency while introducing widespread 302 redirection abuse, cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and cross-site scripting (XSS).
- **Firmware Carving and Supply Chain Analysis:** Because IoT appliances generally run Linux on constrained storage, firmware images contain only essential components or accidentally retained data. Using extraction tools like Binwalk (with recursive Matryoshka carving), analysts can uncover hardcoded static passwords, crackable MD5 hashes, private encryption keys, private certificates, internal GitHub repositories, and network build metadata.

### Technical Details
- **Passive DNS Farming and RFC 1918 Leakage:** Vendor-operated DDNS domains (such as Datto's `dattobackup.com`, Synology's `synology.me`, Western Digital's `remotewd.com`, Meraki's `dynamic-m.com`, and GeoVision's `dipmap.com` / `gvdip.com`) frequently fail to scrub RFC 1918 private IP addresses. Direct unauthenticated DNS queries reveal internal IP schemes, NAT/PAT firewall rules, egress IP addresses, and DHCP lease ranges.
- **Vendor Case Studies:**
  - *Datto Appliances:* Automatically register DDNS records with 120-second TTLs that function as external canaries. Comparing public Shodan results and external DNS records exposes internal IPs (e.g., mapping an external IP directly to internal backup appliances). Datto backup agents also rely on an older CherryPy 3.2.2 web server instance subject to local file inclusion (LFI) and local privilege escalation.
  - *Cisco Meraki:* Templated deployments and internal naming conventions enable tracking of organizations. Meraki DDNS records exposed internal Cisco engineering regression testing racks (e.g., `bxb-r66`), making it possible to correlate Aaron IP registrations and LinkedIn profiles to locate engineering leads.
  - *Synology:* Discloses device names containing keywords such as firewalls, Plex servers, and backup instances, while also allowing unauthenticated enumeration of installed plugins.
  - *GeoVision DVRs:* Vendor-disclosed lfi, XSS, HTML injection, and XML injection flaws remained unaddressed despite vendor claims that automated scanners (Nessus) showed no issues. Legacy DDNS domains scheduled for retirement remained actively resolvable.
  - *Arbitrary Record Injection:* Pyle demonstrated registering an uninitialized Datto unit bought from eBay to inject an internal record pointing to Cloudflare (`1.1.1.1`), effectively creating spoofed, unscrubbed third-party DNS records usable for fast-flux redirection or DDoS redirection.

### Takeaways
To mitigate these systemic threats, organizations and vendors must abandon insecure self-registration services on hardware appliances and eliminate reliance on RFC 1918-leaking dynamic DNS services. The industry needs independent third-party oversight of vendor ecosystems, improved cross-layer training that unites software and network disciplines, human-driven contextual threat analysis rather than sole dependence on automated scanner definitions, and a transition away from HTTP as a universal transport/API model.

talks.title: Barak Sternberg - Extension Land Exploits and Rootkits in Browser Extensions
talks.teaser: LIVE examines Barak Sternberg - Extension Land Exploits and Rootkits in Browser Extensions.
talks.summary:
Browser extensions are installed anywhere, they serve as an integral part of our day-to-day web routine, from AdBlockers to Auto-Translators.
But - do we know what is running inside of them? Do we know what goes deep-down inside their communication routines?
How do they use their internal API’s? And how do their different JS execution contexts work?

In this session, I will explore these unique internal extension API’s, hidden attack-surfaces and show how these concepts can be broken & exploited using new ways!
I start showing how an attacker can "jump" from one low-permissions chrome-app/extension to another, hence elevating its permissions.
Then, I will show how to gain full "browser-persistency" inside extensions' background-scripts context.

Chaining it all together, I show how attacker, starting from low permissions chrome-app, gains a fully-armed "extension-rootkit",
a persistent JS-malware running inside of a “good” extension, along with C&C features, JS injection techniques to any tab/origin, obfuscation-techniques and more.
Eventually, I will present a generic technique, targeting all chrome-users, for taking over any previously installed chrome extension and implant an "extension-rootkit" in it.

REFERENCES:

[1] Chrome Developers: Chrome extensions API Reference, https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/

[2] Chrome Developers: Chrome extensions Manfiest v2/v3 Security References, https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/mv2/getstarted/ & https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/mv3/security/

talks.title: Jenko Hwong - New Phishing Attacks Exploiting OAuth Authentication Flows
talks.teaser: LIVE investigates Jenko Hwong - New Phishing Attacks Exploiting OAuth Authentication Flows.
talks.summary:
OAuth 2.0 device authorization gives users on limited-input devices like TVs an easier way to authenticate against and authorize a cloud website/app by entering a code on a computer/phone. This authentication and authorization flow leads to new phishing attacks that:

- do not need server infrastructure--the login page is served by the authorization provider using their domain and cert

- do not require a client application--application identities can be reused/spoofed

- do not require user consent of application permissions

Since the phish attacks hijack oauth session tokens, MFA will be ineffective as the attacker does not need to reauthenticate. The ability to defend against these attacks is hindered by limited info and functionality to detect, mitigate, and prevent session token compromise.

I'll demonstrate these new phishing attacks, access to sensitive user data, and lateral movement.

Defensive measures against these phishing attacks will be discussed, specifically the challenges in detection, mitigation, and prevention, and the overall lack of support for managing temporary credentials.

Open-source tools have been developed and will be used to demonstrate how users can:

- self-phish their organizations using these techniques

- audit security settings that help prevent/mitigate the attacks

1.0 Evolving Phishing Attacks

talks.title: Policy Panel - Ransomware’s Big Year From Nuisance to Scourge
talks.teaser: LIVE examines Policy Panel - Ransomware’s Big Year From Nuisance to Scourge.
talks.summary: According to a former senior White House official, 2020 was the year that ransomware went from being a nuisance to a full-scale national security threat and a “scourge”. After an awkward adolescence spent shaking down individual users for a couple hundred dollars and a big debut in 2017 with WannaCry and NotPetya , ransomware really hit the big time in 2020. Ransom payments may have topped $400 million plus that year. But those sums are nothing compared to the damage that ransomware campaigns can cause, especially when they hit critical infrastructure like Colonial Pipeline. And even months after Colonial Pipeline, ransomware continues to regularly subvert and cripple enterprises in the US and Europe. Are we not learning the right lessons on defense? Or is it not just an infosec problem, but also an international security issue, with cybercrime being actively wielded – yet again – as a political weapon?

talks.title: Joseph Gabay - DoS Denial of Shopping Analyzing and Exploiting Physical Shopping Cart
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Joseph Gabay - DoS Denial of Shopping Analyzing and Exploiting Physical Shopping Cart.
talks.summary:
Many supermarkets and shopping centers have implemented devices that “lock” their shopping carts if they’re taken outside of an approved boundary (e.g, a parking lot). This talk examines some of the technology that’s used to do this, as well as ways to capture and spoof the control signals to defeat these devices.

We will go over the anatomy of remotely lockable shopping cart wheels, their basic theory, and get into how they’re controlled. We’ll deconstruct some samples of the lock and unlock signals captured using a homemade antenna and a HackRF, and briefly discuss methods of rebroadcasting them – as well as the challenges inherent to this process.

talks.title: Panel - Rebooting Critical Infrastructure Protection
talks.teaser: LIVE investigates Panel - Rebooting Critical Infrastructure Protection.
talks.summary: In 1998 the US government issued the first major policy document on Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP). Since then, CIP has become one of the most fundamental tasks for governments everywhere, and has given birth to a plethora of institutions and processes seeking to manage what is called a “Public Private Partnership” between government, industry, and civil society. But despite all the efforts put into information exchanges, incident management, but also supply chain protection and even national industrial policies, cyber-attacks have not decreased, both in the United States and elsewhere. What else needs to be done? What lessons learned are there from international experiences? And how can the community help best?

talks.title: Policy Panel - HACKERS INTO THE UN Cyber Discussions on War and Peace
talks.teaser: LIVE details Policy Panel - HACKERS INTO THE UN Cyber Discussions on War and Peace.
talks.summary:
As if 2020 and 2021 were not bad enough, the Covid-19 pandemic seemed to have been accompanied by a new rash of bad cyber- attacks on major platforms like Solarwinds and Microsoft, infrastructures worldwide subverted in ransomware campaigns, and even the very organizations researching and fighting the pandemic have been hit.

Meanwhile, the hard work of cyber diplomacy continues, with talks on war and peace in the United Nations reaching a new stage as two working groups presented their final report and a third one is in the process of being born. Mostly the topics are on establishing norms on cyber behavior, rules of the road of what states can do in cyberspace. But where are the hackers in all this? The Internet is famously not run by intergovernmental organizations, so the companies, civil society groups and others should somehow be involved – and one of the UN processes did in fact make a small step in that direction. But the staid ways of pin-striped cyber are hard to change. What is the best way for the community to engage?

talks.title: MAVSH - Attacking from Above
talks.teaser: LIVE explores MAVSH - Attacking from Above.
talks.summary:
Over the course of 2020 and 2021, drone enthusiasts and the FAA have been locked in a series of legal battles over the future of unmanned aviation.

New regulations and restrictions, such as Remote Identification, aim to leave drone and model aviation hobbyists with a grim choice: incur countless financial costs, or lose the ability to fly freely.

Not only do these regulations impact hobbyists, they also restrict our ability to use drones as recon and payload delivery tools, but the FAA gave us a loophole.

In this talk, I'll share my knowledge of the MAVLink protocol and how it can be modified to take advantage of that loophole. I'll also show you how to build a drone capable of 20+ minute flights, potentially multiple miles of range, and hosting a Raspberry Pi 0 W onboard, enabling remote command execution without the use of onboard WiFi or cellular networks ALL while exploiting that loophole.

Come learn how and why the FAA "Can't Stop the Signal"!

talks.title: Matthew Bryant - Hacking G Suite The Power of Dark Apps Script Magic
talks.teaser: LIVE explores Matthew Bryant - Hacking G Suite The Power of Dark Apps Script Magic.
talks.summary:
You’ve seen plenty of talks on exploiting, escalating, and exfiltrating the magical world of Google Cloud (GCP), but what about its buttoned-down sibling? This talk delves into the dark art of utilizing Apps Script to exploit G Suite (AKA Google Workspace).

As a studious sorcerer, you’ll discover how to pierce even the most fortified G Suite enterprises. You’ll learn to conjure Apps Script payloads to bypass powerful protective enchantments such as U2F, OAuth app allowlisting, and locked-down enterprise Chromebooks.

Our incantations don’t stop at the perimeter, we will also discover novel spells to escalate our internal privileges and bring more G Suite accounts under our control. Once we’ve obtained the access we seek, we’ll learn various curses to persist ourselves whilst keeping a low profile so as to not risk an unwelcome exorcism.

You don’t need divination to see that this knowledge just might rival alchemy in value.

talks.title: Hao Xing, Zekai Wu - How I use a JSON 0day to Steal Your Money on the Blockchain
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Hao Xing, Zekai Wu - How I use a JSON 0day to Steal Your Money on the Blockchain.
talks.summary:
Fastjson is a widely used open source JSON parser with 23'100 stars on GitHub. As a basic module of countless java web services, it serves hundreds of millions of users. We managed to find a way to bypass many security checks and mitigations by using the inheritance process of some basic classes, and achieve remote code execution successfully. We will disclose these high-risk and universal gadgets for the first time in this talk.

Now, we can control many important websites and affect millions of users. Let's make things more interesting. We found that this fastjson vulnerability affect a multi-billion-dollar blockchain. We designed multiple complex gadgets based on the features of the blockchain, and exquisitely achieved information leakage and pointer hijacking. Putting all these gadgets together, we achieved remote code execution on the blockchain nodes.

However, generally after remote code execution, we seem to have no better exploit method other than the 51% attack, which will lead to serious accounting confusion. After a detailed analysis of the architecture design of the public blockchain, we found a way from RCE to steal the public blockchain users' assets almost without any notification.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first published attack case on the realization of covertly stealing user assets after RCE on the public blockchain nodes. We will propose a more covert post penetration exploit method for public blockchain nodes in this talk.

Blockchain is not bulletproof to security vulnerability. We will show you how to use classical web vulnerabilities attack the blockchain and how to steal real money from the decentralized cyber world.

talks.summary:
Modern programming languages are, more and more, being designed not just around performance, ease-of-use, and (sometimes) security, but also performance monitoring and introspectability. But what about the languages that never adopted such concepts from their peers? Or worse, what about the languages that tacked on half-hearted implementations as an afterthought? The answer is simple, you write your own and instrument them into the language dynamically.

In this talk, we will discuss the process for developing generalized parasitic tracers targeting specific programming languages and runtimes using Ruby as our case study. We will show how feasible it is to write external tracers targeting a language and its runtime, and discuss best practices for supporting different versions over time.

talks.title: Orange Tsai - ProxyLogon Just Tip of the Iceberg, New Attack Surface on Exchange Server
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Orange Tsai - ProxyLogon Just Tip of the Iceberg, New Attack Surface on Exchange Server.
talks.summary:
Microsoft Exchange Server is an email solution widely deployed within government and enterprises, and it is an integral part of both their daily operations and security. Needless to say, vulnerabilities in Exchange have long been the Holy Grail for attackers, hence our security research on Exchange. Surprisingly, we’ve found not only critical vulnerabilities such as ProxyLogon, but a whole new attack surface of Exchange.

This new attack surface is based on a significant change in Exchange Server 2013, where the fundamental protocol handler, Client Access Service (CAS), splits into frontend and backend. In this fundamental change of architecture, quite an amount of design debt was incurred, and, even worse, it introduced inconsistencies between contexts, leading us to discover this new attack surface.

To unveil the beauty of this attack surface and our novel exploitation, we’ll start by analyzing this architecture, followed by 7 vulnerabilities that consist of server-side bugs, client-side bugs, and crypto bugs found via this attack surface. In the end, these vulnerabilities are chained into 3 attack vectors that shine in different attack scenarios: ProxyLogon, ProxyShell, and ProxyOracle. These attack vectors enable any unauthenticated attacker to uncover plaintext passwords and even execute arbitrary code on Microsoft Exchange Servers through port 443, which is exposed to the Internet by ~400K Exchange Servers.

This attack surface has its unparalleled impact for a reason: security researchers tend to find vulnerabilities from a certain perspective, such as digging for memory bugs, injections, or logic flaws, but we took a different approach by looking at Exchange from a high-level architectural view and captured this architecture-level attack surface, which yielded multiple vulnerabilities. We hope this brings a new paradigm to vulnerability research and inspires more security researchers to look into Exchange Server. Last but not least, we’ll provide hardening actions to mitigate such types of 0days in Exchange.

talks.title: Barak Sternberg - Extension Land: Exploits and Rootkits in Your Browser Extensions
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Barak Sternberg - Extension Land: Exploits and Rootkits in Your Browser Extensions.
talks.summary:
Browser extensions are installed anywhere, they serve as an integral part of our day-to-day web routine, from AdBlockers to Auto-Translators.
But - do we know what is running inside of them? Do we know what goes deep-down inside their communication routines?
How do they use their internal API’s? And how do their different JS execution contexts work?

In this session, I will explore these unique internal extension API’s, hidden attack-surfaces and show how these concepts can be broken & exploited using new ways!
I start showing how an attacker can "jump" from one low-permissions chrome-app/extension to another, hence elevating its permissions.
Then, I will show how to gain full "browser-persistency" inside extensions' background-scripts context.

Chaining it all together, I show how attacker, starting from low permissions chrome-app, gains a fully-armed "extension-rootkit",
a persistent JS-malware running inside of a “good” extension, along with C&C features, JS injection techniques to any tab/origin, obfuscation-techniques and more.
Eventually, I will present a generic technique, targeting all chrome-users, for taking over any previously installed chrome extension and implant an "extension-rootkit" in it.

talks.summary:
Alarm systems are ubiquitous - no longer the realm of banks and vaults only, many people now have them in their homes or workplaces. But how do they work? And the logical follow-up question - how can they be hacked?

This talk focuses on the communication lines in physical intrusion detection systems: how they are secured, and what vulnerabilities exist. We’ll discuss the logic implemented in the controllers and protections on the communication lines including end of line resistors - and all the ways that this aspect of the system can be exploited.

In particular, we’ll release schematics for a tool we’ve developed that will enable measuring end-of-line resistor systems covertly, determining the necessary re-wiring to defeat the sensors, and deploy it without setting off the alarm.

After the talk, you can head over to the Lock Bypass Village to try these techniques out for yourself!
