talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference analyzes smea - Adventures In Smart Buttplug Penetration testing.
talks.summary: Analysts believe there are currently on the order of 10 billions Internet of Things (IoT) devices out in the wild. Sometimes, these devices find their way up people's butts: as it turns out, cheap and low-power radio-connected chips aren't just great for home automation - they're also changing the way we interact with sex toys. In this talk, we'll dive into the world of teledildonics and see how connected buttplugs' security holds up against a vaguely motivated attacker, finding and exploiting vulnerabilities at every level of the stack, ultimately allowing us to compromise these toys and the devices they connect to.

talks.title: XiaoHuiHui - All the 4G Modules Could Be Hacked
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference investigates XiaoHuiHui - All the 4G Modules Could Be Hacked.
talks.summary: Nowadays more and more 4G modules are built into IoT devices around the world, such as vending machines, car entertainment systems, laptops, advertising screens, and urban cameras etc. But no one has conducted a comprehensive security research on the 4G modules. We carried out this initiative and tested all the major brand 4G modules in the market (more than 15 different types). The results show all of them have similar vulnerabilities, including remote access with weak passwords, command injection of AT Command/listening services, OTA upgrade spoofing, command injection by SMS, and web vulnerability. Through these vulnerabilities we were able to get to the shell of these devices. In addition to using wifi to exploit these vulnerabilities, we created a new way to attack through fake base station system, triggered by accessing the intranet of cellular network, and successfully run remote command execution without any requisites. In this talk, we will first give an overview on the hardware structure of these modules. Then we will present the specific methods we use in vulnerability probe. In the final section we will demonstrate how to use these vulnerabilities to attack car entertainment systems of various brands and get remote control of cars.

talks.title: Xiling Gong - Exploiting Qualcomm WLAN and Modem Over the Air
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference examines Xiling Gong - Exploiting Qualcomm WLAN and Modem Over the Air.
talks.summary:
In this talk, we will share our research in which we successfully exploit Qualcomm WLAN in FIRMWARE layer, break down the isolation between WLAN and Modem and then fully control the Modem over the air.

Setup the real-time debugger is the key. Without the debugger, it's difficult to inspect the program flow and runtime status. On Qualcomm platform, subsystems are protected by the Secure Boot and unable to be touched externally. We'll introduce the vulnerability we found in Modem to defeat the Secure Boot and elevate privilege into Modem locally so that we can setup the live debugger for baseband.

The Modem and WLAN firmware is quite complex and reverse engineering is a tough work. Thanks to the debugger, we finally figure out the system architecture, the components, the program flow, the data flow, and the attack surfaces of WLAN firmware. We'll share these techniques in detail, along with the zero-days we found on the attack surfaces.

There are multiple mitigations on Qualcomm baseband, including DEP, stack protection, heap cookie, system call constraint, etc. All the details of the exploitation and mitigation bypassing techniques will be given during the presentation.

Starting from Snapdragon 835, WLAN firmware is integrated into the Modem subsystem as an isolated userspace process. We'll discuss these constraints, and then leverage the weakness we found to fully exploit into Modem.

talks.title: Xiaolong Bai - HackPac Hacking Pointer Authentication in iOS User Space
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference examines Xiaolong Bai - HackPac Hacking Pointer Authentication in iOS User Space.
talks.summary:
Pointer Authentication (in short, PAuth) is the latest security mechanism in iOS. It is proposed to protect the integrity of pointers with hardware-assisted encryption, thus eliminating the threats of code-reuse attacks. In PAuth, a cryptographic signature called PAC is calculated from a pointer value and inserted into the pointer. When the pointer is about to be used, the PAC is extracted and verified whether it is consistent with the original pointer value. In this way, PAuth is able to ensure that the pointers are not tampered. iOS deployed PAuth in user-space system services, protecting pointers that may affect the control flow and preventing code-reuse attacks like ROP and JOP.

However, in our study, we found that a fatal flaw in the implementation of iOS PAuth makes user-space system services till vulnerable to code-reuse attacks. The flaw is: iOS uses the same signing key in different user-space processes. This flaw allows a signed pointer from a malicious process can be correctly verified in a system service, thus making it possible to launch JOP. In this talk, we will explain how we found the flaw and why it is inevitable. In advance, we will demonstrate how to leverage this flaw and launch JOP attacks in a PAuth-protected system service. Also, we will propose a new tool, PAC-gadget, to automatically find JOP gadgets in PAuth-protected binaries.

talks.title: Sheila Ayelen Berta - Backdooring Hardware by Injecting Malicious Payloads
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference details Sheila Ayelen Berta - Backdooring Hardware by Injecting Malicious Payloads.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at DEF CON, security researcher Sheila Ayelen Berta explores methods for backdooring embedded hardware devices controlled by microcontrollers rather than high-end microprocessors. While prior hardware backdoor research has largely concentrated on architectures like x86, AMD, or ARM running complete operating systems, microcontrollers manage critical real-world infrastructure—including automotive Engine Control Units (ECUs), physical security systems, elevators, industrial systems, and robotics. Berta demonstrates how attackers can dump firmware, inject arbitrary payloads directly into hex files, fix program displacements, and flash modified code back to the target chip.

### Key Topics
- **Microprocessor vs. Microcontroller Differences**: Microprocessors feature external memory and buses, Harvard/Modified Harvard architectures, and multi-tasking OS support. Microcontrollers integrate CPU, RAM, ROM/flash, and peripheral registers into a single silicon die with limited stack depth and fixed instruction sets (such as Microchip PIC12, PIC16, PIC18, and 32-bit devices).
- **Firmware Dumping and Disassembly**: Using low-cost official hardware tools (PICkit 3) alongside the MPLAB IDE to read program memory directly into hex files, inspect disassembly views, and map opcodes stored in little-endian format.
- **Payload Construction and Relocation**: Generating assembly opcodes, locating injection offsets, shifting instructions, updating Intel hex checksums, and correcting absolute address offsets (`GOTO` / `CALL`).
- **Injection Vectors**: Three specific injection methods: entry point injection, interrupt vector/polling routine hooking, and stack manipulation via Return-Oriented Programming (ROP).
- **Hardware Defense Mechanisms**: Implementing configuration bits such as boot and data protection to thwart dumping attacks.

### Technical Details
Berta details three payload injection techniques focusing on PIC18 microcontrollers:

1. **Entry Point Injection**: Targeting the reset vector at address `0x0000`, which contains a `GOTO` pointing to the program entry point (e.g., `0x0006` or `0x7F84`). The researcher demonstrates inserting custom machine code directly at the entry point, shifting original bytes, and recalculating per-line checksums (`NOT(sum of bytes) + 1`). This is showcased on an automotive ECU controlling dual fuel injectors: the injected payload causes both petrol and compressed natural gas (CNG) to inject simultaneously instead of transitioning smoothly.

2. **Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) Injection**: Targeting interrupt vectors at address `0x0008` (high priority) and `0x0018` (low priority). Firmware uses polling with `BTFSC` instructions over registers like `INTCON`, `PIE1`/`PIR1`, `PIE2`/`PIR2`, etc., to identify which peripheral triggered an event. In an example targeting the UART/USART receiver flag (`RCIF`, bit 5 of `PIR1`), the routine at address `0x0048` is hooked. The injected payload grabs incoming data from the `W` working register, reconfigures the `TX` pin, and relays received messages over a serial/USB connection or wireless module to an attacker monitor.

3. **Jump Correction & Automated Tooling**: Injecting bytes shifts subsequent code locations. Because PIC18 `CALL` and `GOTO` instructions use 16-bit word offsets (dividing addresses by 2), any jump past the injection site must be incremented by the length of the payload. Berta highlights an automation tool under development that takes the hex file, payload, and offset to automatically patch targets and calculate checksums.

4. **Stack Manipulation & ROP Chains**: Microchip devices manage execution through the stack pointer (`STKPTR`) and top-of-stack registers (`TOSU`, `TOSH`, `TOSL`). By manually adjusting `STKPTR`, writing addresses into the `TOS` registers, and issuing a return (`RETURN` or `RETLW`), execution flow is hijacked. Berta creates a Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) chain stringing together existing firmware gadgets terminated by `RETLW` instructions, visualized by lighting successive LEDs.

### Takeaways
Hardware backdoors in microcontrollers can be achieved without advanced laboratory tools, relying only on a standard programmer, basic disassembly analysis, and careful opcode adjustments. To prevent attackers from extracting firmware to build payloads, developers must properly set hardware security configuration bits—specifically enabling Boot Block Protection (`CPB`) and data protection, rather than relying solely on default code protection bits which still allow memory dumps.

talks.title: Orange Tsai - Infiltrating Corporate Intranet Like NSA Preauth RCE
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference examines Orange Tsai - Infiltrating Corporate Intranet Like NSA Preauth RCE.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, researchers Orange Tsai and Meh Chang from the DEVCORE research team present their research into pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) across leading enterprise SSL VPN appliances, specifically targeting Fortinet (FortiGate) and Pulse Secure. SSL VPNs serve as primary entry points for enterprise networks, making them high-value targets. Because these appliances are closed-source black boxes that rarely offer direct shell access, the researchers first explain how they jailbroke virtual appliances, analyzed their architectures, uncovered critical vulnerabilities, achieved remote code execution, and even weaponized the infrastructure to compromise connected clients.

### Key Topics
- **Appliance Jailbreaking:** Turning black-box appliances into accessible environments. For unencrypted virtual appliances, mounting disks or booting single-user mode suffices. For encrypted systems like Pulse Secure, the researchers bypassed disk encryption via memory forensics during boot, locating spawned Perl processes (`dsconfig.pl`) and patching memory to spawn `/bin/sh`.
- **SSL VPN Attack Surfaces:** Identifying recurring weak points across vendors, including:
  - *WebVPN features:* Reverse proxying complex protocols (HTTP, FTP, RDP) and web resources (JavaScript, Flash, WebSockets), leading to memory corruption or unpatched outdated libraries (e.g., decade-old Libcurl and Libxml).
  - *Native language extensions:* Custom C/C++ extensions in PHP or Perl prone to type confusion, integer overflows, and string handling flaws (e.g., improper `snprintf` handling).
  - *Multi-layer architectural inconsistencies:* Path traversal issues arising from discrepancies between front-end web servers and back-end RESTful services.
  - *Plaintext credential caching:* Both vendors stored comprehensive session files containing active session tokens, usernames, and plaintext passwords directly on disk.
- **Fortinet Exploitation:** A multi-step pre-auth RCE chain and backdoors in FortiGate.
- **Pulse Secure Exploitation:** Chaining an arbitrary file read with command injection via DSSafe module bypasses.
- **Targeting Real-World Environments (Twitter):** Bypassing two-factor authentication and internal interface restrictions to achieve RCE.
- **Weaponization and Client Takeover:** Abusing built-in VPN logon scripts to compromise client operating systems.

### Technical Details
- **Fortinet (FortiGate):**
  - *Arbitrary File Read:* Language selection concatenated user input into a buffer with a `.json` extension appended. By overflowing the fixed-size buffer using excessive slashes (`/`), `snprintf` truncated the `.json` extension, permitting arbitrary file reads and extraction of plaintext credentials from `SSL VPN web session` files.
  - *Heap Overflow:* Located in JavaScript parsing within WebVPN (`0x2000` buffer with no length check). Overcoming Jemalloc constraints and shared-heap instability, the researchers fuzzed connections to overwrite an `SSL` structure's function pointer (`handshake` function) with `system`, using a stack pivot and ROP chain to execute a Python reverse root shell.
  - *Magic Backdoor:* An unauthenticated password update routine allowed resetting any user password using a hardcoded secret key named `magic`.
- **Pulse Secure:**
  - *Pre-Auth Arbitrary File Read:* A logic flaw in HTML5 Access (introduced in version 8.2) loosened path validation, exposing private SSL keys, LDAP/RADIUS configurations, cached WebVPN cookies, and plaintext credentials.
  - *Post-Auth Command Injection & DSSafe Bypass:* While administrative diagnostic options passed inputs to Perl functions, the C++ `DSSafe` module restricted dangerous characters and I/O redirection. The researchers discovered that an incomplete I/O redirection caused parser truncation. By redirecting `stderr` rather than `stdout` (triggering tcpdump errors on non-existent filenames), they formatted error outputs into syntactically valid Perl scripts (using labels like `tcpdump:` and `#` comment symbols) and wrote them into the web cache directory (`setcookie.thtml.ttc`) to execute commands.
  - *Twitter Case Study:* Leveraging the file read on Twitter's SSL VPN yielded plaintext passwords, but 2FA blocked direct login. Bypassing 2FA was achieved by extracting session databases and abusing the "roaming session" feature. The researchers accessed the restricted management interface via WebVPN/SSRF tricks (using `0`), cracked a 10-character SHA-256 admin password hash on a 72-core AWS instance in three hours, and triggered the command injection to obtain a shell.
- **Red Team Weaponization:** Attackers with admin access can modify the "logon script" feature supported across Windows, macOS, and Linux. When users connect via the Pulse Secure client agent, custom scripts execute automatically on the user's endpoint.

### Takeaways
The speakers emphasize several core mitigations for organizations relying on SSL VPNs:
1. Require client-side certificates so unauthorized connections are terminated during SSL negotiation.
2. Enforce multi-factor authentication across all services.
3. Enable complete logging and auditing.
4. Actively monitor and apply vendor security advisories and patches promptly.

talks.title: Evil eBPF Practical Abuses of In-Kernel Bytecode Runtime- DEF CON 27 Conference
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Jeff Dileo - Evil eBPF Practical Abuses of In-Kernel Bytecode Runtime- DEF CON 27 Conference.
talks.summary:
eBPF (or "extended" Berkeley Packet Filter) is a bytecode instruction set and virtual machine used as a safe computing environment within the Linux kernel to perform arbitrary programmatic actions. It is a redesign of Linux's original in-kernel BPF bytecode VM used to power features like tcpdump filters. eBPF has an entirely different set of capabilities and instructions, with its primary goal being to serve as a JIT-able virtual machine instruction set that can be targeted by compilers of a memory-safe "restricted C" language. In the Linux kernel, it is actively being applied to anything and everything to provide performant programmatic capabilities to userland that extend traditionally kernel-based functionality.

In this exploit development focused talk, we will first introduce eBPF and discuss several nefarious techniques enabled by the technology. As we do so, we will cover the respective sets of APIs, file descriptor types, and other eBPF machinery that enable such techniques, building up from various forms of hidden IPC channels to full-fledged rootkits. Within this talk, we will walk through the implementations of the techniques we discuss so that attendees will walk away with the knowledge of how to implement their own variants. Along the way we will discuss novel container breakout techniques and interesting "dual-purpose" eBPF features that enable the development of mutative syscall hooks that work for processes that work for processes already attached by a debugger. Finally, we will provide insight on how defenders should begin to attempt to detect and recover from such abuses, when possible at all.

This presentation significantly extends on work we first presented at 35C3, which focused more heavily on the underlying aspects of general eBPF-based kernel tracing. In contrast, this talk will demo new techniques and include substantially improved versions of techniques presented previously as proofs-of-concept.

talks.title: I Know What U Did Last Summer 3 Yrs Wireless Monitoring DEFCON
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference examines Mike Spicer - I Know What U Did Last Summer 3 Yrs Wireless Monitoring DEFCON.
talks.summary:
For the past 3 years d4rkm4tter has been obsessed with monitoring the wireless networks at DEF CON. This talk will take you on a journey through the successes and failures that lead to the creation of the WiFiCactus and the over 1 TB of data captured. A history of each capture project including a summary of the most interesting pieces of data will be shown.

Many people spread a lot of fear, uncertainty and doubt about the wireless environments during DEF CON. This presentation aims to bring some clarity to what is really happening in the airwaves during one of the largest hacker conferences in the world. This will include presenting data on the attacks and sensitive information that exists in the airwaves. This presentation will demonstrate the risks of using wireless networks and information leaks that can be captured by anyone who is passively listening. Countermeasures and protection strategies will be provided to help you avoid having your data captured by those who might be listening.

With the number of connected devices around us, there has never been a better time to start wardriving or warwalking. Everyone is capable of profiling wireless data around them thanks to cheap hardware and open source tools. As hackers it is important for us to discover issues and vulnerabilities while validating claims of security by software and hardware vendors. Monitoring wireless communication is a great way to start validating those claims. All of the hardware and methods used will be provided so that anyone can do this type of monitoring on their own. Hack the Planet!

talks.title: Apache Solr Injection- DEF CON 27 Conference
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Michael Stepankin - Apache Solr Injection- DEF CON 27 Conference.
talks.summary:
Apache Solr is a search platform used by many enterprise companies to add a full text search functionality to their websites. Often hidden behind firewalls, it provides a rich API to search across large datasets. If this API is used by web applications in a wrong way, it may open a possibility for injection attacks to completely modify the query logic.

In this talk we’ll shed some light on the new type of vulnerabilities for web applications - Solr parameter injection, and provide some useful ways how to achieve remote code execution through it. We also provide exploits for almost all known vulnerabilities for Apache Solr, including the two new RCEs we reported this year.

talks.title: Jiska - Vacuum Cleaning Security Pinky and The Brain Edition
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference analyzes Jiska - Vacuum Cleaning Security Pinky and The Brain Edition.
talks.summary:
Data collected by vacuum cleaning robot sensors is highly privacy-sensitive, as it includes details and metadata about consumers’ habits, how they live, when they work or invite friends, and more. Connected vacuum robots are not as low-budget as other IoT devices and vendors indeed invest into their security. This makes vacuum cleaning robot ecosystems interesting for further analysis to understand their security mechanisms and derive takeaways.

In this talk we discuss the security of the well-protected Neato and Vorwerk ecosystems. Their robots run the proprietary QNX operating system, are locally protected with secure boot, and use various mechanisms that ensure authentication and encryption in the cloud communication. Nonetheless, we were able to bypass substantial security components and even gain unauthenticated privileged remote execution on arbitrary robots. We present how we dissected ecosystem components including a selection of vacuum robot firmwares and their cloud interactions.

talks.title: g richter - Reverse Engineering 4g Hotspots for Fun Bugs Net Financial Loss
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference analyzes g richter - Reverse Engineering 4g Hotspots for Fun Bugs Net Financial Loss.
talks.summary:
“5G is coming” (apparently). That probably means, over the next few years, more and more people are going to be using more and more cellular-connected devices for their day-to-day TCP/IP activities.

The problem is, a lot of existing 4G modems and routers are pretty insecure. We found critical remotely-exploitable flaws in a selection of devices from variety of vendors, without having to do too much work. Plus, there’s only a small pool of OEMs working seriously with cellular technologies, and their hardware (& software dependencies) can be found running in all sorts of places. Their old 4G, 3G and even 2G-era code is going to be running in these 5G-capable devices.

With a small sample of consumer 4G routers as examples, we’re going to talk about how malleable, frustrating, and insecure these devices are. We’ll run through a few examples of existing 4G routers, from low-end bargain-basement end-of-life-never-to-be-fixed to higher-end devices. root is a means to an end, rather than the goal.

talks.title: Nikhil Mittal - RACE Minimal Rights and ACE for Active Directory Dominance
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference details Nikhil Mittal - RACE Minimal Rights and ACE for Active Directory Dominance.
talks.summary:
User rights and privileges are a part of the access control model in Active Directory. Applicable only at the local computer level, a user generally has different rights (through access tokens) on different machines in a domain. Another part of the access control model is security descriptors (ACLs) that protects a securable object. At the domain level, ACL abuse is well known and adversaries have used it for persistence. For user rights, the abuse is mostly with the help of groups (memberships, SID History etc.) or misconfigured delegated rights.

A lesser-known area of abuse and offensive research is a combination of minimal Rights and ACE (hence the term RACE). Often overlooked in audits and assessments, using minimal rights along with favourable ACEs provides a very interesting technique of persistence and on-demand privilege escalation on a Windows machine with much desired stealth.

This talk covers interesting domain privilege escalation, persistence and backdoor techniques with the help of ACLs, minimal user rights and combinations of both. We will discuss how these techniques can be applied using open source tools and scripts. The talk also covers how to detect and mitigate such attacks.

The talk will be full of live demonstrations.

talks.title: Itzik Kotler - Process Injection Techniques Gotta Catch Them All
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference details Itzik Kotler - Process Injection Techniques Gotta Catch Them All.
talks.summary: When it comes to process injection in Windows, there are only 6-7 fundamental techniques, right? Wrong. In this talk, we provide the most comprehensive to-date “Windows process injection” collection of techniques. We focus on Windows 10 x64, and on injections from running 64-bit medium integrity process to another running 64-bit medium integrity process, without privilege elevation. We pay special attention to the new Windows protection technologies, e.g. CFG and CIG. We differentiate between memory write primitives and execution techniques, and discuss memory allocation strategies. Our collection is curated, analyzed, tabulated, with straight-forward, research-grade PoCs. We tested each technique against Windows 10 x64 with and without protections, and we report on the requirements, limitations, and quirks of each technique. And of course – no decent DEF CON presentation is complete without new attacks. We describe a new memory writing primitive which is CFG-agnostic. We describe a new “stack bombing” execution method (based on the memory write primitive above) that is inherently safe (even though overwriting the stack is a-priori a dangerous and destabilizing action). Finally, we release a library of all write primitives and execution methods, so users can generate “tailor-made” process injections.

talks.title: Katherine Pratt - Hacking Your Thoughts Batman Forever meets Black Mirror
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference explores Katherine Pratt - Hacking Your Thoughts Batman Forever meets Black Mirror.
talks.summary:
Companies are coming for your brains. The electricity in your brains, to be more precise. Valve, Facebook, Elon Musk and more are funding research into technologies that will translate neural signals into controls for devices like computers, smartphones, and VR/AR environments. While this would be super exciting, it represents some serious data privacy issues. First: what kind of private information can be elicited from your neural signals? It’s possible to use a specific kind of neural response to visual and audio stimuli to deduce information about the user… like where you bank, who you know, your real identity, etc (Edward Nygma in Batman Forever, anyone?)

More broadly, there is also the issue of what happens when you provide your neural signals to a company. If you’re worried about what Facebook is doing with your information now, imagine what they can do when they have hours of information straight from your brain. If neural data is treated the same as your DNA, commercial companies become the owners of your thoughts (as electrical signals). Will they readily share it with the FBI without probable cause? These kinds of questions, and many more, are starting to surface with neurally-controlled devices and other emerging technologies. This talk will cover all of this and more.

talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference analyzes Joseph Cox - How You Can Buy ATT TMobile and Sprint Real Time Location Data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, investigative journalist Joseph Cox from Motherboard (VICE) details an investigation into how real-time geolocation tracking data from major telecommunications carriers—including AT&T, T-Mobile, Sprint, and Verizon—ended up accessible on the black market. Prompted by an anonymous source connected to the bounty hunting industry, Cox tested the claim by paying $300 to track a consenting person's phone. The test successfully returned a real-time location ping pinpointing the device to Queens, New York within a five-to-six-block radius.

### Key Topics
- **The Location Data Supply Chain**: Rather than direct sales to end users, telecom carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, Sprint) sold access through location aggregators (such as Zumigo), who marketed it for fraud prevention. These aggregators then sold access to data brokers like Microbilt, who marketed mobile tracking to bail bondsmen, car dealerships, and property managers. End users, including bounty hunting firms like Bail Integrity Solutions, ultimately leaked or resold this capability downstream into black-market channels.
- **Technical Data Types**: Geolocation data sold through these pipelines ranged from broad cell phone tower triangulation (covering blocks to several kilometers) to assisted GPS (A-GPS). A-GPS, originally designed for emergency responders (E911), provided granular accuracy down to under 20 meters or specific buildings.
- **CerCareOne and Underground Portals**: Leaked documents from CerCareOne, an invite-only hidden tracking platform catering to around 250 bounty hunter companies, showed administrators (such as Dan Grable) and users tracking targets without any consent notification to the phone. Weak security controls—such as ignoring two-IP whitelisting rules and logins originating from multiple countries—facilitated unauthorized secondary reselling.
- **Social Engineering and Exigent Circumstances**: Even as major carriers announced a halt to third-party commercial data sales following public exposure, attackers continued accessing real-time location data by posing as law enforcement. By spoofing credentials and submitting fraudulent exigent circumstances requests directly to telco representatives, unauthorized actors obtained carrier pings and resold them or used them for illicit repossession and stalking.

### Technical Details
- **Aggregation and Brokerage APIs**: Microbilt offered products like Mobile Device Verify, selling single location verification pings for $4.95 or continuous device monitoring (hourly, daily, weekly) for $12.95.
- **Carrier Consent Controls**: While carriers required explicit user opt-in (via SMS or voice confirmation) for commercial tracking, aggregators lobbied the FCC to weaken consent requirements. Most commercial tracking tools bypassed notifications entirely. Verizon attempted to enforce consent at the carrier level rather than delegating it to brokers, though carrier-level direct queries still suffered from vulnerabilities such as Securus portal abuse.
- **Fraudulent Legal Requests**: Attackers like John Edens exploited emergency override protocols, building rapport with carrier employees to circumvent warrant and subpoena requirements.

### Takeaways
Commercial aggregation and resale of real-time mobile location data inherently leads to unauthorized access and downstream black-market trade. While public reporting forced telcos to cut off aggregator feeds, systemic risks persist due to social engineering of emergency carrier processes, highlighting the severe safety threats posed to targets of stalking, fugitive recovery, and abusive surveillance.

talks.title: Nina Kollars - Confessions of an Nespresso Money Mule
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference explores Nina Kollars - Confessions of an Nespresso Money Mule.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at a security conference (DefCon), Nina Kollars (also known as Kitty), a professor at the Naval War College, recounts how purchasing discounted Nespresso coffee pods on eBay led her to become an unwitting participant in—and subsequent investigator of—a triangulation fraud scheme. After receiving an unprompted, brand-new $280 Nespresso Pixie espresso maker alongside her coffee order, Kollars investigated the origin of the shipment and uncovered how fraudsters exploit the gaps between e-commerce marketplaces and direct-to-consumer manufacturers.

### Key Topics
- **Triangulation Fraud Mechanics**: How cybercriminals use stolen personally identifiable information (PII) or stolen credit cards to purchase goods directly from manufacturers and deliver them to third-party e-commerce buyers, effectively laundering stolen credit into cash.
- **Marketplace & Platform Dynamics**: The role of e-commerce platforms like eBay and vendor fulfillment systems in inadvertently facilitating fraud through search recommendation algorithms, ambiguous review presentation, and reporting limitations.
- **Ad Hoc Fraud Investigation**: Tracking fraudulent seller patterns using spreadsheets, automated searches, account age, seller ratings, and listing characteristics.
- **Human and Ethical Costs**: Dissecting the myth of "victimless crime" in low-level payment fraud, especially its disproportionate impact on elderly or vulnerable populations whose identities are stolen.

### Technical Details
Triangulation fraud operates via a three-part model:
1. **The Fraudster**: Obtains stolen PII or payment card credentials from carding sites and creates fake seller profiles on platforms like eBay, listing goods at steep discounts (e.g., 200 coffee pods at roughly half price).
2. **The Buyer / Money Mule**: The buyer purchases the item via PayPal/eBay, unwittingly providing clean cash to the fraudster.
3. **Manufacturer Fulfillment**: To trigger shipping confirmations and release funds on eBay, the fraudster orders legitimate items directly from the target manufacturer (Nespresso) using the stolen credit line, directing delivery straight to the buyer's home.

Kollars observed multiple anomalies during her experiment. Her first order included a direct-from-Nespresso invoice billed to a different person ("George from Poughkeepsie") rather than the eBay seller ("Sue from Chicago"). When contacting Nespresso customer service, they confirmed the cardholder was charged for both items but declined to share contact details, forwarding the issue to their fraud department.

To study the operation's scale, Kollars automated eBay searches targeting new accounts with zero seller ratings selling 200 capsules for $99. She observed that eBay's interface displayed product review star ratings prominently while burying zero-rating seller metrics, and eBay's recommendation engine suggested similar accounts. Over five attempted purchases (four completed), she received duplicate coffee orders and a $119 milk frother, tracing the accounts until one order was canceled with a polite excuse from the seller. In total, she spent under $400 for nearly $1,000 in retail goods. eBay's reporting tools provided no mechanism to report received fraudulent orders. Kollars compiled invoices, account names, and transaction records and submitted the dossier to the FBI and eBay, after which the observed activity ceased within 30 days.

### Takeaways
Kollars emphasizes that triangulation fraud is not a victimless crime. The cardholders identified were at or near retirement age—vulnerable individuals ill-equipped to detect or mitigate identity theft. Furthermore, because individual transaction values fall beneath corporate loss-prevention thresholds, merchants, platforms, and payment insurers treat such fraud as priced into business operations. This leaves consumers and buyers with an ethical choice either to exploit cheap fraudulent deals knowingly or refuse complicity. To conclude, Kollars auctioned off the received machine for cash at the Tamper Evident Village to benefit the Diana Initiative.

talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference details Damien Cauquil - Defeating Bluetooth Low Energy 5 PRNG for Fun and Jamming.
talks.summary:
Bluetooth Low energy version 5 has been published in late 2016, but we still have no sniffer supporting this specific version (and not that much compatible devices as well). The problem is this new version introduces a new channel hopping algorithm that renders previous sniffing tools useless as devices can no longer be attacked and connections analyzed. This new algorithm is based on a brand new pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) to provide better collision avoidance while kicking out all of our good old sniffing tools.

Unless some random hacker manages to break this not-that-strong PRNG and upgrades his BLE sniffing tool to support this algorithm ;). In this talk, we will explain why this PRNG is vulnerable and how it can be easily defeated to sniff and jam communications between two BLE 5 devices. A new version of BtleJack will be released during this talk, providing an efficient way to sniff BLE 5 connections to our fellow IoT hacker family.

talks.title: Anish Athalye - Want Strong Isolation Just Reset Your Processor
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference explores Anish Athalye - Want Strong Isolation Just Reset Your Processor.
talks.summary:
Today's systems sandbox code through traditional techniques: memory protection and user-kernel mode. Even high-security devices like hardware cryptocurrency wallets use such an architecture. Unfortunately, this arrangement has a history of security bugs due to misconfigured protection hardware, bugs in kernel code, hardware bugs, and side channels.

This talk proposes a new approach to isolation for devices like crypto wallets: separate the user and kernel onto two CPUs and multiplex processes by completely resetting the user processor between tasks so that there is no leakage.

Processor reset is more complicated than might be expected. Simply asserting the reset line isn't enough to clear all CPU-internal state, but it turns out that software can be used to clear this state. However, reasoning about the correctness of such code is challenging. This talk presents a tool that can be used to develop and formally verify the correctness of reset code for a given CPU implementation.

This talk also walks through a design of a wallet based on this reset-based isolation technique, discusses known security vulnerabilities in current designs such as the Ledger and Trezor wallets (including bugs in MPU misconfiguration, system calls, and drivers), and explores how a reset-based design could prevent such vulnerabilities.

talks.title: albinowax - HTTP Desync Attacks: Smashing into the Cell Next Door
talks.teaser: DEF CON 27 Conference analyzes albinowax - HTTP Desync Attacks: Smashing into the Cell Next Door.
talks.summary:
HTTP requests are traditionally viewed as isolated, standalone entities. In this session, I'll introduce techniques for remote, unauthenticated attackers to smash through this isolation and splice their requests into others, through which I was able to play puppeteer with the web infrastructure of numerous commercial and military systems, rain exploits on their visitors, and harvest over $50k in bug bounties.

Using these targets as case studies, I’ll show you how to delicately amend victim's requests to route them into malicious territory, invoke harmful responses, and lure credentials into your open arms. I’ll also demonstrate using backend reassembly on your own requests to exploit every modicum of trust placed on the frontend, gain maximum privilege access to internal APIs, poison web caches, and compromise my favourite login page.

Although documented over a decade ago, a fearsome reputation for difficulty and collateral damage has left this attack optimistically ignored for years while the web's susceptibility grew. By applying fresh ideas and new techniques, I’ll unveil a vast expanse of vulnerable systems ranging from huge content delivery networks to bespoke backends, and ensure you leave equipped to devise your own desync techniques and tailor attacks to your target of choice.

talks.title: CAAD VILLAGE - Joseph Clements - Hardware Trojan Attacks on Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of CAAD VILLAGE - Joseph Clements - Hardware Trojan Attacks on Neural Networks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Joseph Clements, a PhD student from Clemson University working with advisor Dr. Yin He (in the Secure Innovative Research Computing group), presents research on hardware Trojan attacks targeting neural networks. While adversarial machine learning has historically focused on cloud-based implementations—targeting training or inference phases—the emergence of edge computing introduces new constraints and threat models. On edge devices running real-time or offline inference (such as autonomous driving, mobile apps, and wearables), computational and battery limits drive specialized hardware and a fragmented, globalized fabless supply chain. This supply chain model opens the door to hardware-level attacks during the production phase.

### Key Topics
- **Edge Computing & ML Constraints:** Moving inference to the edge eliminates latency and connectivity challenges but introduces severe power and compute limitations, necessitating specialized hardware architectures.
- **Fabless Supply Chain Risks:** The modern horizontal fabless semiconductor business model relies on third-party intellectual property (IP), extensive globalization, and multiple untrusted manufacturing entities.
- **Hardware Attack Landscape:** The speaker classifies hardware threats into four primary categories: IP piracy, counterfeiting (noting integrated circuits account for up to 63% or more of reported counterfeit parts), side-channel attacks (e.g., attacks on AES implementations), and hardware Trojans.
- **Hardware Trojan Fundamentals:** Hardware Trojans consist of two core components: a trigger (which detects a rare internal circuit condition to remain stealthy) and a payload (which executes the malicious alteration).

### Technical Details
Unlike software Trojan attacks on neural networks—which inject triggers and retrain network weights—this hardware-based attack has distinct attributes:
- **No Retraining:** Model weights remain completely untouched; instead, the hardware operations (such as multipliers, adders, or activation function circuits) are modified.
- **Production Phase Implementation:** The attack is inserted during hardware production via untrusted supply chain entities, making it persistent and impossible to remove without scrapping the chip.
- **Attack Methodology:**
  1. *Target Selection:* A target layer and specific operation within it (e.g., multiplier or activation function) are selected. The network is conceptually partitioned into two sub-networks: input-to-target-operation and target-operation-to-network-output.
  2. *Trigger Selection:* An input trigger key is chosen—either a well-crafted trigger structured like domain data or a randomized trigger pattern.
  3. *Intermediate Activation & Perturbation Calculation:* The trigger is fed through the first sub-network to record intermediate activations. A modified adversarial example technique calculates the minimal operational perturbation required at the targeted operation's output to force a malicious misclassification in the second sub-network.
  4. *Hardware Modification:* Hardware Trojans are embedded into a small subset of targeted computing components (e.g., switching between benign and malicious activation function outputs when a rare internal activation is detected).

### Experimental Results
Evaluations across four experimental setups (contrasting well-crafted and randomized triggers) measured:
- **Effectiveness:** On average, 97% of input triggers successfully triggered the targeted malicious classification.
- **Functional Stealthiness:** Evaluated against a golden reference model with standard testing data; 100% of input/output pairs matched benign execution, leaving no detectable functional discrepancies.
- **Behavioral Stealthiness:** Minimized physical and side-channel footprint (timing, power) by altering only a localized subset of neurons (as low as 0.3% of neurons in a layer).

### Takeaways
Hardware Trojans present an effective, persistent, and highly stealthy threat vector against neural networks deployed on edge hardware. As paradigms like federated learning move parts of the training process to edge devices as well, physical hardware security and supply chain provenance must be integrated into machine learning system design.

talks.summary:
# Cruising Cannabis Highway: Major Breaches in Cannabis Software

## Overview
Rex, a full-stack web developer, presents a detailed examination of major security breaches in the cannabis compliance and point-of-sale software industry, with particular focus on MJ Freeway's 2016–2017 breaches. The cannabis industry was valued at $9.2 billion in North America in 2017 and involved a complex supply chain with numerous integration points where security failures could have cascading consequences.

## Industry Landscape
The cannabis supply chain runs from grow-ops through processing facilities to dispensaries and end consumers. At each stage, organizations interface with government compliance tracking systems. Major players in the compliance software space include Metrc (owned by Franwell), BioTrack THC (originally a hospital medication dispenser platform), and MJ Freeway, which pioneered the "seed-to-sale" (C2S) tracking model that became the compliance standard. MJ Freeway was the largest point-of-sale provider across many states and held both dispensary-level and state-level compliance contracts—a potential conflict of interest the speaker highlights.

## The MJ Freeway Breaches
A breach occurred on or about November 19, 2016, followed by multiple additional incidents over roughly two months. MJ Freeway initially claimed "no data loss," citing a third-party security audit, but the reality involved multiple breaches with significant data loss. Personally identifiable information was leaked to the Pirate Bay, source code was posted to GitLab (later removed), and on January 8, the system went offline for all clients. Attackers specifically targeted backups, and in one state, attackers modified live cannabis delivery/restocking information. The outage lasted several months, forcing many clients to abandon the platform.

## Technical Analysis
MJ Freeway's legacy "Gram Tracker" system for dispensary management relied on a 5–6-year-old Drupal core with custom plugins and no upgrade path, making it vulnerable to known CVEs. The newer "MJ Platform" was built from scratch but lacked maturity. The "Leaf Data System" provided state-level compliance tracking. Source code analysis from Git logs revealed:
- Multiple repository splits (CCLeaf, Washington Leaf, etc.), suggesting poor team communication and fragmented development (consistent with Conway's Law)
- Commits from numerous contractors, many using Gmail addresses alongside work addresses
- Evidence of inconsistent development practices and potential information leakage through metadata

## Incident Response and Disclosure
MJ Freeway's communication was poor. Initially, the company claimed it was "not an attack," later pivoting to calling it a "vicious cyber attack." Customers discovered the outage by showing up to work, not through official notification. Reddit posts from industry workers revealed widespread frustration over mixed signals regarding backups and recovery. The company subpoenaed Reddit and Google for information on accounts with first-hand knowledge. Attackers attempted data ransom via Bitcoin, sending emails from spoofed addresses to dispensary owners with samples of stolen data.

## Broader Context
The competitive cannabis software market incentivizes cutting corners to reduce time to market. BioTrack CEO Patrick Veau published an open letter criticizing MJ Freeway over the Washington State handoff process and the reputation risk of association with insecure systems. Legal disputes occurred between BioTrack and MJ Freeway over Puerto Rico state contract bids, involving claims about felony board members. The space is marked by aggressive litigation and market jockeying.

## Attribution Speculation
Rex speculates on possible attackers: foreign state actors (noting contractors from interesting locations), competitors (highly motivated in this space), right-wing anti-weed activists, or advanced bored hackers. He notes that cannabis business victims are unlikely to involve federal law enforcement due to the legal status of cannabis, limiting official investigation and public disclosure.

## Key Takeaways
- Regulations combined with poor compliance practices create massive attack surface
- Highly competitive markets with weak security providers become exploitation targets
- Cannabis industry's federal legal ambiguity prevents traditional law enforcement involvement
- Supply chain complexity (state systems, dispensary systems, third-party integrations, mobile apps) multiplies vulnerability points
- Poor development practices, fragmented teams, and legacy code compound security risks

talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at the DEFCON Data Duplication Village, this talk provides a beginner's guide to the international legal principles governing cyber warfare and international conflict. The speaker uses a piano keyboard analogy to bridge law and technology, mapping international legal concepts—such as the UN Charter, the use of force, and self-defense—to musical notes and octaves. The underlying research was developed during a fellowship at the Harvard Kennedy School's Belfer Center Cybersecurity Project and published with the Houston Law Review.

### Key Topics
- **Defining a Cyberattack**: Under Rule 30 of the Tallinn Manual framework, a cyberattack is defined as an operation expected to cause injury, death, damage, or destruction. Scholars like Matthew Waxman advocate broadening this beyond physical effects to include altering or destroying data and systems, while political leaders like Senator Mark Warner highlight the risks of lacking clear policy thresholds.
- **Legal Regimes & Thresholds**: Starting from "Middle C" (the UN Charter and customary international law), states evaluate armed conflicts under *jus ad bellum* (rules leading up to war) and *jus in bello* (conduct during war). Based on the ICJ's *Nicaragua v. United States* precedent, operations are evaluated by "scale and effects" to determine if they constitute an armed attack.
- **Self-Defense and Attribution**: Under Article 51, states can respond to armed attacks while adhering to necessity and proportionality. Anticipatory self-defense requires evidence of an imminent attack. The talk highlights four attribution frameworks: perfect attribution, perfect non-attribution, perfect selective attribution, and false attribution (fertile ground for false flags).
- **State Responsibility and Non-State Actors**: As highlighted by the 2018 National Defense Strategy, cyber operations frequently involve proxies or non-state actors. Under international law, hostile acts can only be imputed to a state if it exercises effective control over the operation.
- **The Gray Zone (Twilight Zone)**: Operations falling below the "de minimis damage" threshold of an armed attack avoid triggering military self-defense while remaining disruptive. Examples include North Korea's 2014 intrusion into Sony Pictures Entertainment and the 2016 DNC email leaks and disinformation campaigns.

### Technical Details
- **Categories of Cyber Operations**: US Department of Defense classification includes Offensive Cyber Operations (OCO), Defensive Cyber Operations (DCO), and DoD Information Network operations.
- **Use of Force Thresholds**: Common examples identified by former State Department legal adviser Harold Koh that meet the threshold include triggering a nuclear plant meltdown, opening a dam above populated areas, or disabling air traffic control systems.
- **Requirements for Use of Force in Anticipatory Defense**: A state must prove (1) an actual decision by an adversary to exploit vulnerabilities, (2) consequences rising to an armed attack level, and (3) an immediate necessity to act.
- **Non-Forcible Countermeasures**: Acts that do not meet the armed attack threshold limit victim states to UN Security Council appeals (Article 39) and non-forcible measures, such as economic sanctions, diplomatic expulsions, or DOJ legal indictments (e.g., against Iranian and Chinese state-linked actors).

### Takeaways
- International law relies heavily on physical or kinetic thresholds (loss of life or physical destruction), creating challenges when addressing high-impact cyber incidents targeting data, financial markets, or critical infrastructure.
- Gray zone tactics—including psychological operations, disinformation, subversion, and economic coercion—exploit ambiguities in international law to achieve geopolitical aims below the threshold of war.
- While normative frameworks like the Tallinn Manual face participation gaps and slow legal evolution, international standards remain a vital benchmark for peace and collective defense.

talks.summary:
### Overview
At the DEF CON Hardware Hacking Village, programmer John Aho presented on the capabilities and quirks of the low-cost ESP8266 Wi-Fi microcontroller board, culminating in his custom multi-chip creation called the "Beaconator." Aho walked through his transition into microcontrollers, starting from simple Wi-Fi Rickrolls and progressing to massive Wi-Fi beacon frame generation and localized electronic book serving.

### Key Topics
- **ESP8266 Hardware and Ecosystem**: An introduction to the ESP8266, its licensing model (designed by Espressif and produced by various manufacturers), available form factors (such as NodeMCU with 30 pins vs. WeMos boards with 16 pins), and compatible shields (relays, temperature, humidity, and micro SD boards).
- **Rolling Wi-Fi Beacons**: Crafting mock access points by broadcasting 802.11 beacon frames without handling actual connection requests. The speaker referenced Mark Szabo's `fake_beacon_esp8266` as an early project foundation.
- **Impact on Wi-Fi Mapping Tools**: Testing the effects of broadcasting multiple SSIDs on site-survey tools such as Ekahau Wi-Fi Mapper, demonstrating that scanning numerous injected beacons causes mapping software on laptops to lag or crash.
- **The Beaconator Project**: Constructing a high-volume beacon broadcasting rig utilizing roughly 57 ESP8266 units arranged on an aluminum frame powered by an AGM gel lead-acid battery.
- **Embedded File Serving via SPIFFS**: Utilizing SPIFFS (Serial Peripheral Interface Flash File System) to store and serve digital books without external memory.

### Technical Details
- **Beacon Stability and Limitations**: To broadcast a persistent list of randomized-MAC SSIDs reliably visible to client devices, Aho determined that each ESP8266 board functions best when limited to between 13 and 17 broadcast access points. This ensures beacon frames are transmitted frequently enough for receiving devices to register.
- **Wireshark Timestamp Requirement**: ESP8266 beacon frames initially failed to appear in Wireshark packet captures until an internal timer/timestamp field within the beacon frame specification was appropriately populated.
- **Throughput and Scale**: The primary array of 44 modules in the Beaconator cycles through generated lists of approximately 2,800 to 2,900 beacons per unit. During live operation, the device pushes out roughly 130,000 beacon advertisements every 6 seconds, scaling to an estimated 1 million wireless access points and 2 million frames per minute. LED status indicators toggle at loop intervals to monitor operational timing.
- **SPIFFS Book Hosting**: Due to slow read/write speeds when serving web data from micro SD shields, Aho utilized SPIFFS to access the remaining flash memory (up to 3 MB) on select boards. Using public domain texts from Project Gutenberg (including *Frankenstein*, *Alice in Wonderland*, *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes*, and Cory Doctorow's *Little Brother*), four units operated as local open access points offering book downloads.

### Takeaways
Aho emphasized that the ESP8266 represents an inexpensive, highly accessible entry point into hardware experimentation. While the massive beacon generation of the Beaconator was primarily built as an exploratory and humorous proof of concept, massive beacon flood techniques present genuine implications for security operations, such as confusing wireless scanning software or masking other wireless activity. Future concepts discussed include offline disaster survival guides, localized route maps, or mobile mesh-style libraries, alongside the caveat that similar techniques could inevitably be abused for physical Wi-Fi spam.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this ICS Village presentation, Cisco Talos researchers Patrick DeSantis and Carlos Pacho analyze VPNFilter, a multi-year, state-sponsored malware campaign targeting small office/home office (SOHO) and network-attached storage (NAS) devices. Active since at least 2016 and publicly disclosed in May 2018, the malware infected an estimated 500,000 devices globally across more than 75 distinct device models from multiple vendors. The speakers examine the malware's multi-stage architecture and focus specifically on a specialized Stage 3 packet sniffer module designed to monitor Modbus and HTTP traffic.

### Honeypot Architecture and Research Challenges
To capture custom payloads without alerting the threat actor, Talos constructed a high-interaction physical honeypot environment consisting of approximately 40 real devices. Emulation was ruled out to avoid detection, and the devices were deployed across commercial and residential IP space rather than Cisco network ranges. Traffic was captured via one-way network taps connected to isolated analysis workstations to prevent lateral movement into corporate systems. The researchers deliberately flashed firmware containing known vulnerabilities and public exploits. Because every packet on these unutilized devices was non-legitimate, analysis required sorting through gigabytes of malicious traffic per day while managing device limitations where attackers often held more control than administrators.

### VPNFilter Architecture
The speakers clarified that VPNFilter is not a copy of BlackEnergy; its only link is a shared flaw in the RC4 encryption algorithm where S-boxes fail to properly initialize during the permutation stage. The malware operates in multiple stages:
- **Stage 1**: The only persistent component surviving reboots. It locates Stage 2 command-and-control (C2) servers by extracting IP addresses encoded in EXIF metadata (latitude and longitude) of Photobucket images, falling back to a hardcoded domain, or opening a raw socket that passively listens for a TCP SYN packet containing specific magic bytes.
- **Stage 2**: A Meterpreter-like framework that executes shell commands, collects data, handles exfiltration, and supports plugins. Older variants included an embedded kill function to overwrite flash memory (wiping the bootloader's first ~5,000 bytes) and brick the device.
- **Stage 3 Modules**: Extensible plugins including a Tor communication module, an inline interception module named 'ps' that injects JavaScript into port 80 traffic, a dedicated bricking/cleanup module, and a packet sniffer.

### Technical Details of the Modbus Packet Sniffer
Carlos Pacho detailed the Stage 3 packet sniffer module, a statically compiled, stripped Linux ELF binary compiled for the Lexra architecture (an instruction-set variant similar to MIPS) and uploaded to VirusTotal in 2016. Specifically targeting the TP-Link R600 VPN router, the binary requires two runtime arguments: a log directory and a target destination IP address.

The sniffer evaluates incoming traffic matching ipv4, TCP, and a packet length exceeding 150 bytes:
- **Modbus Inspection**: If destination port equals 502 and destination IP matches the provided argument, it logs the connection details to a file formatted as `rep_<timestamp>.bin`. It records only the source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port without logging Modbus payload data.
- **HTTP Inspection**: If traffic is not Modbus, it inspects TCP packets with source ports above 1024 (excluding ports 8080 and 8088) with payloads larger than 20 bytes destined for the specified target IP. It checks for HTTP basic authentication or distinct username and password parameters (discarding the packet if both parameter types are present or if excluded strings match) before saving the entire packet.

### Takeaways
The packet sniffer demonstrates extraordinary targeting, designed for a specific router architecture and requiring a pre-known destination IP address handling both Modbus and HTTP authentication traffic. The researchers noted that while this module passively logs traffic without inline modification capabilities, VPNFilter's overall modular structure gave the actor versatile capabilities ranging from credential theft and ICS monitoring to coordinated destructive bricking.

talks.summary:
R00TZ ASYLUM VILLAGE: Day 2 Morning Session

This DEF CON 26 Roots Asylum track featured multiple speakers addressing young hackers on cybersecurity fundamentals, software security, ethical hacking, and career pathways.

ROB JOYCE (NSA): Joyce outlined the NSA's dual mission—offensive cyber operations (Tailored Access Operations) and defensive security. He described the typical attack chain: reconnaissance, identifying vulnerabilities, establishing persistence, deploying tools, lateral movement, and data collection or destruction. Key defense recommendations: patch management (Windows, iPhone updates), network asset inventory knowledge, and regular backups against ransomware. Joyce highlighted four nations of concern: Russia (attacking US elections and energy grids); China (stealing technical secrets to undercut US businesses); North Korea (hacking Sony Pictures, stealing $81M from banks); Iran (erasing Saudi Arabian systems during geopolitical conflict). He also shared his personal hobby of building elaborate computer-controlled Christmas light displays using a single Raspberry Pi, demonstrating that technical skills learned at DEF CON can be applied creatively.

SARAH ZEO & MUDGE: The pair discussed source code fortification—compiler-based safety features that replace historically unsafe functions with safer alternatives. Critical finding: developers who enable fortification features assume the code is protected without verification. However, measurements show only one-third of binaries actually became fully fortified despite developers checking the "enable safety" box. The remaining two-thirds contain lingering unsafe functions developers are unaware of. The speakers advocated for treating software security like car safety features: testing and measuring rather than assuming. Practical measurement examples included browser security analysis (Chrome and Edge measurably more secure than competitors) and fuzzing (throwing garbage input at programs to expose weaknesses).

ADDIE (TOYMAKERS): Addie presented the DEF CON Roots badge design philosophy across four engagement levels: aesthetic appeal, immediate interactivity (button mashing), moderate depth (terminal access and game play), and expert challenges (hardware/software hacking). The badge theme—1983, the year before Orwell's 1984—emphasized that hackers still have agency to shape the future. Badge mechanics: LED colors (red/green/yellow/off) reflect story choices; the "N" letter indicates overall alignment (red=apocalypse, green=healthy future). Connecting badges with matching alignments allows cooperation; opposing alignments cause game resets. The hardware uses a PIK 32mm microcontroller; multiple microcontrollers on the board allow accessing code for all eight badge types via strapping pin configuration. Different badge types (human, press, goon, contest, speaker, vendor, artist, CFP) have distinct stories and room-specific mechanics.

GADGET GIRL: A 17-year-old high school senior defined a "hacker" as engineer + artist + leader. She emphasized that leadership involves educating the public on what hacking truly means, countering stereotypes of black-hoodie criminals. Practical pathways: STEAM/STEM programs, leadership institutes, university camps, public speaking, robotics competitions (First Lego League, VEX Robotics). She highlighted significant gender disparities: 2% women identify as hackers (NBC), 13% women in engineering workforce (MIT), 25% women in leadership (LinkedIn). Scholarships and programs (NCWIT, Girl Scouts, Girls Who Code) exist for underrepresented groups.

PONY BOY (EMIT BURR, 11 years old): Demonstrated web application hacking using Burp Suite. Live demonstration showed: (1) Direct page access vulnerability—modifying base64-encoded URL parameters to access hidden products; (2) Privilege escalation—changing an "is_guest" parameter from 1 to 0 to change a guest account password; (3) Information disclosure via robots.txt and directory indexing; (4) Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)—converting a POST request to GET format and tricking an admin into clicking a malicious link to hijack their account. Resources: OWASP Top 10 (web vulnerability reference), ZAP proxy (Burp alternative), WebGoat (deliberately insecure application for learning).

RIVERSIDE: Introduced the Wall of Sheep village, which captures unencrypted network traffic at DEF CON to reveal usernames and passwords of attendees not using encryption. Purpose: public awareness and teaching. Extended offerings: Packet Detective and Packet Inspector games for learning packet analysis and threat hunting. Riverside's multi-year involvement exemplifies DEF CON's gift economy—community leaders gain status by contributing, not paying.

AARON OWENS (DARK SKIES): Presented Drone Wars, evolved from a Roots workstation into a full DEF CON village. Highlights: drone racing offers significant prize money (15-year-old won $250,000 in Dubai)—enough to fund elite university tuition. Participants build 3D-printed hover drones from donated parts and learn FPV (first-person view) piloting. Sponsors include Drone Racing League and MultiGP. Future: release drone-based battle games with no-rules engagement.

OVERALL THEME: Roots Asylum bridges offensive and defensive security, hands-on technical skills, and ethical leadership. Speakers emphasized measurement/verification, diverse recruitment pathways, and the importance of educating peers on what "hacker" actually means in a positive sense.

talks.title: IoT VILLAGE - Erez Yalon - Your Smart Scale is Leaking More than Your Weight
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding IoT VILLAGE - Erez Yalon - Your Smart Scale is Leaking More than Your Weight.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at IoT Village, Erez Yalon, Head of AppSec Research at Checkmarx, examines privacy and security failures across the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. Working alongside researcher David Sofas, Yalon highlights how consumer convenience and vendor apathy drive widespread privacy forfeitures. The presentation spans common Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) implementation flaws, deliberate surveillance disguised as consumer software, optical data exfiltration from air-gapped environments, and turning smart speakers into remote eavesdropping tools.

### Key Topics
- **IoT Privacy Realities:** The collision between vendor indifference (low manufacturing cost, rapid churn, zero liability) and user desire for convenience leads to systemic privacy failures across cheap and expensive devices alike.
- **Bluetooth Low Energy Vulnerabilities:** Testing smart locks and wearables revealed that almost all tested devices lacked encryption or used obsolete pairing schemes like 'Just Works' and passkeys, allowing trivial bypasses.
- **Vendor Data Harvesting:** An analysis of a branded smart scale revealed deliberate, extensive data collection routed to servers in China.
- **Covert Optical Exfiltration:** Demonstrating that an infected system can exfiltrate sensitive data across an air gap using smart light bulb modulations.
- **Eavesdropping via Voice Assistants:** Exploiting Amazon Alexa skills to indefinitely record, transcribe, and exfiltrate conversations without continuous user prompting.

### Technical Details
- **Smart Locks & Wearables:** Attacks were performed using HCI (Host Controller Interface) snooping on Android smartphones to capture Bluetooth packets. By inspecting packet captures in Wireshark, researchers extracted six-digit unlock codes and replayed or fuzzed them to open locks in seconds. When HCI snooping failed, proxy-based Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks successfully intercepted unlock payloads. Similar packet-crafting techniques allowed spoofing notifications on smart bands.
- **The AEG Smart Scale Case:** A scale branded by AEG utilized a companion app authored by V-Trust. The application requested excessive Android permissions (such as mounting and unmounting file systems). Network traffic inspection showed the app transmitting unencrypted telemetry to `gather.lotusitc.com` in China. Data leaked included phone IMEI, Wi-Fi SSID, network operator, device model, home and phone MAC addresses, GPS latitude/longitude, and user weight. When notified, AEG took no action, while V-Trust subsequently obfuscated the domain and introduced basic encryption to hide the payloads from researchers without removing data collection.
- **Air-Gap Data Exfiltration via Smart Bulb:** Researchers demonstrated malware modulating a $15-$50 smart light bulb to transmit binary data through blinking. A custom Android app translated blinks back into text. The setup functioned at 100 meters using a telescope in daylight, and researchers noted that invisible blue wavelengths or multi-layer color channels could be utilized to avoid human detection.
- **Amazon Alexa Eavesdropping Skill:** To turn an Amazon Echo Dot into a remote wiretap without physical hardware tampering, researchers developed a rogue Alexa skill (e.g., disguised as a calculator). Normally, Alexa ends sessions or prompts the user audibly after replying. Researchers bypassed this by setting `shouldEndSession` to false and setting the `reprompt` class to an empty string, yielding complete silence while keeping the session open. To extract speech, researchers created a custom wildcard slot named `input` combined with dynamic multi-word sentence templates (up to 15 words). Amazon's speech-to-text service automatically transcribed user conversations and sent the text directly to the developer backend.

### Takeaways
Amazon's Lab126 security team collaborated with Checkmarx to mitigate the Alexa vulnerability by banning empty reprompt strings, screening for eavesdropping skills, and flagging abnormally long sessions. Ultimately, Yalon emphasizes that IoT privacy is a 'Layer 8' (human) issue. Users must demand accountability by avoiding insecure products, and security researchers should continuously audit, break, and publicly expose IoT vulnerabilities to raise industry standards.

talks.title: Matt Wixey - Betrayed by the Keyboard How What You Type Can Give You Away
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Matt Wixey - Betrayed by the Keyboard How What You Type Can Give You Away.
talks.summary:
Attribution is hard. Typically, the most useful identifiers—IP addresses, email address, domains, and so on—are also the easiest things to spoof, obfuscate, or anonymise. Whilst more advanced techniques, such as correlating malicious activity with timezones, or linking attacks through the use of similar techniques or malware, can be useful, they tend to take investigators further away from the individuals responsible; at best, some inference about the country or specific actor group/collective can be made.

In this talk, I present a method for linking incidents to individual attackers with a high degree of accuracy, based on extremely fine-grained behavioural characteristics. This involves an investigatory technique known as "case linkage analysis" (CLA), which uses granular aspects of crime scene behaviours to link common offenders together through statistical comparison. It's been applied to some crime types before, but never to cyber attacks.

I'll cover how CLA works, its advantages and disadvantages, and how it has previously been applied to a range of crimes, from burglary to homicide. I'll place it within the context of personality psychology, biometrics, forensic criminology, offender profiling, and forensic linguistics; and will walk through applying it practically.

I'll then show the results of a novel experiment I conducted applying CLA to network intrusion attacks, which involved logging the keystrokes of volunteer attackers across different simulated intrusions, breaking these down into specific behaviours and syntax, and using these to link individuals to their offences. The end result: the way you type commands, including your choice and order of syntax, switches, and options, can form distinctive behavioural signatures, which can be used to link attackers together. Linking accuracy rates as high as 99% were achieved.

Finally, I'll talk about the implications for both defenders and everyone else (particularly focusing on the privacy implications), explore ways in which these techniques could be defeated, and outline some ideas for future research in these areas.

talks.title: RECON VILLAGE - trustartech - WhiteRabbit Combining Threat Intelligence Public Blockchain
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning RECON VILLAGE - trustartech - WhiteRabbit Combining Threat Intelligence Public Blockchain.
talks.summary:
WhiteRabbit is an open-source tool developed by Trustar engineers Olivia and Nicholas that uses blockchain analysis, threat intelligence, and machine learning to trace ransomware payments and attribute campaigns. The tool exploits Bitcoin's immutable public ledger to cluster Bitcoin addresses associated with ransomware attackers, enabling early warning of campaign activity.

The methodology uses a four-step workflow: (1) harvesting seed addresses from ransom demands in malware samples, (2) expanding clusters using co-spent heuristics via the open-source BlockSID blockchain explorer, (3) monitoring clusters for anomalous balance activity, and (4) mapping blockchain observations to external indicators like IPs or file hashes. The speakers demonstrated this on the CryptoLocker campaign, reconstructing 968 Bitcoin addresses associated with attackers and tracking approximately $11.8 million in illicit funds, with balances peaking at around $140,000 in 2015.

Key findings from the case studies show how ransomware evolution maps to blockchain data. CryptoDefense failed due to a cryptographic bug allowing victims to decrypt files, generating minimal revenue compared to CryptoLocker's $140,000 peak. In contrast, CryptoWall succeeded (~$4 million collected) because it implemented strong RSA cryptography, with 13+ identified clusters; one version accumulated 800 Bitcoin at peak. Bitcoin payments to CryptoLocker clusters began September 7, 2013 (two days after release) and ceased February 2014 (when CryptoDefense launched), validating external timeline events.

The open-source code (github: trustar/white-rabbit) requires BlockSID and a large AWS instance, since the full Bitcoin blockchain occupies approximately 140 gigabytes. Utility functions enable cluster initialization, heuristic configuration, transaction volume computation, and balance history plotting.

The speakers propose positioning Bitcoin addresses in the 'pyramid of pain' threat indicator framework, between hashes and TTPs, because they enable link analysis while creating persistent, immutable evidence of attacker behavior that defenders can disrupt by blocking payment flows. However, significant challenges remain: clustering depends on seed address availability (requiring malware samples), missing whitelists contaminate heuristics with coin-join transactions, computational complexity scales to 140 million clusters blockchain-wide, and ethical concerns around surveillance and discriminatory targeting require community engagement to resolve.

talks.title: Steven Danneman - Your Banks Digital Side Door
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Steven Danneman - Your Banks Digital Side Door.
talks.summary:
Why does my bank's website require my MFA token but Quicken sync does not? How is using Quicken or any personal financial software different from using my bank's website? How are they communicating with my bank? These questions ran through my head when balancing the family checkbook every month.

Answering these questions led me to deeply explore the 20 year old Open Financial Exchange (OFX) protocol and the over 3000 North American banks that support it. They led me to the over 30 different implementations running in the wild and to a broad and inviting attack surface presented by these banks' digital side doors.

Now I'd like to guide you through how your Quicken, QuickBooks, Mint.com, or even GnuCash applications are gathering your checking account transactions, credit card purchases, stock portfolio, and tax documents. We'll watch them flow over the wire and learn about the jumble of software your bank's IT department deploys to provide them. We'll discuss how secure these systems are, that keep track of your money, and we'll send a few simple packets at several banks and count the number of security WTFs along the way.

Lastly, I'll demo and release a tool that fingerprints an OFX service, describes its capabilities, and assesses its security.
