talks.title: Thiago Alves - Hacking PLCs and Causing Havoc on Critical Infrastructures
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Thiago Alves - Hacking PLCs and Causing Havoc on Critical Infrastructures.
talks.summary:
Thiago Alves, a PhD student at UAH and creator of the Open PLC project, demonstrates critical security vulnerabilities in Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) that control critical infrastructure worldwide. PLCs, in use since 1970, rely on legacy protocols designed before the internet existed, leaving them fundamentally insecure.

The Modbus protocol, supported by approximately 90% of PLCs, provides no authentication, encryption, or message integrity verification. Modbus frames contain only a slave ID, function code, data, and CRC (error detection only). Attackers can freely read and write PLC memory without restriction. Alves demonstrates this through live attacks on three different industrial PLCs: Open PLC (Unified platform), Allen Bradley Micro Logic 1400 series, and Schneider Modicon M221.

The injection attack demonstration shows how repeatedly sending simple Modbus frames can switch PLCs from automatic to manual mode and force the heater to remain on, causing total loss of operator control. This attack succeeds identically across all three vendor platforms despite their architectural differences.

For Allen Bradley Micro Logic devices, Alves demonstrates a critical vulnerability he calls 'deadly packets.' By crafting malformed Modbus TCP frames with mismatched length fields, he triggers a buffer overflow in the PLC's memory allocation algorithm. This corrupts the firmware, rendering the device unrecoverable without reprogramming—even after power cycling. Alves worked with Allen Bradley through ICS-CERT to release a firmware patch, but updating operational PLCs remains impractical.

The Schneider Modicon vulnerability is particularly severe. The undocumented 'Unity protocol' operates atop Modbus TCP using reserved function code 0x5A, enabling full system control including memory dumps and OS extraction. Critically, project passwords are stored in plaintext and accessible via the standard 'read project info' function. Alves demonstrates extracting the password 'DEFCON' and using Schneider's own SO Machine Basic software to gain administrative access to the stopped PLC.

Alves introduced the Open PLC project—the first open-source PLC with full source code—supporting multiple platforms (Raspberry Pi, Arduino, industrial devices) and five standard programming languages. However, he acknowledges Open PLC currently mimics existing vendor security practices. His PhD research aims to create a security-hardened version of Open PLC.

Vendors addressed these vulnerabilities by recommending users disable vulnerable protocols and implement network restrictions—shifting security responsibility to operators rather than implementing proper defenses in the devices themselves.

talks.title: Ian Haken - Automated Discovery of Deserialization Gadget Chains
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Ian Haken - Automated Discovery of Deserialization Gadget Chains.
talks.summary: Although vulnerabilities stemming from the deserialization of untrusted data have been understood for many years, unsafe deserialization continues to be a vulnerability class that isn't going away. Attention on Java deserialization vulnerabilities skyrocketed in 2015 when Frohoff and Lawrence published an RCE gadget chain in the Apache Commons library and as recently as last year's Black Hat, Muñoz and Miroshis presented a survey of dangerous JSON deserialization libraries. While much research and automated detection technology has so far focused on the discovery of vulnerable entry points (i.e. code that deserializes untrusted data), finding a "gadget chain" to actually make the vulnerability exploitable has thus far been a largely manual exercise. In this talk, I present a new technique for the automated discovery of deserialization gadget chains in Java, allowing defensive teams to quickly identify the significance of a deserialization vulnerability and allowing penetration testers to quickly develop working exploits. At the conclusion we will also be releasing a FOSS toolkit which utilizes this methodology and has been used to successfully develop many deserialization exploits in both internal applications and open source projects.

talks.title: sghctoma - All Your Math are Belong to Us
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding sghctoma - All Your Math are Belong to Us.
talks.summary:
First of all, it's math. Not meth. So everybody be cool, I'm not gonna touch your central nervous system stimulant substances. Now that this is established, I can start telling my story. And this story, like all good stories, begins where it ends.

Wait, no, not really.

It begins at a birthday party where the sister of a friend asked if I could help her with MATLAB. No matter how horrible memories I had about MATLAB, I just couldn't say no. So the next day, there was I, sitting in my room, installing the trial. And that's when the hacking started...

Believe me, there were a lot to hack in this case! Several gigabytes of installed materials, a few web servers, cloud integration, clustering capabilities, you name it. These software are bloated, they are basically their own little operating systems.

Yup, I used plural. Because I thought why discriminate MATLAB? I should really give a chance to Maple and Mathematica to fail too!. I did, and they did fail, and these failures gave the material for my talk. Basically this will be a dump of exploits (RCEs, file disclosures, etc.), and if you use any of those software and you are at least a bit security conscious, you should definitely listen to it.

talks.summary: Most of us have knowledge of PCB construction. In the past reversing someone's design was an easy task due to the simplicity of the PCB design. Now with BGA's( Ball Grid Array's), manufacturers using several plane layers cover the entire PCB design and obscuring the details of the PCB from view. Thru the use of X-Ray, we are able to reverse engineer virtually anything. Slides will be presented show several PCB designs and how easy it was to reverse engineer the PCB. Also presenting videos of live views and dynamic zoom; this will demonstrate the true power of the X-Ray and its ability to see sub-micron features within the PCB structure and devices while manipulating the PCB.

talks.title: Patrick Wardle - The Mouse is Mightier than the Sword
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Patrick Wardle - The Mouse is Mightier than the Sword.
talks.summary:
In today's digital world the mouse, not the pen is arguably mightier than the sword. Via a single click, countless security mechanisms may be completely bypassed. Run untrusted app? click ...allowed. Authorize keychain access? click ...allowed. Load 3rd-party kernel extension? click ...allowed. Authorize outgoing network connection? click ...allowed. Luckily security-conscious users will (hopefully) heed such warning dialogues—stopping malicious code in its tracks. But what if such clicks can be synthetically generated and interact with such prompts in a completely invisible way? Well, then everything pretty much goes to hell.

Of course OS vendors such as Apple are keenly aware of this 'attack' vector, and thus strive to design their UI in a manner that is resistant against synthetic events. Unfortunately they failed.

In this talk we'll discuss a vulnerability (CVE-2017-7150) found in all recent versions of macOS that allowed unprivileged code to interact with any UI component including 'protected' security dialogues. Armed with the bug, it was trivial to programmatically bypass Apple's touted 'User-Approved Kext' security feature, dump all passwords from the keychain, bypass 3rd-party security tools, and much more! And as Apple's patch was incomplete (surprise surprise) we'll drop an 0day that (still) allows unprivileged code to post synthetic events and bypass various security mechanisms on a fully patched macOS box!

And while it may seem that such synthetic interactions with the UI will be visible to the user, we'll discuss an elegant way to ensure they happen completely invisibly!

Since then, several changes in wifi client devices, including MAC randomisation, significant use of the 5GHz spectrum and an increased variety of configurations has made these attacks harder to conduct. Just firing up a vanilla script gets fewer credentials than it used to.

To address this mana will be re-released in this talk with several significant improvements to make it easier to conduct rogue AP MitM attacks against modern devices and networks.

talks.summary:
Regarding ptmalloc2, many heap exploitation techniques have been invented in the recent years, well documented on the famous how2heap repository, or as writeups of famous CTF challenges (like House of Orange). However, most of them require atleast a libc/heap leak , or fail in non-PIE binaries. My new technique titled House of Roman leverages a single bug to gain shell leaklessly on a PIE enabled Binary. I shall showcase the ease of aligning the heap to perform this attack, thus demonstrating its versatility.

Since this a 20 mins talk, attendees should be aware of basic heap exploitation techniques, like fastbin attacks and unsorted bin attacks, and have a general idea of how the ptmalloc2 algorithm works. As a bonus, I also discuss how to land a fastbin chunk in memory regions with no size alignment (like __free_hook ).

talks.summary:
Voicemail systems have been with us since the 80s. They played a big role in the earlier hacking scene and re-reading those e-zines, articles and tutorials paints an interesting picture. Not much has changed. Not in the technology nor in the attack vectors. Can we leverage the last 30 years innovations to further compromise voicemail systems? And what is the real impact today of pwning these?

In this talk I will cover voicemail systems, it's security and how we can use oldskool techniques and new ones on top of current technology to compromise them. I will discuss the broader impact of gaining unauthorized access to voicemail systems today and introduce a new tool that automates the process.

talks.title: Eric Sesterhenn - In Soviet Russia Smartcard Hacks You
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Eric Sesterhenn - In Soviet Russia Smartcard Hacks You.
talks.summary:
The classic spy movie hacking sequence: The spy inserts a magic smartcard provided by the agency technicians into the enemy's computer, ...the screen unlocks... What we all laughed about is possible!

Smartcards are secure and trustworthy. This is the idea smartcard driver developers have in mind when developing drivers and smartcard software. The work presented in this talk not only challenges, but crushes this assumption by attacking smartcard drivers using malicious smartcards.

A fuzzing framework for *nix and Windows is presented along with some interesting bugs found by auditing and fuzzing smartcard drivers and middleware. Among them classic stack and heap buffer overflows, double frees, but also a replay attack against smartcard authentication.

Since smartcards are used in the authentication process, a lot of vulnerabilities can be triggered by an unauthenticated user, in code running with high privileges. During the authors research, bugs were discovered in OpenSC (EPass, PIV, OpenPGP, CAC, Cryptoflex,...), YubiKey drivers, pam_p11, pam_pkc11, Apple smartcardservices...

talks.title: Christopher Domas - The Ring 0 Facade Awakening the Processors Inner Demons
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Christopher Domas - The Ring 0 Facade Awakening the Processors Inner Demons.
talks.summary: Your computer is not yours. You may have shelled out thousands of dollars for it. It may be sitting right there on your desk. You may have carved your name deep into its side with a blowtorch and chisel. But it's still not yours. Some vendors are building secret processor registers into your system's hardware, only accessible by shadowy third parties with trusted keys. We as the end users are being intentionally locked out and left in the dark, unable to access the heart of our own processors, while select organizations are granted full control of the internals of our CPUs. In this talk, we'll demonstrate our work on how to probe for and unlock these previously invisible secret registers, to break into all-powerful features buried deep within the processor core, to finally take back our own computers.

talks.title: = Richard Thieme - The Road to Resilience How Real Hacking Redeems a Damnable Profession
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for = Richard Thieme - The Road to Resilience How Real Hacking Redeems a Damnable Profession.
talks.summary:
Two years ago Richard Thieme spoke on “Playing Through the Pain: The Impact of Dark Knowledge on Security and Intelligence Professionals” for Def Con 24. He relied on dozens of experiences provided by colleagues over a quarter-century, colleagues from NSA, CIA, corporate, and military. Responses to the presentation have often been emotional and have corroborated his thesis. The real impact of this work on people over the long term has to be mitigated by counter-measures and strategies so scars can be endured or,even better,incorporated and put to use.

In this presentation, Thieme elaborates those strategies and counter-measures. In what is likely his final speech at Def Con, he speaks directly to the “human in the machine” AS a human being. It’s not about leaving the profession: it’s about what we can do to thrive and transcend the challenges. It‘s about “saving this space,” this play space of hacking, work and life, and knowing the cost of being fully human while encountering dehumanizing impacts.

It is easier to focus on exploits, cool tools, zero days, and the games we play in the space that “makes us smile.” It is not so easy to know how to play through the pain successfully. The damage to us does not show up in brain scans. It shows up in our families, our relationships, and our lives.

Thieme is not preaching, he is sharing insights based on what he too has had to transcend in his own life. They call a lot of us “supernormals,” which means we discovered resilient responses to deprivation, abuse, profound loss … or the daily challenges of work that makes clear that evil is real. We are driven, we never quit, we fight through adversity, we create and recreate personas that work, we do what has to be done. It pays to know how we do that and know THAT we know so we can recreate resilience in the face of whatever comes our way.

A contractor for NSA suggested that everyone inside the agency should see the video of “Playing Through the Pain.” A long-time Def Con attendee asks all new hires to watch “Staring into the Abyss,” a talk Thieme did a few years before. This subject matter is seldom discussed aloud “out here” and by all accounts is not taken seriously “inside,” which is perhaps why there have been half a dozen suicides lately at NSA and a CIA veteran said, “I have 23 suicides on my mind, the most recent senior people who could not live with what they knew.”

The assumption baked into this talk: real hacking, its ethos and its execution, provides the tools we need to do this damn thing right.

This talk is in honor of Perry Barlow and the EFF.

talks.title: Seamus Burke - A Journey Into Hexagon Dissecting a Qualcomm Baseband
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Seamus Burke - A Journey Into Hexagon Dissecting a Qualcomm Baseband.
talks.summary: Mobile phones are quite complicated and feature multiple embedded processors handling wifi, cellular connectivity, bluetooth, and other signal processing in addition to the application processor. Have you ever been curious about how your phone actually makes calls and texts on a low level? Or maybe you want to learn more about the internals of the baseband but have no clue where to start. We will dive into the internals of a qualcomm baseband, tracing it's evolution over the years until its current state. We will discuss the custom, in-house DSP architecture they now run on, and the proprietary RTOS running on it. We will also cover the architecture of the cellular stack, likely places vulnerabilities lie, and exploit mitigations in place. Finally we will cover debugging possibilities, and how to get started analyzing the baseband firmware—how to differentiate between RTOS and cellular functions, how to find C std library functions, and more.

We all protect our home networks, but how safe is your data once it leaves on its journey to the latest cat pictures? How does your traffic make it to its destination and what threats does it face on its way? What is BGP and why should you care?

In this talk, I'll explain the basic structure of the network that is the Internet and the trust relationships on which it is built. We'll explore several types of attacks that you may have seen in the news that exploit this relationship to bring down websites, steal cryptocurrency, and monitor dissidents.

Because talking about bringing down the Internet isn't as much fun as doing, I'll show how to create a mini Internet using Mininet and demonstrate the attacks without the need for a BGP router or a lawyer. Finally, because nation states shouldn't get to have all the fun, I'll use Scapy and some novel techniques to demonstrate how a compromised router can be used to prevent attribution, frame a friend, or create a covert communication channel.

talks.title: Joe Rozner - Synfuzz Building a Grammar Based Retargetable Test Generation Framework
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Joe Rozner - Synfuzz Building a Grammar Based Retargetable Test Generation Framework.
talks.summary: Fuzzers have played an important role in the discovery of reliability and security flaws in software for decades. They have allowed for test case generation at a rate impossible by hand and the creation of test cases humans may never conceive of. While there are many excellent fuzzers available most are designed for mutating source files or input in random ways and attempting to discover edge cases in the handling of them. Some others are designed with structured input in mind and use grammars to more strategically generate and mutate possible inputs that adhere to the format defined. These specifically are the ones we care about for the goals of identifying differences between multiple implementations of a single language, finding bugs in parse tree generation/handling of tokens, and handling of the data at runtime once it has been successfully lexically and syntactically analyzed. We'll look at some of the shortcomings of existing fuzzers and discuss the implementation for a new platform designed to make fuzzer creation easier with the goal of being able utilize grammars from the implementations of the languages themselves.

The Teddy Ruxpin is an iconic toy from the 1980's featuring an animatronic teddy bear that reads stories from cassette tapes to children. In late 2017, a new model of the toy was released with improvements including Bluetooth connectivity, LCD eyes, and a companion mobile application. While the new bear features a number of improvements, the Teddy Ruxpin's original ability to add new stories by replacing the included cassettes is no longer applicable, and it requires users to supply files to the bear in a proprietary format.

This presentation aims to show how the new Teddy Ruxpin was reverse engineered down to a very low level in order to create new content. I will reveal the inner workings of the hardware and software within the bear and document the process used to reverse engineer it. I will then examine the communication between the mobile application and Teddy Ruxpin as well as the custom structure of the digital books read by the bear. I will end the presentation by releasing a toolset that allows users to create their own stories followed by a demo showcasing the Teddy Ruxpin greeting the DEF CON audience.

talks.title: Orange Tsai - Breaking Parser Logic Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0Days Out
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Orange Tsai - Breaking Parser Logic Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0Days Out.
talks.summary:
We propose a new exploit technique that brings a whole-new attack surface to defeat path normalization, which is complicated in implementation due to many implicit properties and edge cases. This complication, being under-estimated or ignored by developers for a long time, has made our proposed attack vector possible, lethal, and general. Therefore, many 0days have been discovered via this approach in popular web frameworks written in trending programming languages, including Python, Ruby, Java, and JavaScript.

Being a very fundamental problem that exists in path normalization logic, sophisticated web frameworks can also suffer. For example, we've found various 0days on Java Spring Framework, Ruby on Rails, Next.js, and Python aiohttp, just to name a few. This general technique can also adapt to multi-layered web architecture, such as using Nginx or Apache as a proxy for Tomcat. In that case, reverse proxy protections can be bypassed. To make things worse, we're able to chain path normalization bugs to bypass authentication and achieve RCE in real world Bug Bounty Programs. Several scenarios will be demonstrated to illustrate how path normalization can be exploited to achieve sensitive information disclosure, SMB-Relay and RCE.

Understanding the basics of this technique, the audience won't be surprised to know that more than 10 vulnerabilities have been found in sophisticated frameworks and multi-layered web architectures aforementioned via this technique.

talks.title: Bai and Zheng - Analyzing and Attacking Apple Kernel Drivers
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Bai and Zheng - Analyzing and Attacking Apple Kernel Drivers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Alibaba security researchers Bai and Zheng (Spark) discuss Apple kernel security, focusing on vulnerabilities within Apple kernel drivers (kexts on macOS and integrated drivers in the iOS kernelcache) and presenting static analysis and fuzzing tools to improve driver vulnerability discovery.

### Key Topics
Kernel drivers share the same memory space and privileges as the Mach kernel, making them high-value targets for jailbreaks and kernel exploits. User clients serve as the communication bridge between user-space applications and drivers, implementing callback methods such as `externalMethod`, `clientMemoryForType`, `registerNotificationPort`, and `clientClose`. Even sandboxed applications on iOS retain access to select user clients (such as `IOHIDUserClient` and `IOSurfaceRootUserClient`). Driver vulnerabilities frequently occur because third-party vendors or complex driver codebases often lack strict guarantees.

### Technical Details
- **Vulnerabilities Demonstrated:**
  - *Information Leak in `IOSurfaceRootUserClient`:* Caused by an uninitialized kernel stack variable (`out_channel_handle`) in the channel allocation routine. When the allocation capacity reaches `0xFFFF`, a new object is not added and `out_handle` remains uninitialized on the stack, which is then returned to user space. This leak bypasses Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (kASLR).
  - *Use-After-Free (UAF) in `IOAcceleratorFamily2`:* Found in `asTransaction` where user clients shared a pipe instance. By creating two pipe user clients, attaching a transaction via the first, closing the client with `IOServiceClose` to release the pipe, and completing the transaction from the second client, a UAF is triggered.
  - *Exploitation Strategy:* Exploitation leveraged OSUnserializeXML heap spraying (with controllable header and readable spray data), a fake object with a fake vtable, and a ROP chain. The ROP chain utilized a stack pivot (`rax` to `rdx`, then `rcx` to `rsp`), extracted the `proc` structure and credentials, set `cr_uid` and `cr_svuid` to 0, and cleanly exited kernel mode via thread exception returning to user space to spawn a root shell on macOS 10.13.2 and 10.13.3.
- **Static Analysis with "Rook":**
  Closed-source Apple drivers suffer from stripped symbols, missing types, and unresolved virtual function calls. The authors created **Rook**, an IDA Pro Python static analysis plugin that:
  - Identifies class names and sizes from initialization functions and creates IDA structures.
  - Locates class vtables using pointers to metaclass objects.
  - Recovers virtual function names by mapping overridden kernel virtual functions (leveraging matching names and offsets in child classes).
  - Infers parameter and stack variable types using demangled C++ symbol information and propagates types across control flow graphs.
  - Adds cross-references and allows direct navigation to virtual method implementations on double-click.
  - Generates whole-driver call graphs.
- **Fuzzing with "RookFuzz":**
  Rook was integrated with the driver fuzzer `PassFuzz` (OS X framework). Rook performs static data-flow analysis to infer constraints and user input formats to guide the fuzzer. The authors resolved compatibility issues in PassFuzz for post-macOS 10.11 kernels:
  - Expanded the kernel header read buffer from one page to two pages.
  - Adapted kernel text base detection: because Apple moved the interrupt handler out of the kernel `__TEXT` section to mitigate Meltdown, RookFuzz traverses back from alternative known kernel functions (such as `ml_panic_text`) to locate the kernel text base.

### Takeaways
Drivers remain an accessible and fruitful attack surface for macOS and iOS kernel compromise. Static analysis tooling like Rook bridges the gap between decompiled output and readable source abstractions, significantly aiding both manual reverse engineering and guided kernel fuzzing.

talks.title: Rousseau and Seymour - Finding Xori Malware Analysis Triage with Automated Disassembly
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Rousseau and Seymour - Finding Xori Malware Analysis Triage with Automated Disassembly.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Amanda Russo and Richard Seymour from Endgame introduce Xori, an open-source, browser-based disassembler built in Rust over six months (~36,000 lines of code) to automate malware analysis triage. The tool solves a critical problem: manually analyzing 1,000 samples in three days using traditional methods like IDA Pro is impractical. Xori enables rapid disassembly and analysis of PE executables at scale across any platform (Linux, macOS, Windows).

## Key Topics
The speakers evaluated existing disassemblers (Capstone, Radare2, IDA Pro, Hopper, Binary Ninja) against their requirements: fast development, stability, resilience, cross-platform support, easy-to-integrate JSON output, ease of use, and output accuracy. They adopted insights from multiple tools—particularly Capstone's LLVM/GDB-based approach and Qemu's emulation concepts—and built Xori in Rust to address gaps and bugs in existing solutions.

## Technical Details
**Architecture**: Xori includes a PE loader (similar to Windows's loader), a memory manager, an analysis struct, and a CPU state tracker with loop detection.

**PE Parsing**: Uses the Nom parser combinator framework to safely parse complex PE headers while capturing all metadata (including legacy fields) for later data science analysis.

**Memory & Execution**: Simulates the Windows 7 Thread Environment Block (TEB) and Process Environment Block (PEB) to enable dynamic API call resolution. A giant JSON of Windows DLL exports allows the tool to populate real API addresses during emulation without requiring actual DLL files.

**Disassembly & Emulation**: Supports x86 and x64 architectures. Offers two emulation modes: light emulation (handles registers, stack, some instructions) and full emulation (slower, for packers/encryption). Includes an analysis queue for following control flow through branches and loop detection with configurable limits.

**String Extraction**: Automatically extracts strings pushed onto the stack during emulation, similar to Flareon's plugins. Demonstrated with a shellcode sample that dynamically loads shell32.dll via LoadLibraryA and ShellExecuteA.

**Performance**: Processed 1,000 samples in 20 minutes (~1.25 seconds per sample) on a Dell box with SSD, maxing out all CPUs when run in parallel.

**Output & Integration**: Produces JSON suitable for service integration, grep analysis, function name/import searches, and graph analysis in tools like Angr.

## Takeaways
Xori is open-source and available on GitHub (github.com/endgame/xori) with active community contributions. Rust proved invaluable for rapid development by catching memory bugs at compile-time. The tool demonstrates automation replacing tedious manual reverse engineering for triage workflows. The browser-based UI and CLI options make it accessible for both interactive exploration and automated pipelines. The combination of PE simulation, emulation, and memory management enables detection of dynamic imports and function calls that static analysis alone cannot capture.

talks.title: Riedesel and Hakimian - Tineola Taking a Bite Out of Enterprise Blockchain
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Riedesel and Hakimian - Tineola Taking a Bite Out of Enterprise Blockchain.
talks.summary:
Blockchain adaptation has reached a fever pitch, andthe community is late to the game of securing these platforms against attack. With the open source community enamored with the success of Ethereum, the enterprise community has been quietly building the next generation of distributed trustless applications on permissioned blockchain technologies. As of early 2018, an estimated half of these blockchain projects relied on the Hyperledger Fabric platform.

In this talk we will discuss tools and techniques attackers can use to target Fabric. To this end we are demoing and releasing a new attack suite, Tineola, capable of performing network reconnaissance of a Hyperledger deployment, adding evil network peers to this deployment, using existing trusted peers for lateral network movement with reverse shells, and fuzzing application code deployed on Fabric.

As George Orwell said: "Who controls the past controls the future. Who controls the present controls the past." This talk will demonstrate how a sufficiently armed red team can modify the blockchain past to control our digital future.

talks.summary:
Phone-based mobile money is becoming the dominant paradigm for financial services in the developing world processing more than a billion dollars per day for over 690 million users. For example, mPesa has an annual cash flow of over thirty billion USD, equivalent to nearly half of Kenya's GDP. Numerous other products exist inside of nearly every other market, including GCash in the Philippines and easyPaisa in Pakistan. As a part of this growth, competitors have appeared who leverage ThinSIMS, small SIM card add ons, to provide alternative mobile money implementations without operating their own mobile networks. However, the security implications of ThinSIMs are not well understood.

This talk dives into decade old telecom standards to explore how ThinSIMs work and what attackers of mobile money systems can do when they control the interface between the SIM card and the phone. We will also demo two proof of concept exploits that use ThinSIMs to steal money from mobile money platforms and detail the difficulties of defense.

talks.title: Romailler and Amiet - Reaping and Breaking Keys at Scale When Crypto Meets Big Data
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Romailler and Amiet - Reaping and Breaking Keys at Scale When Crypto Meets Big Data.
talks.summary:
Public keys are everywhere, after all, they are public. These keys are waiting to be reaped by those who know their real value. Hidden behind this public face lurks some potentially dangerous issues which could lead to a compromise of data and privacy.

Leveraging hundreds of minion devices, we built a public key reaping machine (which we are open sourcing) and operated it on a global scale. Collected keys are tested for vulnerabilities such as the recent ROCA vulnerability or factorization using batch-GCD. We've collected over 300 million keys so far and built a database 4 to 10 times bigger than previous public works.

Performing the initial computation on over 300 million keys took about 10 days on a 280 vCPU cluster. Many optimizations allow our tool to incrementally test new RSA keys for common prime factors against the whole dataset in just a few minutes.

As a result of our research, we could have impersonated hundreds of people by breaking their PGP keys, mimicked thousands of servers thanks to their factored SSH keys and performed MitM attacks on over 200k websites relying on vulnerable X509 certificates.

In the end, we were able to do this in an entirely passive way. Going further is possible, but it would lead us to the dark side. Would big brother hesitate to go there?

talks.title: Nevermoe - One Step Ahead of Cheaters Instrumenting Android Emulators
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Nevermoe - One Step Ahead of Cheaters Instrumenting Android Emulators.
talks.summary:
Commercial Android emulators such as NOX, BlueStacks and Leidian are very popular at the moment and most games can run on these emulators fast and soundly. The bad news for game vendors is that these emulators are usually shipped with root permission in the first place. On the other hand, cheating tools developers are happy because they can easily distribute their tools to abusers without requiring the abusers to have a physical rooted device, nor do they need to perform laborious tuning for different Android OS / firmware version. However, luckily for game vendors, commercial Android emulators usually use an x86/ARM mixed-mode emulation for speed-up. As a result, a standard native hooking/DBI framework won't work on this kind of platform. This drawback could discourage the cheating developers.

In this talk, I will introduce a native hooking framework on such a kind of mixed-mode emulators. The talk will include the process start routine of both command-line applications and Android JNI applications as well as how these routines differ on an emulator. The different emulation strategies adopted by different emulators and runtime environments (Dalvik/ART) will also be discussed. Based on these knowledge, I will explain why the existing hooking/DBI frameworks do not work on these emulators and how to make one that works.

Lastly, I will present a demo of using this hooking framework to cheat a game on emulator. With this demo, I will discuss how the dark market of mobile game cheating may develop in the foreseeable future.

Descriptions of full reverse engineering of internal structures and all historical background info needed to understand how the exploit chains for ETERNALBLUE, ETERNALCHAMPION, ETERNALROMANCE, and ETERNALSYNERGY work will be provided.

This talk will also describe how the MS17-010 patch fixed the vulnerabilities, and identify additional vulnerabilities that were patched around the same time.

talks.title: Kim and Choi - Your Watch Can Watch You! Pitfalls in the Samsung Gear Smartwatch
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Kim and Choi - Your Watch Can Watch You! Pitfalls in the Samsung Gear Smartwatch.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, researchers from the HEIT security research lab at Dongguk University in South Korea analyze the security architecture of Samsung Gear smartwatches running Tizen OS 3. While prior security research had evaluated Tizen OS generally, this work focuses specifically on the smartwatch ecosystem, where devices hold highly sensitive user data—such as contacts, calendars, locations, emails, and notifications synchronized from a paired smartphone. The researchers evaluate Tizen's multi-layered access control model, uncover pervasive privilege validation omissions across D-Bus IPC services, and demonstrate how unprivileged malware can abuse exposed APIs to monitor users and exfiltrate sensitive information.

### Key Topics
- **Tizen Security Architecture:** Tizen combines open-source components with proprietary Samsung layers. Access control is maintained via a "3+1" security mechanism: classic UNIX Discretionary Access Control (DAC), Simplified Mandatory Access Control Kernel (SMACK), Cynara (a user-space privilege management daemon), and the Security Manager (a policy configurator).
- **IPC and Privilege Checkpoints:** Applications communicate with privileged service daemons via D-Bus. In theory, privilege checks happen across three defense layers: client-side API libraries querying Cynara, a Cynara-aware D-Bus daemon validating requests mid-transit, and service daemons independently verifying privileges upon receipt.
- **Automated Privilege Analysis Tool (DAN):** The researchers developed DAN (D-Bus Analyzer), a tool designed to fuzz and inspect exposed D-Bus services on remote devices. Using access control errors as an oracle, DAN identifies exposed endpoints where non-privileged requests are accepted.
- **Vulnerabilities Across Core Services:** Systematic auditing identified critical privilege validation bypasses in system services including Wi-Fi (WPA Supplicant), Bluetooth (ProjectX and BlueZ), window/display management (Enlightenment), notification services, and email consumers.
- **App Store Distribution:** The researchers proved real-world exploitability by successfully bypassing Samsung Galaxy Apps verification with a benign-looking watch face app containing obfuscated malware.

### Technical Details
To understand why privilege bypasses occur, the researchers dissected the three privilege checkpoints. The first check occurs inside client-linked shared libraries (e.g., `liblocation`). Because this executes within the client process's own PID, an attacker or malware can simply patch process memory (via `mprotect` and instruction modification) to bypass the check. Consequently, true security depends on the second check (the Cynara-aware D-Bus daemon) and the third check (the target service daemon).

To identify where both subsequent checks fail, DAN gathers bus names from `/usr/share/dbus-1/system.d/` and runtime `ListNames` calls, recursively introspects objects via standard D-Bus introspection, extracts properties via `GetAll`, and invokes every method with random arguments. Because Tizen's D-Bus daemon returns an immediate `AccessDenied` error if a Cynara check blocks an unprivileged message, any other response (such as `InvalidArguments`) indicates that the D-Bus daemon permits non-privileged messages to pass through.

Scanning the Samsung Gear Sport uncovered 269 bus names, over 130,000 readable properties, and over 2,000 callable methods requiring manual review. Critical findings include:
- **WPA Supplicant:** Completely unconfigured and exposed on the shared system bus without D-Bus configuration checks. An unprivileged app can scan BSSIDs and signal strengths, allowing precise geolocation tracking via external geolocation APIs even when location services and GPS permissions are disabled.
- **Bluetooth Subsystem:** ProjectX services exposed methods allowing silent acceptance of pairing requests, forced discovery, and spoofed PIN-entry dialogs to phish user PINs. BlueZ APIs permitted unprivileged disconnects, while unrestricted access to `hcidump` allowed sniffing Bluetooth traffic. Combining forced disconnections with packet dumping allowed attackers to capture re-established link keys.
- **Enlightenment Window Manager:** Exposed methods like `dump_top_level_windows` allowed taking unauthorized screen captures into PNG files.
- **Notification & Email Daemons:** The notification service exposed internal notification data and permitted launching apps on the phone. The `email-consumer` service allowed modifying emails and sending outbound messages via the victim's account. Notably, the private method `email_private_send_mail_noti` relied on a trivial string comparison check against an ID string rather than a Cynara privilege validation.

In a full end-to-end demonstration, an unprivileged watch face app intercepted incoming Google Hangouts notifications, disconnected Bluetooth, captured HCI packets to obtain link keys, took screen captures, and exfiltrated all stolen data to the attacker using the victim's email account.

### Takeaways
The core architectural failure stemmed from treating D-Bus as a hierarchical system rather than a flat shared bus: while high-level middleware had policy files, underlying daemons like WPA Supplicant were left completely unprotected. Furthermore, official store verification in Samsung Galaxy Apps failed to detect these malicious D-Bus calls, allowing an obfuscated proof-of-concept app (`BitWatch`) to be approved and published. Following responsible disclosure to Samsung in April, Samsung acknowledged the issues, merged multiple patches into the Tizen open-source repository, and rolled out firmware updates.

talks.title: Zheng and Panel - Your Peripheral Has Planted Malware An Exploit of NXP SOCs
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Zheng and Panel - Your Peripheral Has Planted Malware An Exploit of NXP SOCs.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Researchers from the Unicorn Team at 360 Technology present research exploring how to bypass secure boot and anti-cloning mechanisms in resource-constrained embedded systems, specifically focusing on NXP microcontrollers based on ARM Cortex-M architecture. In low-cost embedded systems lacking dedicated security hardware such as TPMs or TrustZone, vendors frequently bind firmware execution to a unique ID (UID) etched in silicon to prevent illicit product cloning. The speakers demonstrate how hardware debugging features, specifically the ARM Flash Patch and Breakpoint (FPB) unit, can be repurposed to subvert UID checks, clone proprietary devices, and implant hardware trojans into peripherals.

### Key Topics
- **Embedded Secure Boot Constraints:** Unlike PCs or smartphones with TPMs and TrustZone, resource-constrained microcontrollers rely on on-chip ROM bootloaders and UID-based signature checks to prevent copying.
- **Cloning Economics & UID Protection:** Counterfeiters easily replicate PCBs and dump unprotected flash. To prevent cloning, vendors bind firmware to factory-burned silicon UIDs.
- **ARM FPB Exploitation:** Leveraging the hardware Flash Patch and Breakpoint (FPB) unit to remap code and literal addresses dynamically from flash to SRAM without altering original flash firmware.
- **Peripheral Exploitation via Segger J-Link:** Replicating the Segger J-Link debug probe onto a third-party evaluation board and injecting a BadUSB hardware trojan.

### Technical Details
In NXP Cortex-M microcontrollers, reading the silicon UID is performed via an on-chip ROM API function pointer accessed through command `58`. To circumvent this without reverse-engineering and patching the entire firmware binary, the researchers used the processor's FPB unit.

The FPB unit offers six instruction comparators and two literal comparators. By programming the `FP_COMP` and `FP_REMAP` registers, instructions or literal data fetched from code space can be redirected to arbitrary SRAM addresses. The researchers programmed the FPB before bootloader execution to intercept calls to the ROM API. When command `58` is invoked, it redirects execution to custom SRAM code that supplies a forged UID matching the licensed target, while transparently passing all other commands to the original ROM handler.

To demonstrate real-world impact, the team targeted the Segger J-Link debug probe (which runs on an NXP Cortex-M microcontroller):
1. **Device Cloning:** Firmware extracted from official desktop update software was flashed onto an inexpensive evaluation board. Because code read protection (CRP) levels 1 and 2 allow in-system programming (ISP) erase operations, the board was pre-programmed with an exploit payload in unused flash space that configures FPB hooks at startup, successfully passing license and signature verifications.
2. **Hardware Trojan (BadUSB):** The exploit was extended to implant malware into the peripheral. By using FPB to hook the `SysTick_Handler` interrupt, the device main functionality remained intact while a timer counted down five minutes. Upon expiration, the peripheral assumed USB HID capabilities to execute unauthorized actions on the host machine without user interaction.

### Takeaways
To mitigate attacks abusing hardware debug features:
- Do not leak unencrypted firmware binaries in desktop update packages.
- Explicitly disable the FPB unit before invoking security-critical APIs or completing bootloader verification.
- Fill unused flash regions with trap instructions (such as branch-to-reset) rather than leaving them blank.
- Cryptographically verify signatures across the entire flash memory space rather than subsets of code.
- Carefully evaluate Code Read Protection (CRP) levels; while CRP Level 3 prevents ISP abuse, it completely disables re-programmability.
- Chip vendors should restrict address remapping mechanisms from tampering with critical ROM API entry points.

talks.title: Levinson and Borges - Ill See Your Missile and Raise You A MIRV
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Levinson and Borges - Ill See Your Missile and Raise You A MIRV.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Alex Levinson and Dan Borges introduce the Genesis Scripting Engine, or G-Script (Gscript), an open-source framework developed to rapidly generate cross-platform droppers and stagers. Drawing from their experiences on the Red Team at the National Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition (CCDC), the speakers explain their progression from using raw shell/PowerShell scripts to compiling native Go binaries. Script-based payloads faced significant drawbacks, including PowerShell script block logging and easy forensic recovery of source code. Early compiled prototypes like Genesis used SMB shares to bundle multiple binaries into a single executable, but lacked granular instrumentation. G-Script addresses these challenges by allowing operators to write lightweight scripts in JavaScript (ES5) that compile into standalone, native executables for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Dropper Tooling**: Transitioning from PowerShell/bash wrapper scripts to compiled Go binaries to prevent source recovery and bypass script logging.
- **Architecture of G-Script**: Comprising an engine, compiler, obfuscator, standard library, command-line interface, and interactive debugger (REPL).
- **Isolated Execution & Resiliency**: Bundling multiple independent G-Script scripts and payloads into isolated JavaScript virtual machine runtimes inside a single Go binary, preventing one payload's failure from crashing others.
- **JavaScript-to-Go Native Linking**: Bridging JavaScript with native Go libraries via compiler macros, allowing G-Script to directly call Go functions and third-party packages.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Mapping & Emulation**: Codifying post-exploitation, persistence, and execution techniques as atomic G-Script scripts, enabling realistic threat emulation and vendor detection validation.

### Technical Details
During compilation (`gscript compile`), the compiler parses compiler macros (e.g., file imports or Go package imports) and traverses the JavaScript abstract syntax tree (AST) alongside Go package ASTs. It dynamically generates Foreign Function Interface (FFI) wrappers in Go to expose Go functions to the embedded JavaScript virtual machines. Each script executes inside its own isolated VM runtime, with its entry point defined in a mandatory `deploy()` function. 

Payloads, shellcode, and embedded assets are encrypted using AES-256 with unique keys per VM and are embedded directly into the binary, decrypting only when explicitly requested in memory. The tool features an obfuscation pipeline that runs before and after native Go compilation to randomize function names, addresses, and strip static strings. An interactive debugger (`gscript shell`) provides a REPL environment supporting step-through debugging, type inspection (`typeof` mapped to Go pointer types), and symbol table viewing. Limitations highlighted include large binary sizes characteristic of Go, lack of FreeBSD support, regular expression constraints bound to Go's `re2` engine, restriction to ES5 syntax, and absence of native JavaScript concurrency primitives.

### Takeaways
G-Script enables red teams to codify "persistence and techniques as code" using a collaborative model where multiple operators contribute isolated payloads into one binary. For blue teams and security operations, it provides an auditable method to test whether detection tools detect real behavioral activity rather than relying on brittle file signatures or string matching against known scripts. G-Script version 1 is published as an open-source project on GitHub alongside a repository mapping atomic techniques to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

talks.title: Wesley McGrew - An Attacker Looks at Docker Approaching Multi Container Applications
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Wesley McGrew - An Attacker Looks at Docker Approaching Multi Container Applications.
talks.summary:
Overview
Wesley McGrew presents tactical post-exploitation techniques for attacking multi-container Docker applications, targeting red teamers and penetration testers. The core insight is that traditional network-based offensive skills directly transfer to containerized environments, where internal application communication now flows over TCP/IP protocols instead of remaining in local memory.

Key Topics

Layers of Abstraction: McGrew emphasizes that developers move up the stack of abstraction (from low-level C to high-level frameworks to containerization), while attackers must move down to find exploitable vulnerabilities. Crucially, with multi-container applications, what used to be local in-memory state (variables, data structures) now exists as network-accessible services like Redis databases and PostgreSQL instances—making them targets for post-exploitation manipulation.

Why Post-Exploitation Over Zero-Days: Rather than focusing on Docker-specific zero-day vulnerabilities (which get patched quickly), this talk advocates learning timeless post-exploitation tactics that work after gaining initial access through conventional exploits targeting the outer attack surface (e.g., a vulnerable Joomla image).

Docker Architecture Basics: Containers use OS-level virtualization (lightweight kernel sharing) rather than full hardware simulation, making deployment across development and production environments consistent and quick. Applications compose multiple containers networked together, often with a front-tier (exposed) and back-tier (internal) network.

Technical Details

The demonstration exploits a multi-container voting application:
- Python voting interface, Node.js results server, PostgreSQL database, Redis queue, and a vulnerable Joomla container
- Initial access gained via Metasploit exploit against the Joomla image
- Enumeration revealed internal Docker networks (172.18.x.x, 170.219.x.x ranges) using statically compiled nmap uploaded to the compromised container
- Port forwarding via Meterpreter established tunnels to the PostgreSQL database and Redis server
- Direct database manipulation: inserted votes into PostgreSQL tables
- Redis inspection via netcat in monitor mode showed real-time vote queueing (push/pop operations)
- Arbitrary votes injected into Redis, affecting application state without going through the web interface

Key Vulnerabilities Exploited:
- No authentication on Redis or PostgreSQL (common in tutorial/default configurations)
- Joomla image outdated and vulnerable
- No network segmentation preventing lateral movement between containers
- Lack of tools in minimal container images (busybox) forcing attackers to upload statically compiled binaries

Takeaways

Existing penetration testing methodologies—network reconnaissance, vulnerability exploitation, post-exploitation—apply directly to multi-container applications, democratizing exploitation for red teamers already skilled in network attacks. However, practitioners should proactively familiarize themselves with Docker and Kubernetes before encountering them in real engagements to avoid surprise and paralysis when breaking into containerized infrastructure. The talk positions containerization as an natural entry point for penetration testers expanding into application security testing.

talks.title: Si, Agent X - Wagging the Tail:Covert Passive Surveillance
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Si, Agent X - Wagging the Tail:Covert Passive Surveillance.
talks.summary:
In this modern digital age of technically competent adversaries we forget that there may still be a need to conduct old school physical surveillance against a target. Many organisations utilise surveillance teams and these may be in-house in the case of government agencies or third-party teams contracted for a specific task and their targets range from suspected terrorists to people accused of bogus insurance claims.

Whilst most people think that they may never be placed under surveillance some professions increase this probability. For example, if you are a member of the press with sources that you only meet face to face you could be a target especially if the source is a whistleblower or has information that their employer would rather they didn't give to you. Would it seem far-fetched to think that a hacker, security researcher or a member of the EFF could be placed under surveillance? Maybe even some current and former DEF CON speakers and attendees?

These teams are not the lone Private Investigator sat in their car at the bottom of your street but are highly trained individuals whose job is to remain undetected. Their mission is to observe and identify interactions and document everything they see. They aim to be "The Grey Man", that person, when asked to describe, you are unable to. Their techniques have changed very little over decades because they work.

This talk will focus on mobile and foot surveillance techniques used by surveillance teams. It will also include tips on identifying if you are under surveillance and how to make their life difficult.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Josh Mitchell - Ridealong Adventures: Critical Issues with Police Body Cameras.
talks.summary:
The police body camera market has been growing in popularity over the last few years. A recent (2016) Johns Hopkins University market survey found 60 different models have been produced specifically for law enforcement use. Rapid adoption is fueling this meteoric increase in availability and utilization. Additionally, device manufactures are attempting to package more and more technology into these devices. This has caused a deficiency in local municipalities' skills and budget to accurately assess the attack surface and exposure to the organization. Furthermore, departmental policies and procedures governing the secure deployment of these devices is largely insufficient.

At DEF CON, we will be introducing tactics, techniques, and procedures to assess the security of these devices. We will cover attacks against the physical devices, RF components, smartphone app's, and desktop software. The capabilities demonstrated and discussed will encompass publicly and privately available technologies. Additionally, the talk will cover multiple products and vendors, shedding light on industry wide issues and trends. Finally, we will be releasing software to detect and track various devices and tie these issues into real world events.

talks.title: Blasted Bits - ZOZ
talks.teaser: DEF CON China Beta explores Blasted Bits - ZOZ.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, speaker ZOZ explores rapid, forensic-resistant data destruction mechanisms under a strict one-minute operational constraint. Inspired by previous research presented at DEF CON 19 by Bruce Potter and team, the project addresses the threat of an adversary with nation-state-level forensic capabilities who can recover information from discarded, encrypted, or partially damaged media. The research establishes experimental ground rules: data must be destroyed within a 1U server rack space using internal containment mechanisms (such as concrete buffers or exhaust management) without relying on external facilities, while preventing surrounding equipment from catching fire or activating building fire suppression systems.

### Key Topics
The talk categorizes experimental drive destruction mechanisms into three primary modalities:
- **Thermal Attacks**: Attempting to heat magnetic platters past their Curie point (specifically targeting cobalt-based magnetic layers above roughly 1,000°C) or using the drive's own materials as fuel.
- **Kinetic Attacks**: Physically deforming, mutilating, puncturing, or explosively welding platters and flash memory components to prevent mechanical reading.
- **Electrical Attacks**: Targeting solid-state storage (SSDs) and flash drives by discharging extreme electrical pulses to destroy semiconductor bond wires and internal circuitry.

### Technical Details
- **Thermal Methods**: The speaker tested standard shop plasma torches, cutting cleanly through spinning drive platters within 0.5 seconds. Pure oxygen injection was evaluated to utilize the aluminum substrate itself as combustible fuel. Thermite variations were also tested: standard iron-oxide thermite (3:1 ratio by weight) and copper thermite (4.4:1 copper oxide to aluminum). While copper thermite produced energetic reactions and dispersed elemental copper, the non-magnetic nature of copper left platters potentially readable. External refractory enclosures housing thermite charges failed to uniformly heat disk platters to the required Curie threshold.
- **Kinetic Methods**: Powder-actuated (firing concrete-driving cartridges) and pneumatic nail guns were used to drive fasteners directly through spinning drive platters, demonstrating mechanical deformation and shattering. The speaker then examined directional explosive cutting via shaped charges (the Monroe effect). Using parametric OpenSCAD models, 3D-printed thin-walled geometries (annular and radial grooves) were fabricated and filled with liquid/paste explosive mixtures (sensitized nitromethane matrices). Confinement and blast suppression testing showed that consumer shaving cream placed in the containment volume significantly mitigated the blast pressure wave, keeping explosive deformations within a simulated 1U space.
- **Electrical Methods**: Flash media and microcontrollers were attacked using high-current exploding bridgewires and extreme high-voltage pulses (15,000 volts) routed into common ground pins to overcome power-rail protections. The resulting pulse vaporized internal bond wires and decoupled silicon dies from circuit packaging.

### Takeaways
For magnetic media, high-intensity plasma cutting and mechanical penetration proved effective, while thermite heating remained inconsistent due to aluminum heat sinking. Explosive cutting and welding of platters showed high efficacy but require substantial lateral containment. For solid-state storage, ground-pin high-voltage injection reliably severs internal bond connections. The talk concludes with high-profile operational security cases (such as the arrests of Silk Road's Ross Ulbricht and AlphaBay's Alexandre Cazes), emphasizing that software full-disk encryption fails when adversaries capture devices while in an unlocked or running state.

talks.title: Androsia Securing data in process for your Android Apps - Samit Anwer
talks.teaser: DEF CON China Beta details Androsia Securing data in process for your Android Apps - Samit Anwer.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at DEF CON, Samit Anwer introduces **Androsia**, an automated static analysis and bytecode instrumentation tool designed to protect data in process for Android applications. While data at rest can be secured using ciphers and data in motion via TLS, data in process remains a challenging gray area. Java and Android runtimes routinely leave sensitive data—such as authentication credentials, session tokens, encryption keys, PINs, OTPs, and personally identifiable information (PII)—resident on the heap memory. Developers often assume the garbage collector (GC) will clear this data. However, Java's GC is inherently lazy, triggering only when memory is constrained, and uses a mark-and-sweep algorithm that only reclaims objects unreachable from GC roots. Reachable, unused objects retain sensitive values until process termination, leaving them vulnerable to heap dumps and application compromise. Androsia acts like a proactive garbage collector by determining an object's exact last usage point and immediately instrumenting bytecode to overwrite memory contents with default values.

### Key Topics
- **Data in Process vs. In Rest/In Motion**: Data in process lacks widespread protection mechanisms compared to storage encryption and network encryption.
- **Limitations of Native Garbage Collection**: The mark-and-sweep GC only purges unreachable objects during memory pressure; reachable but unused objects remain in memory indefinitely.
- **Manual Cleanup Deficiencies**: Java APIs like `KeyStore.PasswordProtection.destroy()` depend entirely on manual developer invocation, which is frequently neglected or placed too late in execution.
- **Whole-Program Dataflow Analysis**: Using interprocedural, summary-based dataflow analysis to accurately discover where sensitive objects reach their last point of liveness across methods and execution flows.
- **Intermediate Representations (Jimple)**: Unpacking Android Dalvik bytecode into Jimple (a 3-address, 15-statement IR) using Soot and the Dexpler plugin for streamlined analysis before reinstrumenting and repacking into Dalvik/DEX.

### Technical Details
Androsia leverages the **Soot** bytecode analysis framework alongside **FlowDroid** (to generate a dummy `main` method tying together Android lifecycle callbacks) and the **Dexpler** plugin (to translate Dalvik bytecode to Jimple IR). The analysis operates across three primary scopes: local variables, static fields, and instance fields.

1. **Live Variable Analysis Algorithm**:
   - Calculates definition sets (`def`) and usage sets (`use`) for every statement in reverse execution order (bottom-to-top).
   - Computes live variable exit (`LV_exit`) and entry (`LV_entry`) sets using the dataflow equation: `LV_entry(L) = (LV_exit(L) - def(L)) U use(L)`. Where branches merge, `LV_exit` is the union of successor entries.
   - Identifies the last usage point of a variable when it disappears between the statement's entry set and exit set.
   - Caches per-method results as summaries (tuples of variables and their last use statements), propagating them across call graphs in reverse topological order for static field references.

2. **Handling Loops, Recursion, and Method Calls**:
   - Instrumenting directly after use within a loop or recursive cycle would clear values needed in subsequent iterations, breaking business logic. Androsia detects loops and method calls, hoisting instrumentation outside the loop body or placing it right before method returns.

3. **Instance Field Handling**:
   - For instance fields (e.g., private `StringBuilder` fields), Androsia identifies classes holding sensitive fields, tracks references and aliases of the enclosing object instances, and instruments caller sites at the instance's last use. It injects custom `reset` helper methods inside the target class (calling `delete(0, length())` on `StringBuilder` instances) to cleanly bypass private access modifier constraints.

### Takeaways
- Never rely solely on lazy runtime garbage collection to purge sensitive data from memory.
- Androsia automates the identification of object lifetime and replaces sensitive contents without burdening developers with manual cleanup calls.
- Ongoing and future work includes building out test-driven development to clear remaining bugs and integrating Androsia into CI/CD pipelines so enterprise mobility management (EMM) vendors and organizations can automatically analyze, instrument, and harden Android APKs.

talks.title: Crypto and Privacy Village - Punky Duero - The Key Management Facility of The Root DNSSEC
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Crypto and Privacy Village - Punky Duero - The Key Management Facility of The Root DNSSEC.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Punky Duero, a cryptographic key manager at ICANN, provides an inside look at the Key Management Facility (KMF) and procedures used to secure the Root Zone DNSSEC Key Signing Key (KSK). Rather than diving deep into DNSSEC theory, Duero demystifies the physical security, procedural rituals, and trusted community roles that protect the private root key of the global Domain Name System.

### Key Topics
- **ICANN and IANA Functions**: Clarification of ICANN's role in coordinating top-level IP allocations (via the five Regional Internet Registries) and domain name registries, rather than monitoring general internet traffic.
- **KSK Rollover (2017)**: Explanation of the transition from the operational KSK 2010 to KSK 2017 (an RSA 2048 key generated in October). Duero highlights key milestones, including publication on July 11, packet size changes on September 19, and the critical cutover deadline on October 11, 2017, where un-updated validating recursive resolvers would fail.
- **Physical Security & Defense-in-Depth**: The architecture of the KMF, featuring dual facilities (Virginia and El Segundo), concentric security cages, mantraps, dual-occupancy controls, and sensor networks.
- **Key Ceremonies**: The quarterly, highly scripted three-act ceremony required to sign the root zone's Zone Signing Key (ZSK) responses, audited externally and recorded for transparency.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Security Modules (HSMs)**: The private key is secured inside FIPS 140-2 Level 4 certified HSMs (two per facility). These devices feature tamper-detection sensors designed to zeroize keys if subjected to improper physical movement or electrical tampering.
- **Multi-Party Access & Safes**: Accessing the HSM requires at least three of seven smart cards held by Crypto Officers (a subset of Trusted Community Representatives, or TCRs). Smart cards are stored in safe deposit boxes inside a GSA Class 5 credential safe protected by seismic and triple-biased door sensors. Equipment (HSMs and air-gapped laptops) is kept in a separate hardware safe managed by a different individual under strict segregation of duties.
- **Air-Gapped Execution**: The signing system runs on a bare laptop devoid of wireless interfaces or internal hard drives, booting via CD into a lightweight CentOS environment running custom, publicly available key management software.
- **Physical Access Controls**: Facilities rely on dual-occupancy PIN and card readers (with iris scanners noted as impractical in practice), dual-technology microwave and passive infrared sensors to eliminate false alarms, and 24/7 video monitoring.
- **Ceremony Structure**: Held quarterly with at least 12 distinct individuals, the three-hour ceremony consists of three acts: extracting materials, generating cryptographic signatures for Verisign's root zone management, and returning materials into tamper-evident bags under strict chain of custody. A secondary group of TCRs, including recovery key shareholders, exists to reconstruct the KSK if both primary facilities fail.

### Takeaways
Securing the internet root trust anchor relies fundamentally on strict operational discipline, defense-in-depth, segregation of duties, and transparency. Although popularized by media dramatizations of 'seven keys controlling the internet,' the real protection lies in deliberate, auditable processes, open scrutiny by the technical community, and community-driven trust.

talks.title: Nick Cano - XenoScan Scanning Memory Like a Boss
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Nick Cano - XenoScan Scanning Memory Like a Boss.
talks.summary:
XenoScan is the next generation in tooling for hardcore game hackers. Building on the solid foundation from older tools like Cheat Engine and Tsearch, XenoScan makes many innovations which take memory scanning to a whole new level.

This demo-heavy talk will skip the fluff and show the power of the tool in real-time. The talk will demonstrate how the tool can scan for partial structures, detect complex data structures such as binary trees or linked lists, detect class-instances living on the heap, and even group detected class instances by their types. Additional, these demos will take a look at the tool's extensibility by working not only on native processes, but also on Nintendo games running in emulators. You're not all game hackers, so the talk will also show how XenoScan can be useful in the day-to-day workflow of reverse engineers and hackers.

When I'm not doing demos, I'll be drilling down to the low-level to talk about the nitty gritty details of what's happening, how it works, and why it works.

By the end of the talk, you'll see the true power of a well-made, smart memory scanner. You'll be empowered to use it in your day to day hacking, whether that is on games, malware, or otherwise. For those of you that are really interested in the tool, it is completely open-source and all development is done on an interactive livestream, meaning you can participate in and learn from future development.

talks.title: Salvador Mendoza - Exploiting 0ld Mag stripe information with New technology
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Salvador Mendoza - Exploiting 0ld Mag stripe information with New technology.
talks.summary:
A massive attack against old magnetic stripe information could be executed with precision implementing new technology. In the past, a malicious individual could spoof magstripe data but in a slow and difficult way. Also brute force attacks were tedious and time-consuming. Technology like Bluetooth could be used today to make a persistent attack in multiple magnetic card readers at the same time with audio spoof.

Private companies, banks, trains, subways, hotels, schools and many others services are still using magstripe information to even make monetary transactions, authorize access or to generate "new" protocols like MST(Magnetic Secure Transmission) During decades the exploitation of magstripe information was an acceptable risk for many companies because the difficulty to achieve massive attacks simultaneously was not factible. But today is different.

Transmitting magstripe information in audio files is the faster and easier way to make a cross-platform magstripe spoofer. But how an attacker could transmit the audio spoof information to many magnetic card readers at the same time? In this talk, we will discuss how an attacker could send specific data or achieve a magstripe jammer for credit card terminals, PoS or any card reader. Also, how it could be implemented to generate brute force attacks against hotel door locks or tokenization processes as examples.

talks.title: Professor Plum - Digital Vengeance Exploiting the Most Notorious C&C Toolki
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Professor Plum - Digital Vengeance Exploiting the Most Notorious C&C Toolki.
talks.summary:
Every year thousands of organizations are compromised by targeted attacks. In many cases the attacks are labeled as advanced and persistent which suggests a high level of sophistication in the attack and tools used. Many times, this title is leveraged as an excuse that the events were inevitable or irresistible, as if the assailants' skill set is well beyond what defenders are capable of. To the contrary, often these assailants are not as untouchable as many would believe.

If one looks at the many APT reports that have been released over the years some clear patterns start to emerge. A small number of Remote Administration Tools are preferred by actors and reused across multiple campaigns. Frequently sited tools include Gh0st RAT, Plug-X, and XtremeRAT among others. Upon examination, the command and control components of these notorious RATs are riddled with vulnerabilities. Vulnerabilities that can be exploited to turn the tables from hunter to hunted.

The presentation will disclose several exploits that could allow remote execution or remote information disclosure on computers running these well-known C&C components. It should serve as a warning to those actors who utilize such toolsets. That is to say, such actors live in glass houses and should stop throwing stones.

talks.title: Tomer Cohen - Game of Chromes: Owning the Web with Zombie Chrome Extensions
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Tomer Cohen - Game of Chromes: Owning the Web with Zombie Chrome Extensions.
talks.summary:
On April 16 2016, an army of bots stormed upon Wix servers, creating new accounts and publishing shady websites in mass. The attack was carried by a malicious Chrome extension, installed on tens of thousands of devices, sending HTTP requests simultaneously. This "Extension Bot" has used Wix websites platform and Facebook messaging service, to distribute itself among users. Two months later, same attackers strike again. This time they used infectious notifications, popping up on Facebook and leading to a malicious Windows-runnable JSE file. Upon clicking, the file ran and installed a Chrome extension on the victim's browser. Then the extension used Facebook messaging once again to pass itself on to more victims.

Analyzing these attacks, we were amazed by the highly elusive nature of these bots, especially when it comes to bypassing web-based bot-detection systems. This shouldn't be surprising, since legit browser extensions are supposed to send Facebook messages, create Wix websites, or in fact perform any action on behalf of the user.

On the other hand, smuggling a malicious extension into Google Web Store and distributing it among victims efficiently, like these attackers did, is let's say - not a stroll in the park. But don't worry, there are other options.

Recently, several popular Chrome extensions were found to be vulnerable to XSS. Yep, the same old XSS every rookie finds in so many web applications. So browser extensions suffer from it too, and sadly, in their case it can be much deadlier than in regular websites. One noticeable example is the Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension, which was silently installed on January 10 by Adobe, on an insane number of 30 million devices. A DOM-based XSS vulnerability in the extension (found by Google Project Zero) allowed an attacker to craft a content that would run Javascript as the extension.

In this talk I will show how such a flaw leads to full and permanent control over the victim's browser, turning the extension into zombie. Additionally, Shedding more light on the 2016 attacks on Wix and Facebook described in the beginning, I will demonstrate how an attacker can use similar techniques to distribute her malicious payload efficiently on to new victims, through popular social platforms - creating the web's most powerful botnet ever.

talks.summary: Ever been on a job that required you to clone live RFID credentials? There are many different solutions to cloning RFID in the field and they all work fine, but the process can be slow, tedious, and error prone. What if there was a new way of cloning badges that solved these problems? In this presentation, we will discuss a smarter way for cloning RFID in the field that is vastly more efficient, useful, and just plane cool. We will go over the current tools and methods for long-range RFID cloning, than discuss and demonstrate a new method that will allow you to clone RFID credentials in the field in just seconds, changing the way you perform red team engagements forever.

PEIMA is a brand new method of client side malicious activity detection based on mathematical laws, usually used in finance, text retrieval and social media analysis, that is fast, accurate, and capable of determining when denial of service attacks start and stop without flagging legitimate heavy interest in your server erroneously. However, denial of service attacks aren't the only type of anomalous activity you can look at with PEIMA. Learn what kinds of unusual identifying metrics you can get out of your network and users to help detect intrusions and, ultimately, defend your assets.

talks.title: spaceB0x - Exploiting Continuous Integration (CI) and Automated Build systems
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in spaceB0x - Exploiting Continuous Integration (CI) and Automated Build systems.
talks.summary: Continuous Integration (CI) systems and similar architecture has taken new direction, especially in the last few years. Automating code builds, tests, and deployments is helping hordes of developers release code, and is saving companies a great amount of time and resources. But at what cost? The sudden and strong demand for these systems have created some widely adopted practices that have large security implications, especially if these systems are hosted internally. I have developed a tool that will help automate some offensive testing against certain popular CI build systems. There has been a large adoption of initiating these builds through web hooks of various kinds, especially changes to public facing code repositories. I will start with a brief overview of some of the more popular CI tools and how they are being used in many organizations. This is good information for understanding, at a high level, the purpose of these systems as well as some security benefits that they can provide. From there we will dive into specific examples of how these different CI implementations have created vulnerabilities (in one case to a CI vendor themselves). Last we will explore the tool, its purpose, and a demonstration of its use. This tool takes advantage of the configurations of various components of the build chain to look for vulnerabilities. It then has the capability to exploit, persist access, command and control vulnerable build containers. Most of the demonstration will revolve around specific CI products and repositories, however the concepts are applicable across most build systems. The goal here is to encourage further exploration of these exploitation concepts. The tool is built "modularly" to facilitate this. If you are new to CI and automated build systems, or if you have been doing it for years, this talk and tool will help you to better secure your architecture
