talks.title: Conference Mike Use Their Machines Against Them Loading Code with a Copier
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Conference Mike Use Their Machines Against Them Loading Code with a Copier.
talks.summary:
We've all worked on ‘closed systems’ with little to no direct Internet access. And we've all struggled with the limitations those systems put on us in the form of available tools or software we want to use. I didn't like struggling, so I came up with a method to load whatever I wanted on to a closed system without triggering any common security alerts. To do this I had to avoid accessing the Internet or using mag media. In the end all I needed was an office multi-function machine and Excel. It's all any insider needs.

For my presentation and demo, I'll show you how I delivered a select group of PowerSploit tools to a clean, isolated machine. Of course, Excel has been known as vector for macro viruses for quite some time and some of the techniques--such as hex-encoding binary data and re-encoding it on a target machine--are known binary insertion vectors but I have not found any prior work on an insider using these techniques to deliver payloads to closed systems. You'll leave my presentation knowing why Excel, umm, excels as an insider attack tool, how to leverage Excel features to load and extract arbitrary binary data from a closed network, and what to do if this really frightens you.

talks.title: Wireless Village - Village People - Wireless Capture the Flag Inbrief
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Wireless Village - Village People - Wireless Capture the Flag Inbrief.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At DEF CON 24, the Wireless Village organizers introduced the 13th iteration of the Wireless Capture the Flag (WCTF) competition. Reflecting on the event's evolution from early Las Vegas wardrives to modern IoT, RF, and industrial protocols, the organizers emphasized that the contest's primary objective is hands-on education for both beginners and experienced security practitioners. The CTF features over 100 core challenge flags spanning frequencies from 72 MHz to 5.8 GHz, alongside discretionary points for creative technical accomplishments.

### Key Topics
- **Legal and Operational Rules of Engagement**: Clear boundaries were established regarding radio spectrum behavior. Participants were strictly warned against wideband RF jamming or denial-of-service in the air, with reminders regarding FCC compliance. Contestants were advised to avoid RF tracking on casino floors. Connecting to the competition network serves as mutual authorization for offensive engagement between participants and the village organizers.
- **Mobile Challenges (Fox Hunts and Hide-and-Seek)**: The organizers detailed physical tracking contests across two conference hotels. Traditional Wi-Fi fox hunts transmit ESSID and MAC details via Twitter (@WCTF_us), requiring hunters to locate beacons and verbally identify targets for 750-point bounties. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) hunts introduce tracking of fitness bands and IoT devices, utilizing tools like Blue Hydra. Additionally, an SDR fox operating at 72 MHz plays audio prompts ('What does the Fox say') where physical tokens must be collected.
- **Software-Defined Radio (SDR) & Interactive Games**: The CTF incorporates varied RF tasks manageable with entry-level hardware such as RTL-SDRs and HackRFs. Highlights include 'air painting' (RF watermarking/FFT visualization), a frequency-finding drinking game, and the 'Duck Hunt' challenge requiring players to capture AFSK 'quack' transmissions and transmit properly formatted 'bang' packets to receive MD5 hashes. A high-energy duel challenge involves radio-controlled shock collars strapped to participants' thighs, racing to decode and transmit RF signals directly from empty command consoles.
- **Industrial Control Systems (ICS) / SCADA**: An authentic manufacturing-style ICS setup (representing high-speed automotive or semiconductor lines rather than traditional SCADA) was integrated behind a WEP-protected wireless bridge. Participants progress from cracking WEP to mapping hidden PLC and switch IPs, extracting passwords from 24V I/O blocks, decoding raw industrial button/light I/O byte patterns, hashing PLC firmware dumps, and attempting non-persistent man-in-the-middle attacks on industrial communications.
- **The Classic Wardrive**: Reviving the community wardriving roots from DEF CON 11, the village launched a wardriving competition scored at 0.065 points per unique validated BSSID (doubled to 0.13 points if tagged with GPS coordinates). To avoid legal issues under 9th Circuit rulings, raw PCAP packet captures were banned; contestants were required to submit native NetXML files (from Airodump-ng or Kismet) packaged in an XZ-compressed tarball before the Sunday deadline.

### Technical Details
- **Frequency Coverage**: 72 MHz up to 5.8 GHz.
- **Wi-Fi Challenges**: Includes WEP cracking entry vectors, automated WPA dictionary attacks with supplied wordlists, real-world enterprise WPA configurations, and handshake captures.
- **SDR Techniques**: AFSK packet decoding/transmitting, waterfall pattern recognition, daisy-chained RF power plug manipulation, and RTL-SDR baseline monitoring around 900 MHz.
- **ICS Protocols & Hardware**: Switch password retrieval, PLC configuration dumping via USB to retrieve SHA-1 hashes, and sniffing button state byte patterns within I/O data fields.

### Takeaways
Participants can compete effectively using minimal hardware (such as a $40 Wi-Fi card or an $18 RTL-SDR), with extensive educational documentation provided via wctf.us and sdr.ninja. The organizers encouraged peer collaboration, shoulder-surfing, and hands-on learning, framing the event as a realistic penetration testing environment where organizers defend, detect, and interact directly with contestants.

talks.title: Jay Healey - Feds and 0Days: From Before Heartbleed to After FBI Apple
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Jay Healey - Feds and 0Days: From Before Heartbleed to After FBI Apple.
talks.summary:
Does the FBI have to tell Apple of the vuln it used to break their iPhone? How many 0days every year go into the NSA arsenal -- dozens, hundreds or thousands? Are there any grown-ups in Washington DC watching over FBI or NSA as they decide what vulns to disclose to vendors and which to keep to themselves? These are all key questions which have dominated so much of 2016, yet there's been relatively little reliable information for us to go on, to learn what the Feds are up to and whether it passes any definition of reasonableness.

Based on open-source research and interviews with many of the principal participants, this talk starts with the pre-history starting in the 1990s before examining the current process and players (as it turns out, NSA prefers to discover their own vulns, CIA prefers to buy). The current process is run from the White House with "a bias to disclose" driven by a decision by the President (in because of the Snowden revelations). The entire process was made public when NSA was forced to deny media reports that it had prior knowledge of Heartbleed.

talks.title: Richard Thieme - Playing Through Pain: The Impact of Secrets and Dark Knowledge
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Richard Thieme - Playing Through Pain: The Impact of Secrets and Dark Knowledge.
talks.summary:
Dismissing or laughing off concerns about what it does to a person to know critical secrets does not lessen the impact when those secrets build a different map of reality than "normals" use and one has to calibrate narratives to what another believes. The cognitive dissonance that inevitably causes is managed by some with denial who live as if refusing to feel the pain makes it disappear. But as Philip K. Dick said, reality is that which, when you no longer believe in it, refuses to go away. And when cognitive dissonance evolves into symptoms of traumatic stress, one ignores those symptoms at one's peril. But the constraints of one's work often make it impossible to speak aloud about those symptoms, because that might threaten one's clearances, work, and career. The real cost of security work and professional intelligence goes beyond dollars. It is measured in family life, relationships, and mental and physical well-being.

The divorce rate is as high among intelligence professionals as it is among medical professionals, for good reason - how can relationships be based on openness and trust when one's primary commitments make truth-telling and disclosure impossible?

Richard Thieme has been around that space for years. He has listened to people in pain because of the compelling necessities of their work, the consequences of their actions, the misfiring of imperfect plans, and the burdens of - for example - listening to terrorists slit someone's throat in real time, then having to act as if they had a normal day at the office. Thieme touched on some of this impact in his story, "Northward into the Night," published in the Ranfurly Review, Big City Lit, Wanderings and Bewildering Stories before collection in "Mind Games." The story illuminates the emotional toll of managing multiple personas and ultimately forgetting who you are in the first place.

The bottom line is, trauma and secondary trauma have identifiable symptoms and they are everywhere in the "industry." The "hyper-real" space which the national security state creates by its very nature extends to normals, too, now, but it's more intense for professionals. Living as "social engineers," always trying to understand the other's POV so one can manipulate and exploit it, erodes the core self. The challenge is not abstract or philosophical, it's existential, fired into our faces every day at point blank range, and it constitutes an assault on authenticity and integrity. Sometimes sanity is at stake, too, and sometimes, life itself. In one week, two different people linked to the CIA told Thieme that going into that agency was like becoming a scientologist. Think about what that analogy means. For his own sake and sanity, Thieme has thought about it a lot and that's what this talk is about - the real facts of the matter and strategies for effective life-serving responses.

talks.summary:
Is the Internet going to live up to its promise as the greatest force for individual freedom that the world has ever known? Or is the hope for a global community of creative intellectual interaction lost…for now?

In last year’s Black Hat keynote—entitled "Lifecycle of a Revolution"—noted privacy and civil liberties advocate Jennifer Granick told the story of the Internet utopians, people who believed that Internet technology could greatly enhance creative and intellectual freedom. Granick argued that this Dream of Internet Freedom was dying, choked off by market and government forces of centralization, regulation, and globalization. The speech was extremely popular. Almost 8000 people watched it at Black Hat. It was retweeted, watched and read by tens of thousands of people. Boing Boing called it "the speech that won Black Hat (and DEF CON )."

This year, Granick revisits the state of the Internet Dream. This year’s crypto war developments in the U.S. and U.K. show governments’ efforts to control the design of technologies to ensure surveillance. The developments also show that governments see app stores as a choke point for regulation and control, something that couldn’t easily happen with general purpose computers and laptops but which could be quite effective in a world where most people access the network with mobile devices.

Also in the past year, the European Court of Justice embraced blocking orders and ISP liability in the name of stopping copyright infringement, privacy violations, and unflattering comments from ever being published online. The effect of these developments is to force Internet companies to be global censors on the side of online civility against the free flow of information and opinion. If we want to realize some of the promise of the Internet utopian vision, we are going to have to make some hard political choices and redesign communications technology accordingly. The future could look a lot like TV, or we could work to ensure our technology enshrines individual liberties. This talk will help attendees join that effort.

talks.title: Jake Kouns - Cyber Who Done It: Attribution Analysis Through Arrest History
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Jake Kouns - Cyber Who Done It: Attribution Analysis Through Arrest History.
talks.summary:
There have been over 20,000 data breaches disclosed exposing over 4.8 billion records, with over 4,000 breaches in 2015 alone. It is clear there is no slowdown at all and the state of security is embarrassing. The total cybercrime cost estimates have been astronomical and law enforcement has been struggling to track down even a fraction of the criminals, as usual.

Attribution in computer compromises continues to be a surprisingly complex task that ultimately isn’t definitive in most cases. Rather than focusing on learning from security issues and how companies can avoid these sorts of data breaches in the future, for most media outlets the main topic after a breach continues to be attribution. And if we are honest, the media have painted an "interesting" and varied picture of "hackers" over the years, many of which have caused collective groans or outright rage from the community.

The Arrest Tracker project was started in 2011 as a way to track arrests from all types of "cyber" (drink!) and hacking related incidents. This project aims to track computer intrusion incidents resulting in an arrest, detaining of a person or persons, seizure of goods, or other related activities that are directly linked to computer crimes.

The Arrest Tracker project currently has 936 arrests collected as of 4/23/2016. How does tracking this information help and what does the data tell us? A lot actually! Who is behind these data breaches and what are the demographics such as average age, gender, and nationality? Which day of the week are you most likely to be arrested? How many arrests lead to assisting authorities to arrest others? How many work by themselves versus part of a group? These observations, and a lot more, paint an interesting picture of the computer crime landscape.

talks.title: Crypto and Privacy Village - Mat Caughron, Trey Blalock - Revocation the Frailty of PKI
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Crypto and Privacy Village - Mat Caughron, Trey Blalock - Revocation the Frailty of PKI.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Crypto and Privacy Village presentation, speakers Matt (Mat Caughron) and Trey Blalock discuss the operational realities, scalability challenges, and privacy implications of certificate revocation in public key infrastructure (PKI). Rather than disclosing zero-day vulnerabilities, the presentation evaluates how the industry manages distrusting compromised certificates across web browsers, operating systems, and servers, contrasting traditional mechanisms with modern alternatives.

### Key Topics
The speakers trace the history of revocation from direct manual distrust on individual devices to network-based mechanisms. Manual management remains available on operating systems such as macOS (via Keychain and the `security` CLI tool) and Windows GUI tools, but scaling internet trust necessitated automated protocols. Two primary historical mechanisms were examined:
- **Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs):** Bundles of revoked certificates hosted via DER/PEM files defined in RFC 5280. While historically standard, crl files continually expand in size as untrusted certificates accumulate, creating bandwidth and scaling bottlenecks. Some implementations, like Mozilla Firefox, compress and distribute periodic blocklists to mitigate this.
- **Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP):** Designed as an online database-style query over ASN.1/HTTP to check specific certificate statuses in real time. Required for Extended Validation (EV) certificates, OCSP shifts infrastructure burdens to Certificate Authorities (CAs) to maintain high-availability responders.

### Technical Details
- **OCSP Mechanics & Implementation:** The speakers demonstrate retrieving certificate chains, extracting issuer information, and issuing OpenSSL queries directly to responder URIs (e.g., querying DefCon certificate status). While OpenSSL can run lightweight responders, the speakers highlight that commercial CAs predominantly rely on PrimeKey's Enterprise Java Bean Certificate Authority (EJBCA) backed by Java and Oracle, creating a software monoculture.
- **Privacy and Data Leaks:** OCSP queries generate outbound, unencrypted HTTP requests that reveal the client IP address, timestamp, browser user-agent, and the target domain being visited. This effectively exposes browsing histories of HTTPS sites to CA responder operators and network eavesdroppers—posing serious risks to privacy and whistleblowers. Responders utilizing EJBCA audit logging can record entire transaction streams.
- **Failure Modes and Caching:** OCSP checks rely on client and responder validity caching windows. Responses distinguish between hard fail (terminating connections on query failure) and soft fail (allowing connections through if responders are unreachable), the behavior of which varies widely across operating systems and browsers.
- **SSH Key Revocation Lists (KRLs):** The speakers highlight that revocation concepts extend beyond TLS. OpenSSH 6.8 introduced Key Revocation Lists (`RevokeKeys` directive) to track compromised SSH key hashes.
- **Emerging Alternatives:** To address OCSP drawbacks, the industry explores short-lived certificates (valid for days or weeks, aligning with automated issuance like Mozilla's ACME project), OCSP stapling / OCSP Must-Staple (where servers fetch and bundle signed status proofs), and Google's Certificate Transparency (CT) public logs.

### Takeaways
The speakers emphasize that the capacity to revoke trust reliably is as crucial as the capacity to establish it. However, real-time revocation protocols like OCSP represent significant privacy liabilities. Relying parties and administrators should recognize that client implementations vary in caching and failure handling, investigate emerging solutions like OCSP Must-Staple and Certificate Transparency, and maintain vigilance over certificate chains.

talks.title: Nate Cardozo - Crypto State of the Law
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Nate Cardozo - Crypto State of the Law.
talks.summary: Strong end-to-end encryption is legal in the United States today, thanks to our victory in what’s come to be known as the Crypto Wars of the 1990s. But in the wake of Paris and San Bernardino, there is increasing pressure from law enforcement and policy makers, both here and abroad, to mandate so-called backdoors in encryption products. In this presentation, I will discuss in brief the history of the first Crypto Wars, and the state of the law coming into 2016. I will then discuss what happened in the fight between Apple and the FBI in San Bernardino and the current proposals to weaken or ban encryption, covering proposed and recently enacted laws in New York, California, Australia, India, and the UK. Finally, I will discuss possible realistic outcomes to the Second Crypto Wars, and give my predictions on what the State of the Law will be at the end of 2016.

We’ll survey the arguments being advanced by prosecutors, the resulting case law, and the ethical dilemmas facing technology companies. The session will cover the rights and civil liberties we’ve already lost, and review the current threats to our collective freedoms. We’ll cover what an individual needs to know if they want to avoid compelled decryption, and keep their data private. talks.title: Crypto and Privacy Village - Alisha Kloc
talks.teaser: Logs Aren't Enough analyzes Crypto and Privacy Village - Alisha Kloc.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Defcon's Crypto and Privacy Village, Alicia Kloc—a privacy Technical Program Manager at Lyft with prior security engineering experience at Google and Boeing—argues that traditional security logs are fundamentally insufficient for detecting insider abuse of user data. Standard security logging focuses on unauthorized system breaches (external attacks), capturing when, where, and what occurred. However, defending user data from employees requires distinguishing legitimate business activity from internal data misuse, such as stalking, curiosity, or fraud. To bridge this gap, organizations must implement dedicated Data Access Logs (DALs) that capture internal user data interactions and establish formal investigation processes.

### Key Topics
- **Security Logs vs. Data Access Logs (DALs):** Traditional security logs track machine and authentication events (e.g., SSH login attempts), recording timestamp, hostname, and action. DALs must specifically record human interactions with user data and introduce critical context: the actor (who), the target user (whom), and the business justification (why).
- **Prevention and Foundation:** Logging only records actions after the fact. Organizations must first establish preventive measures: clear job role definitions, enforcing strict and updated Access Control Lists (ACLs), segmenting databases (e.g., breaking large monoliths into separate tables/databases per function), assigning unique credentials instead of shared root/admin access, and drafting clear internal access policies.
- **Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) vs. Custom Systems:** Organizations building their own tools can directly incorporate DAL logging and justification prompts. For COTS software, teams can deploy custom intermediate administrative front-ends or adapt existing vendor logging mechanisms.
- **Investigation Team and Legal Alignment:** Logs require monitoring and analysis. Organizations need dedicated analysts (either as an independent team or within an existing Security Operations Center) equipped with automated parsing rules and strong legal support, as handling employee abuse involves potential terminations and employment law implications.

### Technical Details
- **Six Core DAL Attributes:** A complete DAL requires logging: `who` (the actor/human making the access; machine tasks and users accessing their own data should be omitted), `whom` (the target user or users), `what` (the specific user data accessed), `where` (the specific interface, tool, or database queried), `when` (timestamp), and `why` (the business justification, such as a customer support ticket or bug ID).
- **Query vs. Target Logging:** DALs must track both the input query (e.g., search text, SQL query, clicked link) and the resulting target account. Discrepancies between what was searched (e.g., William Gates from Wyoming) and what was accessed (e.g., Bill Gates) serve as primary indicators of malicious intent.
- **Logging Placement:** DALs should be captured as close to the source actor as possible—specifically in the front-end application interface—because backend authorization/database servers typically lack contextual business justifications and user search queries.
- **Data Structure & Granularity:** DAL events can be formatted in Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), XML, or Syslog strings. When an actor uses multiple tools, each actor-tool-query event must generate a distinct log entry rather than bundling accesses under a single blanket justification.
- **Detection Indicators:** Analysts and automated parsing rules should flag red flags, including keyboard-walk justifications (e.g., "ASDF", "1234"), identical surnames between actor and target, accesses to high-profile accounts (presidents, executives, public figures), repeated deep-dive tool usage over time, and attempts to access friend or family accounts without official tickets.

### Takeaways
Relying exclusively on standard security logs leaves organizations blind to internal employee data abuse. Establishing user data privacy requires capturing granular Data Access Logs with mandatory business justifications, implementing least-privilege architectural controls, and maintaining an investigation team backed by legal counsel to enforce accountability and maintain user trust.

talks.title: Marc Newlin - MouseJack: Injecting Keystrokes into Wireless Mice
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Marc Newlin - MouseJack: Injecting Keystrokes into Wireless Mice.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Marc Newlin, a security researcher at Bastille Networks, presents findings on 16 vulnerabilities affecting wireless keyboards and mice from 16 vendors across 4 different transceiver families. The vulnerabilities primarily target non-Bluetooth proprietary wireless protocols and include keystroke injection, keystroke sniffing, forced pairing, and denial-of-service attacks. Most affected devices cannot be patched due to hardware limitations such as one-time programmable (OTP) memory.

## Key Vulnerabilities
Newlin identifies three main keystroke injection scenarios: (1) unencrypted keystrokes sent directly to USB dongles, (2) encrypted keystrokes generated without knowledge of AES keys due to poor implementation, and (3) forced pairing attacks allowing attackers to pair malicious devices with victim dongles. Additional vulnerabilities include keystroke sniffing on completely unencrypted protocols and malicious macro programming affecting gaming mice like the Logitech G900.

## Technical Details
Most vulnerable devices use Nordic semiconductor nRF24L transceiver chips configured with identical parameters: 2 Mbps data rate, 5-byte address length, 2-byte CRC, and automatic ACK/retransmit. This standardization enables a single fuzzer and decoder to work across all affected devices. The Logitech Unifying protocol, identified as the most complex, implements AES encryption only for standard keyboard keys while leaving mice, multimedia keys, and some data unencrypted. Counter-mode AES implementations prove vulnerable because many devices accept duplicate counter values, allowing attackers to generate arbitrary encrypted keystrokes through XOR operations with observed ciphertext. Completely unencrypted protocols from MOSART, Signia, and GE/Jasco transceivers transmit keystroke data in cleartext. White-label hardware from OEMs like Chicony contributes to the vulnerability's breadth, with vendors unaware of underlying protocol weaknesses.

## Affected Vendors
All major vendors in the market show vulnerabilities: Logitech, HP, Microsoft, Dell, Anker, Lenovo, Toshiba, Amazon, Gigabyte, Insignia, ShhhMouse, HDE, GE/Jasco, RadioShack, EagleTec, and Kensington. Notification timeline: November disclosure to Amazon, Dell, Lenovo; February public disclosure for Logitech; April disclosure of bypasses; responses varied from firmware updates to no response.

## Tools and Demonstration
Newlin developed custom firmware for Logitech Unifying dongles enabling keystroke injection attacks without expensive Crazy Radio hardware. Range testing achieved 225 meters with directional antenna. Practical demonstrations included forced pairing to create new paired devices and keystroke injection to execute commands (opening command prompt and adding user accounts). An Android app capable of detecting and classifying wireless devices is planned for release.

## Takeaways
The vulnerabilities represent an industry-wide problem affecting consumer, enterprise, and gaming devices. Hardware design choices prevent retroactive patching for most devices in the field. Vendors lack visibility into OEM protocol implementations. Bluetooth devices were explicitly not evaluated, leaving that attack surface unaddressed in this research.

Nearly every piece of modern home theater equipment has HDMI support and most modern mobile devices actually have HDMI-capable outputs, though it may not be obvious. Lurking inside most modern HDMI-compatible devices is something called HDMI-CEC, or Consumer Electronics Control. This is the functionality that allows a media device to, for example, turn on your TV and change the TV’s input. That doesn’t sound interesting, but as we'll see in this presentation, there are some very surprising things an attacker can do by exploiting CEC software implementations. talks.title: David An - When the Secretary of State says Please Stop Hacking Us
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding David An - When the Secretary of State says Please Stop Hacking Us.
talks.summary: Two major roadblocks in cyber diplomacy are the "attribution problem," and the related "disclosure dilemma." If there is indeed an attribution problem--when a country cannot be sure which other state is hacking it because a third country could be using it as a proxy--then a country could never accuse another countries of state-sponsored cyber attacks. Yet, countries routinely accuse others of cyber attacks, the public sees this in newspapers almost every day, and it is often an important topic in bilateral dialogues. Furthermore, the disclosure dilemma occurs when a country has both incentives and disincentives to disclose details on how it was hacked. On one hand, evidence will prove its case, but on another hand, evidence will make the attacker more savvy and careful not to repeat the same mistakes next time. Disclosure could create a stronger adversary. These are major concerns in the practice of cyber diplomacy today.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Christian Frichot - Hooked: Browser Meshed Networks with WebRTC and BeEF.
talks.summary:
One of the biggest issues with BeEF is that each hooked browser has to talk to your BeEF server. To try and avoid detection, you often want to try and obfuscate or hide your browsers, particularly if you're heavily targeting a single organization. Don’t worry Internet-friends, those crazy pioneers at Google, Mozilla and Opera have solved this problem for you with the introduction of Web Real-Time Communications (WebRTC). Initially designed to allow browsers to stream multimedia to each other, the spec has made its way into most Chrome and Firefox browsers, not to mention it’s enabled by default.

Using this bleeding-edge web technology, we can now mesh all those hooked browsers, funnelling all your BeEF comms through a single sacrificial beach-head. Leveraging WebRTC technologies (such as STUN/TURN and even the fact the RTC-enabled browsers on local subnets can simply UDP each other), meshing browsers together can really throw a spanner into an incident-responders work. The possibilities for a browser-attacker are fairly endless, channeling comms through a single browser, or, making all the browsers communicate with each other in round-robin. This is just another tool tucked into your belt to try and initiate and maintain control over browsers.

This presentation will present a background into WebRTC, and then demonstrate the WebRTC BeEF extension. (Bloody JavaScript...)

talks.title: Colby Moore
talks.teaser: Spread Spectrum Satcom Hacking examines Colby Moore.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Colby Moore details his security research into reverse engineering and exploiting the GlobalStar simplex data service—a bent-pipe satellite network used broadly across consumer and enterprise sectors. Aiming to complete the project on a budget under $1,000, Moore demonstrated how an attacker can passively intercept, despread, decode, and actively spoof or clone satellite transmissions used by tracking systems, emergency beacons, and SCADA infrastructure.

### Key Topics
- **Satellite Architecture and Simplex Data Service**: GlobalStar relies on Low Earth Orbit (LEO) bent-pipe satellites that repeat uplinked signals at around 1.6 GHz down to terrestrial ground stations. Simplex transmissions are unidirectional, repeating packets multiple times to compensate for the lack of bidirectional handshakes.
- **Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS)**: GlobalStar simplex channels use DSSS with Binary Phase Shift Keying (BPSK). Moore explains how narrow-band data is spread across wider bandwidth using pseudorandom noise (PN) sequences, providing processing gain and Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) capabilities.
- **Signal Recovery and Demodulation**: Using public FCC filings, academic papers, and leaked Axon spec sheets, Moore identified critical transmission parameters (a 255-chip PN sequence at 1.25 Mchips/s and a ~100 bps data rate). Using software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, he captured raw IQ samples and recovered the global PN code used across devices.
- **Packet Inspection and Vulnerabilities**: The recovered packets lacked encryption, digital signatures, or integrity protections beyond a basic checksum. Data payloads plainly exposed hardware identifiers and GPS latitude/longitude coordinates.
- **Cloning and Injection**: Beyond radio-frequency spoofing, Moore found an uncalled internal debug console (`writeESN`) inside GlobalStar's macOS update utility for Spot Trace devices, enabling trivial hardware serial number cloning.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Setup**: Hardware was assembled under budget using an Ettus USRP SDR (~$600), an antenna with left-hand circular polarization sourced from eBay, and a low-noise amplifier (Mini-Circuits, ~$150).
- **Signal Processing Flow**: The receiver sampled at 4 MHz (resampled/interpolated to 5 MHz) to maintain an integer number of samples per chip. Moore used Python and custom signal-processing scripts to slide and correlate the incoming signal against the 255-chip PN code. Once correlation peaks were locked and phase/frequency differential was corrected, mixing the incoming signal with the recovered PN sequence despread the data back into a narrow-band BPSK signal around 100 Hz.
- **Packet Decoding & Spoofing**: Despread bits were low-pass filtered and run through a PSK demodulator. The decoded binary matched the published packet format, beginning with a preamble, device ID, payload (latitude and longitude encoded as binary integers multiplied by a degree-per-count value), and a checksum. Uplink transmission requires only ~0.2 watts of power and an amplifier.

### Takeaways
- **Lack of Encryption in Critical Systems**: Simplex networks frequently protect data solely through security by obscurity, leaving critical infrastructure, aviation tracking (e.g., FAA VFR flight plans via Lockheed Martin), SCADA systems (pipelines, oil, gas, water sensors), and personal emergency beacons exposed to eavesdropping and spoofing.
- **Patching Difficulties**: Because bent-pipe satellites and deployed simplex transmitters lack bidirectional communication or over-the-air firmware update mechanisms, field remediation is extremely difficult. The only viable path forward is applying application-layer encryption prior to transmission.
- **Vendor Response**: Moore reported findings to GlobalStar approximately 180 days prior, but noted that defensive statements asserting passive monitoring were insufficient given the purely passive, undetectable nature of satellite sniffing.

talks.title: Jason Haddix - How to Shot Web: Web and mobile hacking in 2015
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Jason Haddix - How to Shot Web: Web and mobile hacking in 2015.
talks.summary:
# Overview
Jason Haddix, Director at Bug Crowd, presents practical web and mobile hacking methodology focused on bug bounty hunting. The talk emphasizes the philosophical and tactical differences between rapid vulnerability discovery (bug bounties) and comprehensive penetration testing, using an 80/20 rule favoring speed and target selection over exhaustive coverage.

# Discovery & Reconnaissance
Haddix outlines a multi-stage discovery process beginning with subdomain enumeration using recon-ng, which scrapes Google, Bing, and NetCraft for domain-related subdomains. He recommends targeting underassessed properties: recently acquired companies, mobile versions, subdomains, and redesigned sections rather than flagship applications already under security testing. Port scanning is demonstrated as effective (citing an 8,000+ dollar Facebook bug found via port scanning). Directory brute-forcing uses wordlists compiled by internet-wide crawling (raft, robots.txt parsing, and OWASP SecLists). Platform identification leverages headers, JavaScript analysis (via Retire.js for known vulnerabilities), and WordPress plugin scanning (Wpscan). Open-source intelligence includes exploit databases, Shodan/Censys, and Wikipedia acquisition records. Ben (Haddix's colleague) contributed an automated framework aggregating 200+ bug bounty program scopes and running subdomain discovery against them via recon-ng and Intrepid framework.

# Vulnerability Testing Techniques
**Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)**: Multi-context payload bypass strings designed to evade filters across different web contexts; tested in search parameters, customizable themes, imported third-party data (e.g., Facebook imports), file upload names, and Flash parameters.

**SQL Injection**: Blind SQL injection is predominant; SQLmap with tamper scripts and DBMS-specific syntax used to bypass blacklists. Common injection points: order, sort, filter parameters.

**File Upload & Inclusion Attacks**: Local File Inclusion (LFI) tests server filesystem interaction using common parameters (file, path, locale); malicious uploads include polyglot files (PDFs that are also ZIPs) and DOS attacks (sparse files). Remote File Inclusion (RFI) targets parameter values like filename, folder, template; common bypasses involve URL encoding tricks.

**CSRF Bypass**: Four primary techniques—removing the token, removing the parameter value, adding headers, or changing request method. Tool CsFixer automates detection across an entire domain.

**Privilege Escalation & Logic Flaws**: Testing low-privilege user access to admin functions (add/delete users, payment receipt viewing, account info changes) using Burp AutoRepeater. Logic flaws include step manipulation (skipping checkout steps), negative quantity exploitation, and receipt/payment manipulation.

**Mobile Testing**: Frida used to inspect iOS data storage, encryption values, and file handling.

# Tools & Resources
Core tools: Recon-ng (reconnaissance), Burp Suite (request manipulation and CSRF testing), SQLmap (SQL injection automation), Retire.js (JavaScript vulnerability profiling), Wpscan (WordPress scanning), OWASP SecLists (fuzz strings), Shodan/Censys (internet-wide service discovery), Intrepid framework (API intelligence gathering), Frida (mobile inspection), and custom Ruby/Python scripts.

# Practical Workflow
Haddix demonstrates a 15-30 minute testing window: register account, reset password, test forms, examine security cookies, enumerate user IDs in URLs, test file uploads, and apply fuzz strings. Time-limited testing balances breadth with viability of findings.

# Key Takeaways
Bug bounty success prioritizes target selection and rapid vulnerability discovery over comprehensive assessment. Subdomain enumeration and acquisition tracking yield underexplored attack surfaces. Multi-context bypass payloads, automated scripting, and tool chains (Burp with tamper scripts, custom detection tools) amplify findings. Logic flaws and step manipulation remain underappreciated but lucrative vulnerabilities.

Then, an astute researcher discovered that the OSX/XSLCmd malware which pre-dated the disclosure, exploited this same vulnerability as a 0day! The talk will conclude by examining Apple’s response, a second patch, that appears to squash ‘rootpipe’…for now.

There have been talks that have identified the risks that are caused by the inherent trust between the OS and any device attached by USB. I found in my research that most of the available payloads for the USB rubber ducky would be stopped by common enterprise security solutions. I then set out to create a new exploit that would force the victim to trust my Man-In-The-Middle access point. After my payload is deployed, all Wi-Fi communications will be readable, including usernames, passwords and authentication cookies. The attack will work without the need of elevating privileges, which makes it ideal for corporate environments.

talks.title: Geoff Walton and Dave Kennedy - Pivoting Without Rights: Introducing Pivoter
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Geoff Walton and Dave Kennedy - Pivoting Without Rights: Introducing Pivoter.
talks.summary: One of the most challenging steps of a penetration test is popping something and not having full administrative level rights over the system. Companies are cutting back on administrative level rights for endpoints or how about those times where you popped an external web application and were running as Apache or Network Service? Privilege escalation or pillaging systems can be difficult and require extensive time if successful at all. One of the most challenging aspects around pentesting was the need to have administrative level rights, install your tools, and from there leverage the compromised machine as a pivot point for lateral movement in the network. Well, the time has changed. Introducing Pivoter – a reverse connection transparent proxy that supports the ability to pivot with ease. Pivoter is a full transparent proxy that supports the ability to use limited rights on a system to pivot to other systems and attack transparently from your system at home. Port scans, exploits, brute forcing, anything you could do like you were on that network is now available through Pivoter. As part of this talk, we’ll be releasing a new Metasploit module for shell DLL injection for AV evasion, a Linux version of Pivoter, a Windows version of Pivoter, and a PowerShell version of Pivoter. msf> run pivoter -> pentest as if you are on the internal network even if you don’t have admin rights. Also during this talk, we’ll be releasing a new major release of the Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET) which incorporates Pivoter into the payload delivery system.

talks.title: Packet Capture Village - Brian Wohlwinder and Andrew Beard
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Packet Capture Village - Brian Wohlwinder and Andrew Beard - I See You.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At the Packet Hacking Village during DEF CON 23, Andrew Beard of Fidelis Cybersecurity reflected on passive network monitoring conducted at DEF CON 22. In connection with the Wall of Sheep, Fidelis deployed a commercial off-the-shelf network visibility appliance hooked up to the village's common data tap. The passive listener captured approximately 500 MB of metadata over three days (August 8–10), representing more than six million transactions. The presentation reviewed the surprisingly high prevalence of plain text credentials, improperly secured mobile devices, and sensitive personal and financial data exposed on an untrusted conference network.

### Key Topics
- **Traffic Composition and Protocol Breakdown**: Unencrypted HTTP and SSL/TLS made up the vast bulk of traffic. Contrary to expectations for DEF CON, VPN usage was remarkably low (under 7%), with more plain text Teredo IPv6 tunnels observed than actual VPNs (mostly OpenVPN, IPsec, and proprietary options). Beard speculated that attendees who knew how to secure their connections likely avoided conference Wi-Fi entirely.
- **The "Fish in a Barrel" Protocols**: Mail protocols (POP3, IMAP, and SMTP), FTP, Telnet, and IRC routinely exposed credentials in the clear. Plain text credentials appear in the initial packets of these sessions during authentication before any content transfer occurs.
- **Disproportionate Risk of Email**: While mail traffic constituted only a tiny slice of total network volume (grouped in the <7% "other" category), POP3, IMAP, and SMTP accounted for roughly 75% of all scraped credentials. This disparity stemmed largely from mobile devices (predominantly iPhones) configured years prior that continuously beaconed in the background every 10–15 minutes without user awareness.
- **Provider Implementations**: Major providers (such as Google, Yahoo, AOL, and Outlook.com) automatically mandate or probe for SSL/TLS in client configurations, preventing credential exposure on the Wall of Sheep. In contrast, smaller or third-party email providers lacked enforced encryption, leaving users vulnerable unless they manually enabled SSL.

### Technical Details
- **Plain Text and Encoded Credentials**: POP3, IMAP, and FTP transmitted authentication commands directly over the wire in plain text. HTTP traffic frequently leaked credentials via query strings in URLs or through HTTP Basic Authentication (`Authorization: Basic`), which simply uses base64 encoding rather than encryption. Tools like Bro were highlighted for scripting extraction of URLs and base64-decoded credentials from network streams.
- **Session Key Hijacking**: In one observed case involving an office supply and toner retailer, initial authentication used HTTPS, but subsequent requests reverted to unencrypted HTTP while transmitting a session key in an `API` header formatted as basic authorization. Replaying this header within the session timeout window granted full access to the user's active session and stored credit card info.
- **Data Leakage in Applications**: An unencrypted URL payload from the Taobao mobile app was found beaconing default home location coordinates before obtaining a GPS lock.
- **Sensitive Data in Email**: The speakers highlighted two major incidents involving unencrypted email: an attached 2014 W-4 tax form containing an employee's full name, home address, signature, and Social Security number; and a message thread involving a representative of the band The Orb coordinating the pickup of a $6,500 cash or check balance in Las Vegas, creating an immediate social engineering risk.

### Takeaways
- **Defense in Depth**: Securing data solely in transit is insufficient if sensitive materials sit unencrypted at rest in an email inbox. Sensitive attachments should use document-level encryption (such as AES-encrypted ZIP files, PGP, or S/MIME).
- **Audit Mobile Settings**: Users should verify that email clients explicitly require SSL/TLS across incoming and outgoing servers rather than assuming background traffic is secure.
- **Zero Trust on Networks**: Every network must be treated as inherently untrusted, particularly public networks and conference Wi-Fi environments where passive sniffers and taps operate.

talks.title: BioHacking Village - Walter Powell - Parallels in BioSec and InfoSec
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BioHacking Village - Walter Powell - Parallels in BioSec and InfoSec.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this BioHacking Village presentation, speaker Walter Powell (handle Mr. Brimley) explores the foundational parallels between biological security (biosecurity) and information security (infosec). Drawing from an extensive background of five years in information security, nineteen years in IT, and prior agricultural farming experience, Powell argues that professionals in either field already possess the operational mindset needed to succeed in the other. Both domains operate under a pervasive threat environment with rapidly evolving, adaptive threats that require systematic defenses.

### Key Topics
- **Shared Language and Metaphors:** The presenter highlights overlapping terminology between cybersecurity and biology, such as viruses, worms, infections, and watering hole attacks. For instance, a computer virus behaves like a biological virus by acting as an obligatory parasite needing a host to replicate, whereas worms self-propagate independently.
- **Pervasive and Adaptive Threat Environments:** Whether dealing with billions of environmental bacteria and shifting immune responses or hostile Internet traffic evading security countermeasures, both fields manage environments where external forces continuously evolve against existing protections.
- **The Four Core Defensive Concepts:** Defense in both fields is structured around four essential pillars: isolation, sanitation, monitoring, and education.
- **Real-World Case Study (Jeni's Splendid Ice Creams):** Powell uses an outbreak of *Listeria* at Jeni's Splendid Ice Creams to demonstrate systemic failure in basic hygiene, cross-contamination prevention, and testing programs, comparing the organizational negligence to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) breach.
- **Contrasts and Consequences:** The speaker contrasts biosecurity and infosec in terms of threat delivery, error margins, and the gravity of failure, noting that biosecurity enforces significantly harsher legal, operational, and life-safety consequences.

### Technical Details
Powell structures practical defensive workflows across four shared operational categories:
1. **Isolation:** Creating fully controlled, segregated environments. In infosec, this involves firewalls and application proxies to isolate production environments from the broader Internet; in biosecurity, it entails physically isolated, sterile workspaces.
2. **Sanitation:** Maintaining clean systems to remove vulnerabilities. In infosec, this encompasses vulnerability patch management, up-to-date antivirus definitions, pruning decommissioned accounts, and maintaining access control lists (ACLs). In biosecurity, it equates to standard sterile procedure, including wiping surfaces with bleach solutions and autoclaving glassware.
3. **Monitoring:** Actively tracking the integrity of the environment. In infosec, this is achieved by watching intrusion detection systems (IDS) and host intrusion prevention systems (IPS). In biosecurity, it relies on checklists tracking sterilization dates, spill logs, and shift cleaning schedules.
4. **Education:** Enforcing procedures against human shortcutting. In infosec, this means preventing risky behaviors like plugging in unknown CDs or disabling USB devices. In biosecurity, it means enforcing strict hygiene rules, such as mandatory hand washing and changing coveralls after breaks.

These principles are illustrated through the Jeni's Ice Cream incident, where Wisconsin regulators detected *Listeria*—an environmental bacterium resilient to freezing. An FDA inspection revealed that lack of testing, poor sanitation, grime, and unmanaged risks (such as allowing employees to garden during breaks without subsequent hand-washing or coverall changes) led to contamination traced to a single pint-filling machine. The result was a $2.5 million product recall, suspended operations, and facility rental expenses.

### Takeaways
While the defensive paradigms are closely aligned, biosecurity allows much thinner margins for error due to over a century of agricultural safety precedents compared to roughly two decades of serious infosec practices. Infosec faces remote attack surfaces, but failures primarily result in financial or reputational damage. In contrast, biosecurity requires physical presence, yet failures directly endanger human lives. Consequently, biosecurity features aggressive automatic responses (such as culling entire herds or issuing immediate complete recalls) and carries severe legal ramifications, ranging from negligence lawsuits and fraud charges to involuntary manslaughter or depraved indifference. Powell concludes that software EULAs disclaiming all liability have no equivalent in biology, meaning infosec practitioners entering biohacking must respect the significantly higher stakes of physical systems.

talks.title: Crypto and Privacy Village - Marina
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Crypto and Privacy Village - Marina - Hacking Quantum Cryptography.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at the Crypto and Privacy Village, Marina, a physicist and security engineer, explores how fundamental quantum mechanics underpins both the threats and defensive capabilities of quantum computing. Framing the universe as a massive quantum system, she demystifies core physics principles to explain why quantum computers threaten current public key cryptography and how quantum mechanics simultaneously offers a physical solution through quantum key distribution.

### Key Topics
- **Foundations of Quantum Mechanics**: The historical progression from classical thermodynamics and the ultraviolet catastrophe to Max Planck's energy quanta, Albert Einstein's photoelectric effect (light as photons), and Louis de Broglie's wave-particle duality for matter.
- **Wave Functions and Measurement**: Mathematical representations of quantum states, superposition (e.g., Schrödinger's cat), orthogonal bases, and wave function collapse upon observation/probing, illustrated using a three-polarizer experiment.
- **Qubits and Superposition**: Moving from classical bits to two-dimensional Hilbert space states (visualized on the Bloch sphere), scaling parallel computational capacity exponentially ($2^n$) across coupled qubits.
- **Cryptographic Implications (Shor's Algorithm)**: How Shor's algorithm leverages the Quantum Fourier Transform to rapidly find periods and factor large prime numbers, threatening classical public-key cryptosystems like RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography without forward secrecy.
- **Quantum Cryptography & BB84 Protocol**: Utilizing the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the no-cloning concept to enable secure key exchange over a quantum channel where eavesdropping introduces detectable errors.
- **Engineering Challenges**: Practical obstacles in maintaining coherence and isolating multi-qubit systems from environmental decoherence, alongside various physical implementations (ion traps, superconducting qubits, quantum dots).

### Technical Details
The speaker demonstrates how quantum states are represented in bra-ket notation and manipulated across orthogonal measurement bases. In an illustrative experiment using polarizing filters, inserting a 45-degree polarizer between horizontal and vertical polarizers restores light transmission because the diagonal filter represents a linear combination of the two states, effectively changing the measurement basis.

In cryptography, Shor's algorithm utilizes quantum interference via the Quantum Fourier Transform so that incorrect answers cancel out while correct periodic factors form constructive peaks, allowing rapid integer factorization. To counter quantum computing threats, the BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol allows Alice and Bob to establish a shared secret. Alice sends single photons randomly polarized across two non-orthogonal bases (rectilinear and diagonal). Bob independently measures each photon using a randomly chosen basis. Over an authenticated classical channel, they compare which bases they used, discarding mismatched instances and retaining matching measurements (roughly 50%) as their key.

Because observing a quantum state collapses its superposition, an eavesdropper (Eve) attempting to intercept and measure the photons must pick a basis, inadvertently disturbing the quantum states. If Eve measures with the incorrect basis, she introduces errors—lowering Bob's expected agreement rate on check bits to approximately 25% instead of the standard 50%. Alice and Bob can detect this elevated error rate by comparing a subset of parity/test bits over the classical channel.

### Takeaways
While building fault-tolerant quantum computers remains a significant engineering challenge—particularly combating decoherence and environmental noise—experimental progress is advancing rapidly across academia, industry (such as IBM), and intelligence agencies. Because classical public-key cryptography lacking forward secrecy will be rendered insecure once large-scale quantum computers arrive, security practitioners must understand quantum mechanical fundamentals and prepare for transitions to quantum-safe alternatives like quantum key distribution.

We'll even talk about creative ways to merge algorithms to further increase entropy and key strength. If you've ever wanted to learn how crypto can give you an advantage as a hacker, then this talk is for you. talks.title: IoT Village - K Reid Wrightman
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding IoT Village - K Reid Wrightman - Vulnerability Inheritance in PLCs.
talks.summary:
K Reid Wrightman from Digital Bond Labs discusses vulnerability inheritance in programmable logic controllers (PLCs), focusing on insecure third-party libraries that vendors bundle into their products. He challenges the narrow definition of vulnerabilities that excludes design flaws, arguing that any mechanism allowing unintended system modification should be considered a vulnerability.

The primary focus is CODIS, a ladder logic runtime by 3S Software used by approximately 300 industrial control vendors including Mitsubishi and Bosch. CODIS Version 2 contains multiple critical design flaws: no authentication for uploading ladder logic, unauthenticated ability to start/stop PLCs, directory traversal vulnerabilities allowing arbitrary file access, and processes running with root privileges. These issues enable attackers to upload malicious code (rootkits) without any credentials. Version 3, while using a more complex UDP/TCP protocol, suffers similar problems, including a dangerous CRC verification mechanism that uses packet data as a function pointer index, potentially enabling arbitrary code execution. When Wrightman disclosed these issues, 3S Software acknowledged security was not a priority and added optional authentication they themselves claimed would not stop determined attackers.

Wrightman examines affected vendors including Hitachi (EH-plus controllers using CODIS v3 with no firmware update mechanism) and Sano Deni (running CODIS v2.3 with additional VxWorks backdoor vulnerabilities from 2005). He discovers multiple vendors—Festo, CBA, and others—appear to share OEM firmware, yet none detected security problems before product release, suggesting inadequate internal testing and no meaningful red team involvement.

The second major library discussed is Pronos by KW Software (now Phoenix Contact), which has nearly identical vulnerabilities: unauthenticated logic upload/download and no authentication for process control. Affected vendors include Emerson and Contron, notably including an Iranian indigenous PLC manufacturer.

Wrightman presents internet scanning metrics showing the scale: in 2013, he and Aaron Leverett found 600 CODIS controllers online at ~$1.50 per device cost. By the talk date, Shodan searches reveal 2,200+ controllers directly on the internet for ~1 cent per device. The speaker emphasizes the difficulty in getting ISPs and system owners to take vulnerable systems offline, noting most ISPs decline responsibility and owner cooperation is rare.

Key recommendations include vendors maintaining accurate third-party software component lists, implementing proper firmware update mechanisms addressing design issues rather than just bugs, and conducting red team testing before product release. He criticizes vendors for deflecting responsibility and notes that design flaws in industrial control protocols (such as authentication bypass) persist for years without fixes, unlike traditional bugs which receive quicker patches.

talks.title: FX - Attacking Control Routing and Tunneling Protocols *
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding FX - Attacking Control Routing and Tunneling Protocols *.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Def Con presentation, the speaker examines methods for attacking network control, routing, and tunneling protocols. Beginning from local-area redirection concepts such as ARP spoofing and routing table manipulation, the talk expands into active and passive router discovery, exploitation of dynamic routing protocols (IGRP, RIP, OSPF, and BGP), manipulation of first-hop redundancy protocols (HSRP), and vulnerabilities in unencrypted encapsulation protocols like Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE).

### Key Topics
- **Local Redirection and Discovery:** Local traffic manipulation via tools like Hunt, Ettercap, and THC Parasite, alongside router discovery techniques using CDP, passive listening, IRDP, autonomous system (AS) scanning, and protocol scanning with Nmap.
- **Control and Discovery Protocols:** Abusing IRDP (ICMP Router Discovery Protocol) and ICMP redirects to alter host routing tables, noting implementation differences between Windows and Linux.
- **Dynamic Interior and Exterior Routing Protocols:** Exploiting Cisco's IGRP (lack of authentication, metric manipulation), RIPv1/RIPv2 (broadcast/multicast abuse, cleartext or non-standard authentication, routing loops), OSPF (link-state advertisement manipulation and design flaws), and BGP-4 (TCP session attacks, underlying IGP targeting, and route injection).
- **First-Hop Redundancy (HSRP):** Hijacking virtual router IP and MAC addresses via multicast priority manipulation and exploiting weak cleartext authentication.
- **Tunneling and GRE Exploitation:** Piercing private RFC 1918 networks by encapsulating traffic inside GRE tunnels, bypassing perimeter access filters, and receiving return traffic via routed paths across the Internet.

### Technical Details
- **ARP and Local Redirection:** Demonstrating how ARP replies can be injected to position an attacker in the middle, and how modifying local routing entries can route traffic through intermediate routers even after direct blocks are implemented.
- **IRDP & ICMP Redirects:** IRDP announcements insert routes with specific preferences, which Windows systems readily adopt on boot. ICMP redirect attacks require crafting packets containing the first 64 bits of the offending payload; Windows registers these as `/32` host routes directly in the routing table, whereas Linux stores them inside the `/proc` filesystem.
- **IGRP & RIP Attacks:** IGRP relies on autonomous system numbers up to 65,535 and calculates metrics using delay, hop count, and reliability without authentication. Injecting fake updates allows attackers to steal traffic, redirect sessions to rogue authentication servers, or induce TTL routing loops. RIPv1 broadcasts over UDP port 520, while RIPv2 adds netmasks and multicast support; split horizon with poison reverse fails to prevent loops when only two routers participate.
- **OSPF & BGP:** OSPF utilizes link-state advertisements (LSAs) with built-in "fight back" mechanisms, which can be bypassed by intercepting and modifying LSAs in transit between routers. For BGP-4 (running over TCP port 179), attacks often target the underlying Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) carrying BGP peering traffic or leverage misconfigured BGP community attributes.
- **HSRP Virtual Address Takeover:** Cisco's HSRP coordinates standby routers via multicast hello packets using a cleartext authentication string (up to 8 characters). Injecting packets claiming a higher priority allows an attacker to transparently claim the active virtual IP and virtual MAC address.
- **GRE Tunneling Attack and Live Demo:** The speaker details a scenario where a corporate headquarters connects to a branch office over an unencrypted GRE tunnel to link RFC 1918 private address spaces. By deploying a custom "attack router" that encapsulates packets addressed to an internal target into GRE with the HQ router as the source, perimeter firewalls accept and decapsulate the packet. Return traffic routes via default gateways and exits back out to the Internet, effectively making supposedly unreachable private addresses reachable. A live demonstration using Cisco routers and a tool named Viper illustrates this attack.

### Takeaways
- Routing and control protocols frequently suffer from weak security mechanisms, relying on plaintext credentials or non-standard authentication schemes.
- First-hop and dynamic routing protocols can be manipulated to redirect, inspect, or disrupt traffic transparently to client endpoints.
- Unencrypted encapsulation mechanisms such as GRE do not offer perimeter isolation, and private IP addressing schemes (RFC 1918) do not provide security against tunneling attacks.

talks.title: Cult of the Dead Cow
talks.teaser: Activism Panel * analyzes Cult of the Dead Cow.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at a cybersecurity conference by the Cult of the Dead Cow (cDc), this panel discussion—titled "Hacktivism and Human Rights: Using Technology to Raise the Bar"—bridges the gap between the hacking community and international human rights advocacy. Introduced by Reid Fleming and featuring a keynote by Dr. Patrick Ball (Deputy Director of the Science and Human Rights Program at the American Association for the Advancement of Science, AAAS), alongside panelists Greg Walton, Drunken Master, and Deth Veggie, the session defines hacktivism not as destructive disruption or cyberterrorism, but as the constructive application of science, large-scale data analysis, and software development to defend human rights and speak truth to power.

### Key Topics
- **Redefining Hacktivism:** The speakers explicitly distinguish constructive hacktivism from cyberterrorism, information warfare, or arbitrary denial-of-service attacks against repressive regimes. They emphasize using technology to uphold human rights grounded in international agreements such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
- **Scientific Data and Quantitative Analysis:** Dr. Patrick Ball illustrates how anecdotal evidence of human rights abuses can easily be dismissed by repressive governments as rogue actions or crossfire. However, aggregating massive datasets—such as documenting over 200,000 killings in Guatemala or tens of thousands of violations in El Salvador—provides statistically defensible proof that atrocities are systematic state policy, including genocide.
- **Targeted Advocacy vs. Mass Disruption:** Indiscriminate actions like spamming or mail-bombing embassies are easily filtered and dismissed as undisciplined. Effective pressure requires disciplined, focused strategies coordinated with established human rights groups that understand institutional levers and reformist dynamics.
- **The Hacktivismo Declaration and Tooling:** Discussion covers the release of the Hacktivismo Declaration, an effort grounded in international human rights covenants to advocate for anti-censorship and free expression, as well as upcoming tools like Peekabooty and Martus.

### Technical Details
- **Relational Databases for Accountability:** In El Salvador, Dr. Ball's team documented over 9,000 testimonies, 17,000 victims, and 29,000 violations alongside 14,000 career history segments of military officers. Executing large relational SQL-style joins between violation records and command timelines generated individual statistical dossiers on officers, directly tying senior commanders to hundreds of executions and disappearances, ultimately forcing roughly 100 officers out of power.
- **Historical Field Implementations and Cryptography:** Earlier field databases (such as CIIDH in Guatemala) utilized 40-table relational structures in FoxPro for DOS on monochrome Toshiba 386 laptops, relying on PGP, PKZIP, disk wiping utilities, and sneakernet aggregation. A lost laptop during operations resulted in zero data leakage due to rigorous cryptographic discipline.
- **Usability Constraints (Ellison's Law):** Carl Ellison’s observation is highlighted: the user base for strong cryptography declines by half with every additional keystroke or click required. Technical tools must be simple for non-technical grassroots field workers to operate.
- **The Martus Project:** An open-source (GPL), Java-based cross-platform client-server project designed to securely record testimony text, encrypt it locally to prevent data loss from hardware theft or destruction, and automatically replicate encrypted data across remote servers with optional public web-searching capabilities. It is being localized for languages including Khmer, Tamil, and Sinhala via Unicode.
- **Peekabooty:** An upcoming peer-to-peer anti-censorship client developed under the Hacktivismo initiative to bypass nation-state internet filtering on low-spec hardware. The panel debates open-source peer review versus adversary discovery dynamics during rollout.

### Takeaways
The panel emphasizes that technical skills—such as writing Perl scripts, developing privacy-preserving tools, stripping embedded tracking IDs from documents, improving document translators, and securing data management systems—are among the most valuable donations hackers can make to human rights organizations. Hackers are urged to engage constructively with established civil liberties organizations (such as EFF, EPIC, CDT, and CPSR) and human rights networks, applying their skills to build resilient, freedom-respecting software.

At DEF CON 24, DARPA will challenge machines to play this game for the first time, with the winner taking home a $2 million prize. This talk will include a first public look at the machines, teams, technology, and visualization behind Cyber Grand Challenge. The technology: machines that discover bugs and build patches? Visualization: the product of CTF players working with game designers, this talk will include a live interactive demo of a graphical debugger for everyone that will let an audience follow along in real time. The machines: we’re bringing high performance computing to the DEF CON stage. The event: In 2016, machines will Capture the Flag! Follow DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge on Twitter: #DARPACGC

talks.title: Dennis Maldonado - Are We Really Safe?
talks.teaser: Bypassing Access Control Systems explores Dennis Maldonado - Are We Really Safe?.
talks.summary:
Dennis Maldonado, security consultant at Kale Consulting and co-founder of Houston Lockport, presents research on critical vulnerabilities in Linear brand access control systems (A1000, A2000, AM3 Plus models). These systems control doors, gates, and barriers at apartment complexes, office buildings, and commercial facilities.

**Key Vulnerabilities:** The systems ship with a hardcoded default password of "123456"—exactly six numeric digits with no rate limiting or lockout mechanism, yielding only one million possible passwords. A single master physical key works across all Linear controllers despite no evidence of users changing the lock. The device enclosure provides direct access to relay buttons that manually open all doors. Commands execute without authentication despite returning no confirmation. All access logs can be remotely deleted to hide evidence. The tamper monitor uses a simple magnet that can be defeated.

**Local Attacks:** Pressing "0" and "2" on the keypad triggers a password prompt; entering the default "123456" followed by specific command sequences (e.g., "31#9999#9999#99#") creates permanent backdoor entry codes in under 10 seconds. Possession of the master key, lock picking, or opening the enclosure allows direct relay manipulation. The tamper switch can be bypassed with a magnet.

**Remote Attacks:** When networked via a serial-to-TCP converter (default port 4660), systems are vulnerable to: (1) brute force password guessing using a Python script that tests common codes then iterates through all possibilities; (2) unauthenticated command execution—commands execute even without sending a password, though no confirmation is returned; (3) relay control to open doors for 2 seconds or lock relays persistently in open/closed states; (4) log deletion by initiating a log download that deletes data from controller memory; (5) password reset via database updates; (6) denial of service by sending incomplete database updates that freeze the device; (7) firmware destruction via overwriting.

**Device Enumeration:** Attackers can locate these systems by sending UDP broadcasts to port 55954 (devices respond), scanning for serial-to-TCP converters on port 4660, or sending password request strings that validate whether devices are Linear controllers and using default credentials.

**Tools Released:** Maldonado developed three open-source tools on GitHub: (1) Access Control Attack Tool—a Python command-line utility accepting serial or IP connections to trigger relays, lock/unlock doors, delete logs, upload configurations, and execute denial of service attacks; (2) Device discovery tool sending UDP broadcasts to identify Linear controllers and validate default password usage; (3) planned nmap and Metasploit modules. All operate over the serial protocol backbone, bypassing the management software (Access Base 2000).

**Architecture:** Linear controllers use a serial communication protocol with hex-encoded strings and checksums. The TCP/IP kit converts serial to TCP connections, enabling remote management. The protocol has a fixed packet header (5A A5), data length fields, node identification, command bytes (01 to 0F for various operations), data payload, and checksum validation.

**Recommendations:** Change default passwords (though limited to 6-digit numeric codes); change physical locks; use direct serial connections instead of networked TCP/IP; enable authentication on serial-to-TCP converters (rarely implemented); keep systems offline unless remote access is essential; implement active alerting for tamper events rather than passive logging.

**Broader Context:** Maldonado emphasizes similar vulnerabilities likely exist across other vendors (Synex, Chamberlain, DoorKing, LiftMaster) but may manifest differently. He frames this research as opening discussion about physical access control security and plans continued research on other systems. The talk highlights that these ubiquitous systems protecting critical infrastructure have been inadequately secured and are easily compromised through local keypad manipulation, master key access, or unauthenticated network commands.

talks.title: Charlie Miller & Chris Valasek - Remote Exploitation of an Unaltered Passenger Vehicle
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Charlie Miller & Chris Valasek - Remote Exploitation of an Unaltered Passenger Vehicle.
talks.summary: Although the hacking of automobiles is a topic often discussed, details regarding successful attacks, if ever made public, are non-comprehensive at best. The ambiguous nature of automotive security leads to narratives that are polar opposites: either we’re all going to die or our cars are perfectly safe. In this talk, we will show the reality of car hacking by demonstrating exactly how a remote attack works against an unaltered, factory vehicle. Starting with remote exploitation, we will show how to pivot through different pieces of the vehicle’s hardware in order to be able to send messages on the CAN bus to critical electronic control units. We will conclude by showing several CAN messages that affect physical systems of the vehicle. By chaining these elements together, we will demonstrate the reality and limitations of remote car attacks.

talks.title: Zoz - And That's How I Lost My Other Eye...Explorations in Data Destruction (Fixed)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Zoz - And That's How I Lost My Other Eye...Explorations in Data Destruction (Fixed).
talks.summary:
### Overview
Inspired by a previous DEF CON 19 presentation by Bruce, Deviant, and Shane on rapid physical data destruction in data centers, speaker Zoz explores aggressive, rapid physical methods to render hard disk drives (HDDs) and solid-state storage unrecoverable within a 1U or multi-U server rack constraint. The experiment aims to satisfy operational criteria: triggering destruction within 60 seconds, containing collateral damage inside the equipment rack, preventing the release of dangerous hazards to human bystanders, and resisting sophisticated laboratory extraction techniques like magnetic force microscopy or forensic reconstruction.

### Key Topics
- **Physical Data Center Threat Models:** Evaluating risks from physical data center raids and endpoint seizures (citing Silk Road and Snowden disclosures), emphasizing that cryptographic protection fails once physical devices and active keys are seized.
- **Thermal Destruction:** Evaluating the practicality of heating magnetic media past the Curie point (1,115°C for cobalt alloys) to permanently erase data.
- **Kinetic and Percussive Methods:** Utilizing mechanical tools, powder-actuated systems, and explosive forces to warp, shatter, or weld platters and casings.
- **Electrical and Inductive Eradication:** Investigating high-voltage discharge and capacitor banks against flash media and integrated circuits.
- **Blast Mitigation and Containment:** Employing common materials to dampen blast shockwaves and hot gases within confined rack spaces.

### Technical Details
Zoz divides the experimental testing into three core approaches:

1. **Thermal Methods:**
   - *Plasma Cutters:* Proved highly effective and easy to contain, piercing drives in approximately 40 seconds. However, disk platters seized thermally rather than continuing to spin, showing that multiple cutter heads would be needed across the drive surface.
   - *Oxygen Injection:* Drilling vent points and injecting oxygen allowed the hard drive metal to combust, though oxygen delivery tubing melted before achieving complete platter consumption.
   - *Thermite and Thermate:* Standard iron thermite (powder and slurries) largely failed to reliably destroy platters due to the immense heat-sinking capacity of aluminum drive chassis. Slurries failed to sustain heat. Pre-inserted thermate (with barium nitrate) and copper thermite produced violent reactions, yet forensic analysis showed significant intact platter sections remained readable.

2. **Kinetic and Explosive Methods:**
   - *Nail Guns:* Both a 0.22-caliber powder-actuated concrete nail gun and a pneumatic cylinder system easily penetrated cast aluminum casings and perforated platters, representing a highly feasible mechanical solution.
   - *High Explosives and Shaped Charges:* Testing examined liquid binary mixtures, linear ring charges, radial shaped charges, and oil well perforators. Heavy detonations compressed and explosively welded platters or shattered casings entirely. Oil well perforators caused extreme penetration, puncturing through steel backing plates. 
   - *Blast Suppression:* Using shaving cream as a compressible foam matrix effectively damped the explosive impulse, shockwave, and flash when detonating charges in a simulated 1U steel enclosure.

3. **Electrical Methods:**
   - *Capacitor Banks & High Voltage:* Applying high voltage directly across flash drive power and ground lines blew flash chips off their circuit boards and decapped microcontrollers, offering potential for flash drive destruction.

### Takeaways
Conventional expectations regarding thermite for drive destruction are often misleading; drive enclosures act as substantial heat sinks that can preserve media beneath thermal crusts. In contrast, mechanical penetration (such as pneumatic or propellant-driven pins) and plasma cutting offer high feasibility in data center footprints. Controlled, damped explosive mechanisms can also achieve complete platter deformation, while high-voltage surges show promise against solid-state media.
