talks.title: Chris Littlebury - Home Alone with localhost: Automating Home Defense
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Chris Littlebury - Home Alone with localhost: Automating Home Defense.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, penetration tester Chris Littlebury explores practical, automated techniques to augment residential physical security without violating legal boundaries regarding booby traps. Drawing from his personal experiences living in high-crime areas and having his vehicle targeted, Littlebury focuses on proactive deterrence: making a home appear continuously occupied, integrating custom sensors with existing monitored alarm systems, defending against RF-based attacks, and generating disorientation tactics to thwart intruders.

### Key Topics
- **Deterrence via Occupancy Simulation:** Exploring the evolution of home automation from early X10 hardware power-line transmission to modern smart bulbs, emphasizing randomized lighting schedules rather than static timers.
- **Smart Lighting and Hardware Integration:** Utilizing Wi-Fi-enabled LED bulbs (such as LIFX and Philips Hue) alongside smart switches (such as Belkin WeMo), and discussing their respective power draws, form factors, and API accessibility via Python and Ruby.
- **Home Defense Server Architecture:** Designing a Raspberry Pi-based central controller that interfaces with hardwired alarm loops, wireless panic buttons, and sensor networks to trigger both subtle automations and emergency alerts.
- **Presence Detection and Adaptive Scheduling:** Tracking occupant presence without manual input by monitoring Wi-Fi beacon frames and MAC addresses using tools like Tshark and Scapy, combined with an automated weather-based cron system.
- **Wireless Threat Detection and Physical Deterrence:** Detecting RF replay attacks or jamming targeting 345 MHz and 900 MHz alarm/Z-Wave bands using radio direction-finding techniques, alongside non-lethal, high-stress deterrents to encourage immediate intruder retreat.

### Technical Details
- **Controller & Infrastructure:** Built around a Raspberry Pi running backend microservices (implemented in Python with Flask or Ruby with Sinatra) hosted on separate ports to avoid single points of failure. An external powered USB hub with a hard drive was utilized for external swap to preserve the SD card against high read/write cycles.
- **Alarm System Bridging:** Littlebury tied the Raspberry Pi directly into standard alarm panel loops (open or closed circuits) via relays, allowing custom PIR sensors or Raspberry Pi outputs to trigger the commercial alarm. He also demonstrated soldering transistors directly across wireless alarm panic buttons to simulate silent panic alarms sent directly to monitoring companies.
- **Lighting Control & Vulnerabilities:** Highlighted LIFX bulbs (1000 lumens, 17W draw) and Philips Hue (8.5W draw), noting their color capabilities and APIs. Littlebury cautioned against WeMo smart switches due to unreliability, cycling vulnerabilities that could pose fire hazards, and odd behavior such as briefly shutting off at midnight.
- **Presence Tracking (Scapy & Tshark):** Rather than aggressive Bluetooth polling (which disrupted device wireless interfaces), Littlebury captured 802.11 beaconing frames. Using a flat file of known device MAC addresses, a Python Scapy script logged observed packet timestamps into a database to infer occupant departure and apply away-mode lighting rules.
- **SmartCron & Direction Finding:** Integrated developer weather APIs to dynamically schedule lighting offsets around daily sunrise, sunset, cloud cover, and UV index. For wireless defense, Littlebury implemented an RF direction-finding system (PicoDopp using the Agrello DF message format) leveraging the Doppler effect across 345 MHz and 900 MHz to pinpoint transmitter bearings outside the residence.
- **Intrusion Deterrence:** Discussed methods to create an inhospitable environment during a break-in, such as strobing every bulb red, triggering 12V solenoids to simulate noises upstairs, and theoretical concepts utilizing 12V-driven model rocket igniters to trip firecrackers sequentially as loud acoustic deterrents.

### Takeaways
Littlebury emphasizes that home defense automation should act as a supplement to professional monitoring rather than a complete replacement. By combining occupancy simulation, presence-aware scheduling, RF direction-finding, and reactive environmental triggers, homeowners can effectively stack the odds in their favor while strictly avoiding dangerous, illegal booby traps.

talks.title: Christopher Campbell - The $env:PATH less Traveled
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Christopher Campbell - The $env:PATH less Traveled.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Christopher Campbell presents research on privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Windows package managers, particularly Chocolatey and OneGet. As a PowerSploit developer, Campbell demonstrates how misconfigured PATH environments and improper package installation practices create exploitable escalation opportunities.

## Key Topics

**Package Managers:** Campbell discusses OneGet (Microsoft's new package manager in PowerShell v5), Chocolatey/NuGet, and PSGet. These tools simplify software management and third-party patching (Adobe, Java, Flash) on Windows, but inherit vulnerabilities from repositories and packages.

**Download Security Issues:** Early versions of PSGet and Chocolatey downloaded installation scripts over HTTP and piped them directly to PowerShell's Invoke-Expression (IEX), creating man-in-the-middle risks. Chocolatey fixed this upon notification.

**Repository Abuse:** When Campbell tested Chocolatey's public repository by hashing all packages, he found 100 packages with unknown hashes; 31 contained malware detections, including one straight Trojan uploaded by a user.

## Technical Details

**PowerShell v3 Console Host Exploitation:** PowerShell searches for PSConsoleHost.cmd and related files in the PATH. An attacker can write a malicious PSConsoleHost.cmd to any PATH directory. When an administrator opens PowerShell, the payload executes automatically, escalating privileges without user interaction.

**Chocolatey Installation Vulnerabilities:** Older Chocolatey versions dropped all package files into C:\chocolatey\bin with improper permissions allowing any user to write to binaries. This affected hundreds of packages, including SysInternals tools. Campbell demonstrated a real-world attack: during remote administrative updates (cinst commands), an attacker can inject a net user add command to achieve domain admin simply by waiting for the next scheduled update.

**PATH Variable Exploitation:** Binaries placed in C:\ root often inherit permissions allowing users to write to the folder. This creates DLL preloading and PATH hijacking opportunities affecting services that use the PATH to load libraries.

## Takeaways
All package managers inherit vulnerabilities from repositories and packages. File permission misconfigurations during installation and HTTP downloads remain critical issues. Proper file permissions and HTTPS are essential mitigations. Campbell references prior work including the "Encyclopedia of Windows Privilege Escalation" talk and credits Rob Reynolds (Chocolatey), Matt Graber, harmjOy (Power Up author), and Microsoft's PowerShell security team for their fixes.

talks.title: Christopher Campbell - The Secret Life of Krbtgt
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Christopher Campbell - The Secret Life of Krbtgt.
talks.summary: A tale of peril and woe, Krbtgt is the domain account that you just can't quit. Quiet and harmless, it has been with your enterprise since you first installed Active Directory. Although disabled, it has witnessed years of poor configurations, remote code execution vulnerabilities and bad administrator passwords. Come hear Krbtgt's story and see why its days should be numbered. If you don't laugh, you'll cry. This talk is targeted at Windows administrators, penetration testers and incident handlers and will explore why Microsoft's implementation of Kerberos is not the answer to its many credential problems.

talks.title: Christopher Soghoian - Blinding The Surveillance State
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Christopher Soghoian - Blinding The Surveillance State.
talks.summary: We live in a surveillance state. Law enforcement and intelligence agencies have access to a huge amount of data about us, enabling them to learn intimate, private details about our lives. In part, the ease with which they can obtain such information reflects the fact that our laws have failed to keep up with advances in technology. However, privacy enhancing technologies can offer real protections even when the law does not. That intelligence agencies like the NSA are able to collect records about every telephone call made in the United States, or engage in the bulk surveillance of Internet communications is only possible because so much of our data is transmitted in the clear. The privacy enhancing technologies required to make bulk surveillance impossible and targeted surveillance more difficult already exist. We just need to start using them.

talks.title: Kallenberg and Kovah - Extreme Privilege Escalation On Windows 8/UEFI Systems
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Kallenberg and Kovah - Extreme Privilege Escalation On Windows 8/UEFI Systems.
talks.summary: The UEFI specification has more tightly coupled the bonds of the operating system and the platform firmware by providing the well-defined "runtime services" interface between the OS and the firmware. This interface is more expansive than the interface that existed in the days of conventional BIOS, which has inadvertently increased the attack surface against the platform firmware. Furthermore, Windows 8 has introduced APIs that allow accessing this UEFI interface from a userland process. Vulnerabilities in this interface can potentially allow a userland process to escalate its privileges from "ring 3" all the way up to that of the platform firmware, which includes permanently attaining control of the very-powerful System Management Mode (SMM).

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of David Dorsey - Why Don’t You Just Tell Me Where The ROP Isn’t Suppose To Go.
talks.summary: Using a ROP chain to bypass operating system defenses is commonplace and detecting this technique while executing is still difficult. This talk will discuss a method built on Intel’s dynamic binary instrumentation tool, Pin, to dynamically detect ROP attacks against the Microsoft Windows operating system. The method is designed to detect ROP attacks that use the return instruction and the indirect call instruction. We will discuss how we determine if a return or indirect call is jumping to a valid location. Then we will show examples of the method working, discuss its effectiveness, and its limitations. After the talk, the source code for the pintool will be released.

talks.summary: Internet of Things devices are often slow and resource constrained. This makes them the perfect target for network-based timing attacks, which allow an attacker to brute-force credentials one character at a time, rather than guessing the entire string at once. We will discuss how timing attacks work, how to optimize them, and how to handle the many factors which can prevent successful exploitation. We will also demonstrate attacks on at least one popular device. After this presentation, you will have the foundation necessary to attack your own devices, and a set of scripts to help you get started.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Paul Drapeau and Brent Dukes - Steganography in Commonly Used HF Radio Protocols.
talks.summary: Imagine having the capability to covertly send messages to an individual or a larger audience, without the need for large centralized infrastructure where your message could be observed, intercepted, or tampered with by oppressive governments or other third parties. We will discuss the opportunities and challenges with steganography implementations in widely used amateur radio digital modes, and present a proof of concept implementation of hiding messages within innocuous transmissions using the JT65 protocol. This technique could theoretically be used to implement a low cost, low infrastructure, covert, world wide short message broadcasting or point to point protocol. No messages in codes or ciphers intended to obscure the meaning thereof were actually transmitted over the amateur bands during the creation of this talk.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in - David Wyde - Client-Side HTTP Cookie Security: Attack and Defense.
talks.summary: HTTP cookies are an important part of trust on the web. Users often trade their login credentials for a cookie, which is then used to authenticate subsequent requests. Cookies are valuable to attackers: passwords can be fortified by two-factor authentication and "new login location detected" emails, but session cookies typically bypass these measures. This talk will explore the security implications of how popular browsers store cookies, ways in which cookies can be stolen, and potential mitigations.

talks.title: Panel- Ephemeral Communications: Why and How?
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Panel- Ephemeral Communications: Why and How?.
talks.summary: Ephemeral communications applications are increasingly popular ways, especially among younger users, to communicate online. In contrast to “once it’s on the Internet, it’s forever”, these applications promise to delete information rapidly, or to maintain anonymity indefinitely, lowering inhibitions to share sensitive or personal content. There are several types of these applications, as well as ephemeral or anonymous publication use of mainstream tools, with unique security features and general utility. Key people from the major ephemeral applications will debate where the market is, where it’s going, and how these systems can best balance user desires with technical and legal requirements.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Panel - Diversity in Information Security.
talks.summary: Discussion from the point of view of a diverse panel of leading representatives currently in or thinking of becoming part of the Information Security industry. This panel will give you insight to the evolutionary landscape of diversity in the hacking community. We will present statistical evidence showing the lack of sub-culture representation in the hacking community and while these numbers have been decreasing we can still work to encourage cultural variance. By analyzing how diversity is critical to improving the information security industry we will explore positive approaches to encourage recruiting and retention of deficient subcultures, removing of unconscious bias’ and discouraging inclusiveness, and introduce the audience to a wide variety of existing support structures. There will be no witch hunt here, there will be no judgement, only information. All of this and more will be answered with open and honest dialogue into one of the most controversial issues currently within our community.

Live demonstrations will be given to show how these flaws lead to facility and system compromise, even against the most secure access control systems and card types being sold to the market today. Attacking Cisco VoIP services requires limited knowledge today with the Viproy Penetration Testing Kit (written by the presenter). It has a dozen modules to test trust hacking issues, signalling attacks against SIP services and Skinny services, gaining unauthorised access, call spoofing, brute-forcing VoIP accounts and debugging services using as MITM. Furthermore, Viproy provides these attack modules in a penetration testing environment and full integration. The presentation contains live demonstration of practical VoIP attacks and usage of new Viproy modules.

talks.title: Felix Leder - NinjaTV - Increasing Your Smart TV’s IQ Without Bricking It
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Felix Leder - NinjaTV - Increasing Your Smart TV’s IQ Without Bricking It.
talks.summary: Smart TVs are growing in popularity. Set-top boxes like Apple TV, Roku, or WD TV can make your “normal” TV "smart" and Smart TVs even smarter. Despite their functionality, they’re often missing interesting features, like bit-torrent, VPN and even specific TV channels. This presentation is about how to hack into WD TV set-top boxes and how to add experimental functionality without the risk of bricking it. Whether you want to add exotic TV channels, watch right from bit-torrent, or are crazy enough to do bitcoin mining on your TV – you are in charge. We will demonstrate several methods to become root using everything from remote exploits to hardware hacking. Unfortunately, just becoming root isn’t sufficient to make persistent changes. Because stronger modifications put your device at risk of bricking or of losing specific services, you must dig deeper. We are going to present and release our "adjusted" firmware that keeps all the manufacturer's encryption and service DRM keys intact. The firmware is minimally invasive and enables customization without risk. Patching becomes as easy as an SMB software upload. For those who want get deeper and dirtier, we will explain the firmware structure, how to extract the relevant encryption keys, and discuss the protected software modules. This includes a short overview of relevant tools to do hot-patching, live-debugging, and pointers to get started on reverse engineering core applications.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Gene Bransfield - Weaponizing Your Pets: The War Kitteh and the Denial of Service Dog.
talks.summary: WarKitteh: In my job I have to deliver frequent Information Security briefings to both technical and non-technical professionals. I noticed that as the material got more technical, I began to lose the non-technical crowd. Therefore, I started including humorous pictures of cats and made the briefings include stories about those cats. This worked, and I soon became notorious for my presentation style. After delivering one of those presentations, an audience member offered to lend me their cat tracking collar. The collar contained a GPS device and a cellular component and would track your cats movements throughout the neighborhood. Me being the guy I am, I thought “All you need now is a WiFi sniffing device and you'd have a War Kitteh.” I laughed, and started working on it.

Several vulnerabilities found with the XRDP server will be briefly discussed, including two that may be exploited for RCE prior to authentication. These attacks are typically based on a piggy-back application (such as the Remote Desktop Connection Client, mstsc.exe), the piggy-back application performs a benchmarking operation, and then fuzzing begins through a parallel set of the piggy-back instances attacking each event sequentially.

It has always been easier to attack than to defend on the Internet, even back to 1979 when it was written that "few if any security controls can stop a dedicated" red team. We all accept this as true but the community rarely ever looks at the longer term implications of what happens to the internet if one side has a persistent advantage year after year, decade after decade. Is there a tipping point where the internet becomes no longer a Wild West but Somalia, a complete unstable chaos where the attackers don't just have an advantage but a long-term supremacy? This talk will look at trends and the role of hackers and security researchers.

But, when every year the Las Vegas Metro SWAT Team stages for an interdiction of your convention, you know you have something "different". From crawling through Air Ducts to surreptitiously "acquiring" telco equipment, these are the stories of DEF CON you don't often hear about. The stories of yesteryear that not only helped shape defcon but also the people who make up today's hacker and infosec communities at large. DEF CON is the event that helped spawn a generation of hackers and changed the landscape of information security. So come join us for a trip down memory lane as we reveal some of the secrets and stories of what architected the mystery, myth and legend of the hacker community you see today... Now that the statues of limitation have passed.

In March 2014 I spoke at the annual TED conference about why hackers are a vital part of the information age. I claimed that the world actually needs hackers, and that they play an important social, political and technology role. At first I thought I will encounter objection, but I found out I was preaching to the choir. Surprisingly,
many of the smart, powerful, rich people at TED thought hackers were just great. Then I realized: I was preaching to the WRONG choir. It’s the hackers who are the change agents, and the only ones who can make a difference when it comes to the future of the net. That’s why this talk will speak to the heart of the hacking community about the practical things hackers can do to create a positive impact on the world. Essentially, it’s about being a good hacker while staying out of jail and making the world a better place – with things like community outreach projects, crypto parties, voluntary red teams, responsible disclosure and stopping the spread of FUD.

talks.title: - Zach Fasel - Logging ALL THE THINGS Without All The Cost With Open Source Big Data Tools
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of - Zach Fasel - Logging ALL THE THINGS Without All The Cost With Open Source Big Data Tools.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented on the Party Track, speaker Zach Fasel steps in as a replacement speaker to deliver a defensive security talk on enterprise logging. He explains that traditional logging architectures—often reliant on simple Syslog setups, regex, grep, or costly commercial tools with volume-based licensing—fail to scale or adequately serve security monitoring needs. Emphasizing that defenders need to collect and monitor logs without being financially penalized by data volume, Zach presents open-source big data tools, specifically the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), as well as alternatives like Fluentd and Graylog2, to build scalable, cost-effective logging pipelines.

### Key Topics
- **The Cost and Scaling Problem of Commercial SIEMs:** Commercial logging products frequently rely on volume-based licensing models, forcing organizations to selectively discard logs or spend significant portions of their IT budget simply to ingest data.
- **Open-Source Big Data Alternatives:** Logstash, Elasticsearch, and Kibana (ELK) provide an open-source framework capable of ingesting, indexing, searching, and visualizing high-volume log data. Alternatives noted include Graylog2 and Fluentd.
- **Ingestion and Input Sources:** Capturing data across disparate environments requires flexible inputs. Zach outlines methods for Linux/Unix/Mac via Syslog agents or Logstash agents (supporting TCP/TLS), Windows event ingestion using tools like Nxlog, Snare, or Windows Event Collector via Group Policy, network devices via Syslog and SNMP traps, application-level security events, and cloud services (AWS CloudTrail, Google Apps Reports API, Box Events API, Salesforce LoginHistory).
- **Parsing and Filtering with Grok:** Rather than relying purely on complex regular expressions, Logstash uses Grok patterns to simplify parsing varied formats (such as PAM authentication logs). Logstash can also enrich logs with metrics, GeoIP lookup data, reverse DNS, multiline parsing, key-value extraction, URL decoding, and data anonymization.
- **Automated Security Actions and Alerting:** Rather than passive storage, Logstash outputs can trigger automated responses via scripts or commands using the `exec` output (e.g., automated firewall updates or switch port shutdown), deliver notifications via PagerDuty, HipChat, or email, or forward structured data to custom web applications for dynamic evaluation.
- **Elasticsearch Security and Performance Hardening:** Out of the box, Elasticsearch lacks native authentication and uses multicast clustering. Production setups require placing an Nginx reverse proxy with basic authentication (htpasswd) in front of Elasticsearch, network segmentation, and adjusting index sizes (e.g., hourly instead of daily for heavy loads) or placing Redis queuing layers ahead of Logstash indexers.

### Technical Details
Zach details Logstash’s operational pipeline, which consists of shippers/agents, brokers/queues (such as Redis) for buffering, indexers for parsing and tagging, and search/storage backends in Elasticsearch. He provides concrete configuration examples, including parsing PAM Unix logs in Logstash by identifying modules, tagging authentication and authorization phases, and extracting fields like user, session ID, and remote host without writing complex custom regexes. For alerting, he illustrates an output filter that evaluates failed logins against threshold metrics (e.g., more than two failures for a specific user in a 60-second window) to trigger immediate email alerts or call an external script via `exec`.

### Takeaways
Zach concludes that open-source logging stacks offer an affordable, highly customizable alternative to expensive vendor platforms, though they require technical expertise and manual security controls (such as reverse proxy authentication and network isolation). Furthermore, he highlights the Open PCI Project, an initiative aimed at freely sharing configuration files, parsing rules, prebuilt VMs, and hardening guides across the security community to eliminate security obscurity and lower the barrier to robust defensive logging.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Lucas Morris and Michael McAtee - ShareEnum: We Wrapped Samba So You Don’t Have To.
talks.summary: CIFS shares can tell you a lot about a network, including file access, local administrator access, password reuse, etc.. Until now most people have relied on add-ons to scanning tools to implement Microsoft’s complicated network APIs. Some tools wrap existing clients, such as smbclient, or use RPC calls; however, this is inefficient. What we need is a scanner that utilizes the closest thing we can get to Microsoft’s SMB libraries to scan network shares efficiently and quietly. ShareEnum uses the underlying Samba client libraries to list shares, permissions, and even recurse down file trees gathering information including what is stored in each directory.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Metacortex and Grifter - Touring the Darkside of the Internet. An Introduction to Tor.
talks.summary: This is an introduction level talk. The talk itself will cover the basics of Tor, Darknets, Darknet Market places, and Bitcoin. I will start by giving the audience an overview of Tor and how it works. I will cover entry nodes, exit nodes, as well as hidden services. I will then show how you connect to Tor on both Linux/OSX and Windows and demo it off. Once we are connected to Tor, I am going to show how to find Tor hidden services and then demo off browsing around some marketplaces. Once the audience has a solid grasp on what the market places offer, I am going to start dealing the process of purchasing something off of it. I will cover bitcoin and bitcoin mining. After we know about how bitcoin works, we will cover purchasing items. I will cover purchasing PO Box's and the pickup of packages. talks.summary: Of all the technologies revealed in the NSA ANT catalog, perhaps the most exotic is the use of RF retroreflectors for over-the-air surveillance. These tiny implants, without any power supply, transmit information intercepted from digital or analog communications when irradiated by radio signals from an outside source. This modern class of radar eavesdropping technology has never been demonstrated in public before today. I've constructed and tested my own RF retroreflectors, and I'll show you how they work and how easy they are to build with modest soldering skills. I'll even bring along some fully assembled units to give away. Now you can add RF retroreflectors to your own NSA Playset and play along with the NSA!

talks.summary:
### Overview
This transcript captures the DEF CON 22 Contests and Events Awards Ceremony. The session begins with Pyro announcing his departure after running DEF CON contests, events, and villages for five years. Leadership transitions to Grifter (taking over villages), alongside Hackajar and Coleslaw (taking over contests and events). The ceremony proceeds at a rapid pace—using a gong to keep presentations concise—as organizers present results, statistics, and prizes across community initiatives, technical challenges, and creative hacking competitions.

### Key Topics
- **Charity and Health Initiatives:**
  - *Be the Match:* DEF CON continued its partnership with the National Marrow Donor Program registry, recording 112 sign-ups (its second-highest year) and noting past matches that led to life-saving transplants.
  - *Mohawk Contest & Art Donations:* Ed reported 255 Mohawks, raising $4,220.76 for the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) and $1,820 for Hackers for Charity ($6,040.76 total). Artist Eddie separately donated $4,100 to EFF and $4,100 to charity. Hackerspace HACK also raised $213.
- **Technical and Hacking Contests:**
  - *Wireless CTF:* 17 teams competed, with team "All Cats" taking top honors after four days of challenges; the Wireless Village also featured 25 speakers.
  - *Crack Me If You Can:* The password cracking competition saw Team Hashcat place first, with Team Pro in second and a Carnegie Mellon team winning $600 for releasing writeups and tool updates.
  - *Network Forensics Puzzle Contest:* 264 teams registered across seven rounds. Team Dofer took first place (49 hours, 3 minutes), while Top Pole and Team Blue tied for second (52 hours, 7 minutes).
  - *Zero-Day Vulnerability Submissions:* In a router exploit contest, 150 zero-days were submitted, leading to full router compromises (highlighted submitters included Craig Young from Tripwire, Michael Lucy, and Chase Schultz).
  - *Tamper Evident Contest:* Competitors explored physical security; the winning team discovered a new 15-second exploit against padlock seals typically used on gas meters.
  - *Zapping Rachel (FTC Robocall Challenge):* Partnering with the Federal Trade Commission to combat automated spam calls, 100 participants competed across three phases (honeypot challenge, circumvention, and data analytics), competing for $17,000 in prizes.
- **Gaming, Hardware, and Creative Contests:**
  - *DEF CON Bots:* Contestants engineered hardware, electronics, and software for robots shooting lasers at moving targets (won by TMX).
  - *Database & Crypto Games:* "Abstract" hosted a SQL-command space battle (26 million database events) and a Defcoin-powered robot combat game (35,000 Defcoin transactions), won by Sis Fix.
  - *Badge Counterfeiting:* Entries produced replicas of human, Queercon, and Lost badges using dental plaster, ballpoint pen on vinyl, and titanium.
  - *Community Classics:* Hack Fortress (Team Fortress 2 combined with hacking), Hacker Jeopardy, Hacker Pyramid, Scavenger Hunt, Crash and Compile, Beverage Cooling Contraption Contest, and SECTF for Kids.

### Technical Details
- **Database/Cryptocurrency Scale:** The Defcoin robot battle generated 35,000 transactions (accounting for nearly 99% of network activity that weekend), while the SQL game processed over 26 million database events.
- **Hardware & Physical Security:** Hardware challenges ranged from custom-built targeting robots to rapid physical bypasses of utility tamper seals in under 15 seconds.
- **Telecommunications Defense:** The FTC's multi-stage challenge targeted automated telephony abuse, tasking researchers with honeypot design, circumvention analysis, and data analytics on call records.

### Takeaways
The DEF CON 22 Contests and Events Ceremony highlights how the hacker conference merges technical rigor with community support. From raising over $14,000 for charities and expanding the bone marrow donor registry, to evaluating zero-day exploits, hardware engineering, and anti-robocall research, the contests serve as both entertainment and a venue for practical security problem-solving.

talks.summary:
### Overview
At DEF CON 7 in July 1999, Michael J. Martinez, a technology reporter for abcnews.com, delivered a talk examining the strained dynamic between mainstream news media and the underground hacker community. Acknowledging that mainstream media coverage of hackers was growing rapidly and here to stay, Martinez shared insights into how newsrooms function, the editorial constraints reporters face, and how hackers can engage productively with journalists to improve coverage and accuracy.

### Key Topics
- **Mainstream Media Influx and Mechanics**: Martinez explained that generalist reporters from outlets like the *New York Times*, *The Wall Street Journal*, and *60 Minutes* were entering the space without deep technical backgrounds. Most journalists write for non-technical audiences—translating complex topics for ordinary readers—and face tight deadlines.
- **The Editorial "Telephone Game"**: Stories undergo editing, fact-checking, copy editing, and layout changes (plus video, standups, and anchors in broadcast news). Martinez emphasized that technical nuances often get altered or diluted across these editing layers.
- **Sensationalism and Preconceptions**: Hacking stories drive readership and page views because they are seen as cool, dangerous, and dramatic. However, this dynamic is amplified by cultural preconceptions shaped by movies like *War Games* and *The Matrix*, leading many uninformed reporters to depict all computer intrusion under uniform stereotypes.
- **Hacker vs. Cracker Terminology**: Attendees challenged Martinez on mainstream media's failure to distinguish between ethical hackers and malicious actors ("crackers" or "script kiddies"). Martinez explained that the mainstream public and news editors view the terms through popular culture usage, and malicious actors often call themselves hackers. While he referenced resources like Eric Raymond's Jargon File to educate editors and use accurate terminology, shifting mainstream vernacular remains a slow battle.
- **Source Credibility and Verification**: Unlike corporations with extensive public relations apparatuses, underground communities lack formal clearinghouses. Generalist reporters frequently struggle to find credible sources, verify skills on IRC, and separate genuine experts from posers.

### Technical Details & Ethical Dilemmas
- **Legal Boundaries and Anonymity**: Martinez cautioned hackers about interactions with journalists, reminding them that journalistic source protection does not shield them from law enforcement investigations if illegal acts are disclosed. Hackers were warned not to invite journalists to observe active illegal intrusions or provide contraband (such as "wares" or exploits).
- **Exploit and Tool Releases**: Martinez discussed tools like Back Orifice 2000 (cDc) and malware incidents like ExploreZip. While recognizing the value of demonstrating flaws to push vendors like Microsoft into addressing vulnerabilities, Martinez noted the mainstream perception remains negative when dangerous utilities are distributed broadly to the public.
- **Hactivism and Free Speech**: Addressing politically motivated hacks, Martinez noted that while a motive might be reported, taking down third-party websites inherently interferes with others' speech and commercial activities, which invariably earns negative press with general audiences.

### Takeaways
To improve media coverage and clear the hacker community's public perception, Martinez offered practical guidance:
- **Direct Journalists to Credible Sources**: Point reporters to recognized technical repositories, documentation (e.g., Raymond's Jargon File), and knowledgeable individuals, while calling out posers.
- **Clearly Explain the "Why"**: Reporters often know who, what, when, and where, but struggle to explain the technical philosophy and underlying motivations behind actions or exploit releases.
- **Provide Smart, Constructive Feedback**: Avoid sending hostile, abusive flame emails or 2,000-word diatribes. Concise, professional, and fact-focused criticism often leads to ongoing, productive source relationships.
- **Protect Personal Security**: Avoid sharing illegal tools, private emails, or advance notice of criminal acts, as reporters cannot act as accomplices and have civic responsibilities.

talks.title: Huagang Xie - Linux Kernel Security with LIDS
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Huagang Xie - Linux Kernel Security with LIDS.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Huagang Xie introduces the Linux Intrusion Detection System (LIDS), an open-source security extension designed to protect the Linux kernel and operating system against unauthorized access and tampering. Xie discusses the security shortcomings of traditional Unix access control—where gaining root access grants unrestricted power—and explains how LIDS enforces mandatory access control (MAC) and least privilege to create a trusted kernel environment.

### Key Topics
- **Kernel and Application Untrustworthiness:** Growing complexity leads to unavoidable software bugs, untrusted applications, and vulnerabilities to local/remote root exploits, trojans, worms, and rootkits.
- **Mandatory Access Control (MAC) and Least Privilege:** Enforcing rules that cannot be bypassed even by the superuser (root), such as restricting read access on sensitive files like `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/passwd` exclusively to designated binaries (e.g., the login binary).
- **LIDS Architecture:** Core components include an Access Control database, hook checking center, administration interface, and logging mechanism that mediates interactions between subjects (processes) and objects (files, directories, devices).
- **Attack and Defense Vectors:** Mitigating administration compromises, raw I/O manipulation (`/dev/kmem`, `/dev/kcore`), rootkit kernel module insertions, `LD_PRELOAD` privilege abuse, and ShellCode in command arguments or environment variables.
- **Kernel Patching and Tooling:** Compiling vanilla Linux kernels with LIDS patches, setting up configuration files in `/etc/lids`, and using utility tools (`lidsconf` and `lidsadm`).

### Technical Details
- **Kernel Structures and System Calls:** LIDS adds pointers to the kernel's `task_struct` (`lids_sys_acl`) and uses structures like `secure_inode` identified by inode and device numbers. Processes inherit ACLs on `fork()` via `copy_lids_acl` and configure their permissions on `execve()` using `lids_set_acls`. System calls such as `chmod` are intercepted with functions like `lids_check_base`.
- **Securing Administration:** To prevent unauthorized administrative override, LIDS uses a 16-character/116-bit MD5 kernel password, limits administrative sessions by checking restricted login TTYs (local vs. remote console or serial ports), and seals the kernel with `lidsadm -I`.
- **Defense Mechanisms:**
  - **Module & Raw I/O Restrictions:** Disables `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` and `CAP_SYS_MODULE` by default, blocking direct writes to memory/raw devices and blocking unauthorized insertion or deletion of loadable kernel modules (`insmod`/`rmmod`).
  - **Virtual File System (VFS) Protection:** Files can be marked as Read-Only (e.g., `/bin/login`), Append-Only (e.g., log files), or Deny Access/Hidden (e.g., `/etc/shadow`).
  - **`LD_PRELOAD` Sanitization:** Checks for `LD_` environment variables on execution and strips LIDS ACL privileges to prevent hijacking privileged binaries.
  - **ShellCode Detection:** Lightweight kernel checking of parameters and environment variables halts execution of local exploit payloads.

### Takeaways
LIDS converts standard Linux systems into fortified, least-privilege environments by implementing mandatory access controls directly into the kernel. By blocking common attack vectors at the system call boundary (such as dynamic kernel modification, module rootkits, and unauthorized credential access), LIDS ensures that compromising root does not grant attackers full control over the host.

talks.title: FX
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate FX and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Defcon presentation, FX from Phenoelit explores security weaknesses across network routing devices, cellular network infrastructure, mobile handsets, and Cisco router exploitation. Beginning with an analysis of Enterasys Matrix switches, the speaker moves into telecommunications architectures covering GSM and GPRS, demonstrates multiple client-side vulnerabilities in a Siemens mobile phone, and concludes with an in-depth technical walkthrough of exploiting Cisco IOS via remote memory leaks and buffer overflows.

### Key Topics
- **Network Switches and Protocol Flaws:** Examination of Enterasys Matrix switches, highlighting poor TCP/IP management handling, predictable TCP initial sequence numbers, and flawed OSPF routing packet processing that can disrupt networks.
- **GSM and GPRS Backbone Exploitation:** Architectural breakdown of mobile phone networks (HLR, SGSN, GGSN) and attack vectors involving the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP) and Wireless Application Protocol (WAP) gateways.
- **Mobile Device Vulnerabilities:** Flaws identified in the Siemens S55 handset, spanning Bluetooth connection exhaustion, file handling limits, Java VM crashes, unauthorized information disclosure, dialer manipulation, and malformed image handling.
- **Cisco IOS Remote Exploitation:** Deep dive into remote exploitation techniques on Cisco routers using memory leakage via UDP Echo and an HTTP integer overflow to achieve runtime memory patching or configuration overwrite.

### Technical Details
- **GPRS & GTP Attacks:** FX explains that GPRS infrastructure relies on standard IPv4 backbones. Using guessable Access Point Names (APNs), attackers can attempt authentication into internal corporate networks. Furthermore, the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP) operates over UDP without authentication. Having access to a machine inside a provider's network enables an attacker to issue spoofed UDP packets to establish, alter, or terminate user contexts, redirect backbone traffic, adjust accounting records, or force subscriber roaming between SGSNs. Additionally, connectionless WAP session protocol (WSP) over UDP port 9200 allows attackers to send anonymous, spoofed HTTP requests billed to other subscribers.
- **Siemens S55 Handset Weaknesses:**
  - *Bluetooth & File System:* Repeated pairing prompts can overwhelm the UI and exhaust connection slots. Flooding the device with thousands of files crashes the inbox workflow, as the deletion interface only handles 255 files at a time.
  - *Java Virtual Machine:* Missing midlet names in `.jad` files trigger unhandled null pointer exceptions causing a white screen of death. Overly long midlet names corrupt underlying file system structures. Non-standard vendor Java classes expose sensitive data like missed call logs and IMEI numbers, while UI timing discrepancies allow midlets to trick users into approving billable SMS transmissions.
  - *GIF Parsing:* Processing animated GIFs with offset virtual screen coordinates causes out-of-bounds memory writes, permanently crashing handsets if applied as wallpapers.
- **Cisco IOS Remote Exploitation:**
  - *Memory Disclosure:* The UDP Echo service in IOS 11.x and below contains an information leak where claiming a packet length larger than the transmitted payload returns up to ~19 KB of raw IO memory. This leak enables IOS image and memory layout fingerprinting, as well as sniffing in-flight transit data like Telnet passwords (implemented in `phenoelit-ios-sniff`).
  - *Exploitation Pipeline:* FX pairs this information leak with an HTTP server integer overflow (present in 11.x through 12.2), triggered after transmitting 2 GB of data so that a signed integer wraps negative. Shellcode is delivered via UDP Echo into IO memory ring buffers. Once the address is identified via the memory leak, the HTTP stack return address is overwritten.
  - *Shellcode Execution:* Two Shellcode approaches were presented: runtime IOS patching (disabling authentication routines on active Telnet and enable prompts while fixing the call stack to prevent crashes) and image-independent NVRAM configuration patching (scanning NVRAM for password strings, replacing credentials, and recalculating the checksum).

### Takeaways
To mitigate mobile risks, the speaker advises turning off unnecessary wireless interfaces like Bluetooth and infrared in untrusted environments, avoiding unverified Java applications, keeping firmware updated, and avoiding exposed GPRS VPN configurations. For core network infrastructure, administrators must disable non-essential legacy services like UDP Echo, restrict direct incoming network traffic to management interfaces, adopt out-of-band management architectures, monitor routers via IDS, and keep operating system software updated.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Jaya Baloo - Government IP_TAPPING: Vendors & Techniques.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, freelance interception consultant Jaya Baloo explores the technical architectures, legal implications, standards, and commercial vendor landscape behind government lawful interception (LI) of IP traffic, with a primary focus on Europe and the Netherlands. Baloo explains that lawful interception involves legally warranted surveillance where network operators or Internet Service Providers (ISPs) capture and deliver target data—ranging from metadata correlations to full content and TCP taps—to a Law Enforcement Monitoring Facility (LEMF).

### Key Topics
- **Legal & Evidentiary Issues:** Baloo highlights key legal complexities in collecting digital evidence, including jurisdictional admissibility variations between the US and Europe, challenges in proving attribution without biometric markers, and judges/juries making non-scientific evaluations of technical data. In the Netherlands, intercepted digital data is legally treated as secondary rather than primary evidence.
- **Interception Architectures:** Interception methods have evolved from legacy passive physical taps (vampire clamps in Telco wiring closets) to semi-active and active interception deployed within ISP domains. Modern designs often rely on hardware splitters separating public production networks from isolated private LI environments to prevent performance degradation and ensure the tap remains invisible to targets.
- **Standards and Handover Protocols:** The presentation details the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) framework and Dutch guidelines (TIIT), defining three core Handover Interfaces: HI1 (administrative warrant metadata and intercept keys), HI2 (Intercept Related Information / IRI such as timestamps and session duration), and HI3 (the actual content of communication).
- **Handling Encryption:** Network operators are only mandated to decrypt traffic or supply keys if they provide the encryption service (such as ISP-managed SSH). If targets deploy end-to-end encryption independently (e.g., PGP), operators pass raw ciphertext, leaving decryption to authorities. Mention is also made of tools like the FBI's Magic Lantern keystroke logger used to capture passphrases directly at the endpoint.

### Technical Details
- **Dutch Technical Architecture:** A lawful interception warrant desk routes orders to ISPs. The target's data flow is captured by S1 units (switches or routers that apply timestamps, generate SHA hashes of initial packets, and encrypt data), funneled via an S2 concentrator router over IPsec or TLS tunnels across the internet using X.509 certificates, managed by S3 administrative servers, and terminated at government T1 collection boxes before decryption and handoff to agency-specific T2 monitoring facilities.
- **Commercial Vendors & Hardware:** Vendors must support ETSI and CALEA compliance. Notable commercial vendors include Verint (Comverse Infosys), the dominant market leader using Top Layer switches; Nice Systems (NiceTrack), utilizing proprietary hardware running on Windows NT with claims of topic extraction, language detection, and GIS location tracking; ADC/SS8, specialized for large bandwidth and satellite environments; and Acurus, which faced limitations such as a 50 concurrent tap ceiling per system.
- **Operational Challenges:** Filtering and packet reassembly pose major strain on network switches, which struggle to quickly apply dynamic filters without dropping packets. Past tools like the FBI's Carnivore frequently failed to track RADIUS disconnects, causing accidental illegal interception of unrelated subscribers. Additionally, high-bandwidth DSL connections require substantial peering pipe capacity to LEMFs.

### Takeaways
Compliance is mandatory for public communication providers in the EU, backed by severe non-compliance penalties (such as fines up to $250,000 or executive house arrest in the Netherlands). High capital expenditures ($100,000 to over $700,000 per ISP system) are typically borne by operators, balanced somewhat by per-warrant government reimbursements. Looking forward, Baloo anticipates challenges including borderless EU-wide interception mandates, data retention burdens, public WLAN interception questions, and quantum cryptography's potential to render link interception detectable.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Matt Shannon - _vti_fpxploitation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Matt Shannon from KPMG's Information Risk Management Group examines the security architecture, protocol mechanics, and common attack vectors associated with Microsoft FrontPage Server Extensions. Despite being widely deployed across tens of thousands of web servers, FrontPage is frequently misunderstood and poorly secured. Shannon breaks down the underlying communication flow, introduces his custom reconnaissance and brute-forcing tool called FP Exploiter, demonstrates post-exploitation strategies using malicious Active Server Pages (ASP), and outlines hardening best practices.

### Key Topics
- **FrontPage Architecture and History:** Developed originally by Vermeer Technologies in 1995 before being acquired by Microsoft in 1996, FrontPage relies on components and dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) prefixed with `_vti_`. FrontPage client-server interactions take place over HTTP using specialized Vermeer RPC packets and endpoints such as `author.dll`, `admin.dll`, `shtml.exe`, and `_vti_rpc`.
- **Authentication and Information Disclosure:** The protocol begins by querying `_vti_inf.html`, which provides server version data and file locations embedded in HTML comments. This information reveals whether the host is running Unix/Apache (`.exe` handlers) or Windows/IIS (`.dll` handlers), and pinpoints OS versions (NT 4.x vs. 2000/XP 5.x). Vermeer RPC packets can also inadvertently leak physical drive paths.
- **Debugging the Back End:** Using Microsoft's free WinDbg tool attached to the `inetinfo` process alongside the Microsoft Symbol Server, Shannon analyzes how FrontPage Server Extensions function internally. DLLs like `fp4awel.dll` handle document arrays and file queries, presenting potential opportunities for memory corruption or buffer overflows in routines such as `DSPContext::GetFile`.
- **Automated Exploitation (FP Exploiter):** Shannon developed FP Exploiter, a tool with command-line and Perl/GTK interfaces designed to scan Class C IP ranges for IIS-based FrontPage servers. It checks for anonymous access via the "Everyone" account and performs brute-force password grinding against user-defined or default accounts (defaulting to `administrator` to avoid account lockouts).
- **Post-Exploitation via ASP:** Once write access is obtained via FrontPage, attackers can upload ASP scripts to pivot through the environment. Key tools discussed include Michael Brinkley's *SQL Ultimate* (allowing SQL Server Query Analyzer access via browser) and *cmdasp.asp* (enabling remote command execution, network reconnaissance with `netstat` and `ipconfig`, and internal network enumeration).
- **Hardening and Securing FrontPage:** Securing FrontPage relies on enforcing strong passwords (over eight characters), renaming the default administrator account, applying least privilege through FrontPage-specific role permissions, and strictly restricting access to administrative DLLs/files (`admin`, `author`, `_vti_rpc`) to internal corporate IP ranges or VPNs.

### Technical Details
FrontPage authentication utilizes unique `_vti_` HTTP headers alongside NTLM challenge-response sequences over HTTP POST requests rather than generic NTLM authentication. Reverse-engineering revealed that FrontPage builds a complete array listing of web documents on the stack prior to servicing retrieval requests. For attacking authenticated instances, default administrative accounts are preferred targets because they typically do not incur lockout policies, while standard user accounts may lock out during brute-force attempts.

### Takeaways
The primary security risk surrounding Microsoft FrontPage stems less from exotic zero-day exploits and more from administrative misconfiguration, default out-of-the-box deployments, and weak password management. Stealthy attackers who gain authoring access can deploy disguised ASP backdoors to compromise backend database servers and internal file shares, making IP-level restrictions and rigorous credential policies essential defenses.

talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at DEF CON, this panel explores the technical evolution, legal battles, and cultural impact of peer-to-peer (P2P) networking following the decline of Napster. Former Napster executives, security consultants, and documentary filmmakers discuss why Napster fell, how decentralized architectures evolved to evade centralized points of failure, the realities of digital copyright enforcement, and the emergence of mobile ad-hoc coordination ("smart mobs").

### Key Topics
- **Napster's Fall and Realities**: Contrary to popular belief that the courts or the RIAA solely destroyed Napster, internal conflict between the board of directors and partner Bertelsmann played a decisive role. Furthermore, 80% of Napster's traffic was out-of-print "back catalog" material that was otherwise unavailable to consumers, alongside international music and bootlegs.
- **Music Industry & Copyright History**: The panel contrasts the historical response to mechanical reproduction (player pianos and the compulsory license) with current digital rights management. They critique the record industry's claim that declining CD sales were driven entirely by piracy, attributing drops to platform shifts (the transition from CDs to MP3s), lower hit production quality, and macroeconomic cycles.
- **Evolution of P2P Architecture**: Napster utilized a centralized, dynamic real-time directory index over HTTP, creating a single point of failure legally and architecturally. Successor protocols like Gnutella decentralized the index across all participating clients to eliminate centralized liability, while Freenet added encrypted, trusted-peer clustering modeled after dissident communications.
- **Smart Mobs and Ad-Hoc Networks**: Extending decentralized concepts into mobile networks, demonstrators and political activists utilize wireless PDAs, cell phones, and blogs to coordinate in real time ("smart mobs" or "live hives"), circumventing centralized media and static infrastructure.

### Technical Details
- **Napster Architecture**: Built simple transactional semantics on top of HTTP (GET/PUT/SEARCH) with a centralized real-time directory that tracked connected users and their file availability dynamically.
- **Gnutella vs. Napster**: Gnutella removed the centralized index, distributing search queries across connected peer clients. While this offered legal distance for service providers, users remained susceptible to forensic analysis due to predictable default client configurations, static ISP IP addresses, and well-known network ports.
- **Freenet**: Implemented trusted pair and clustered data transfers to provide anonymity and resist network-level censorship and surveillance.

### Takeaways
Centralized file-sharing architectures are vulnerable to single-point legal and infrastructural shutdowns, driving an inevitable migration toward distributed and encrypted networks. Because consumer behavior gravitates toward convenient digital reproduction and access to out-of-print media, laws and industry business models must adapt rather than attempt to criminalize technological evolution. Furthermore, decentralized peer networks and wireless ad-hoc communication have outgrown file sharing, actively enabling decentralized civic and political mobilization globally.

talks.title: Cameron nummish Hotchkies,Blind SQL Injection Automation Techniques
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Cameron nummish Hotchkies,Blind SQL Injection Automation Techniques.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Defcon, Cameron Hotchkies of hex90 presented on automating data extraction from blind SQL injection vulnerabilities. While standard SQL injections may return data directly through query reshaping or database error messages, blind SQL injections occur when the application does not return query results or errors, instead subtly answering boolean (true/false) questions. Although blind vulnerabilities are just as dangerous, they often grant administrators a false sense of security and are frequently neglected because manual exploitation by asking tens of thousands of boolean questions is tedious, slow, and impractical. To address this, Hotchkies developed and presented Squeal, an automated exploitation tool written in C# designed to extract schemas and table data from Microsoft SQL Server.

### Key Topics
- **Forms of SQL Injection**: Hotchkies categorized SQL injection exploitation into three methods: query redirection/reshaping (formatting and displaying results on page), error-based injection (inducing verbose errors, particularly in Microsoft SQL Server, to reveal data and schema), and blind injection (inferring data bit by bit using binary yes/no logic).
- **Mathematics of Blind Extraction**: Extracting data manually requires converting data (characters, dates, or binary) into ASCII integer values. Using binary search algorithms, an attacker can identify character values in roughly 7 requests per character rather than linear guessing. However, fully dumping schemas and records quickly accumulates into thousands of queries, making manual execution unfeasible.
- **True/False Response Differentiation**: Automated tools must distinguish between true and false HTTP responses. Hotchkies analyzed why traditional approaches fail:
  - *String Comparison*: Fails due to dynamic content like timestamps, requested URLs, or page counters.
  - *MD5 Hashing*: A single-character change drastically alters the entire hash, rendering diffing useless.
  - *DOM/HTML Tree Parsing*: Computationally heavy, complex to parse on malformed HTML, and insensitive to purely textual content changes inside existing nodes.
- **Linear ASCII Sum Representation & Differential Filtering**: Squeal splits HTTP responses into lines by carriage returns and computes the ASCII sum of characters per line. Squeal applies two filtering layers:
  1. *Subtractive Filter*: Identifies and removes identical line sums across baseline true and false pages, discarding markup unrelated to query outcomes.
  2. *Dynamic Baseline Filter*: Compares multiple true requests (e.g., `1=1` vs `2=2`) to detect and eliminate dynamically changing elements like times or query echoes.
  Once dynamic noise is stripped, simple array index matching replaces numerical tolerance thresholds.

### Technical Details
- **Tool Architecture & Features**: Squeal was built in C# (.NET / Mono 1.0+) with WinForms and GTK# interfaces. It supports GET and POST requests, custom HTTP headers/cookies for authenticated sessions, proxy routing, string injection handling, and query termination using `--` for SQL Server. Extracted data and attack signatures are saved in XML format.
- **Schema Extraction Process**: Squeal targets SQL Server system metadata (such as `sysobjects` and column definitions). It first queries table counts, followed by table IDs (using 64-bit long integers), table name lengths, and character ASCII values. It then extracts column counts, sequential column IDs, column names, and internal data type IDs (`xtype`). Once columns and data types are mapped, records are dumped row by row.
- **Limitations & Challenges**: Exploitation generates massive amounts of HTTP traffic (e.g., 2,700+ requests for just four sample records), which risks filling server logs or causing unintended denial of service on small servers. In addition, web pages lacking carriage returns disrupt Squeal's line-based sum algorithm unless pre-processed (e.g., with HTML Tidy or alternative delimiters). The version presented lacked request throttling/delays.

### Takeaways
Blind SQL injection poses identical data leakage risks to classic injection methods. Manual testing severely underestimates the severity of blind injection because automation tools can systematically dump entire databases in minutes. Hotchkies emphasized that developers must remediate these vulnerabilities by utilizing parameterized queries and stored procedures across frameworks (.NET, Java, PHP) rather than relying on suppressing error messages.

As always, the panelists look forward to answering your questions.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Alexey Smirnov & Tzi-cker Chiueh, DIRA: Automatic Detection.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Alexey Smirnov presents DIRA, a compiler-based tool developed jointly with his advisor Tzi-cker Chiueh at Stony Brook University. DIRA targets control hijacking attacks—predominantly buffer overflow vulnerabilities used by computer worms to compromise hosts and propagate across networks. While traditional defense mechanisms focus solely on detecting an attack and terminating the program, DIRA provides a unified architecture for three essential security tasks: attack detection, attack identification (automatic signature generation), and attack repair (restoring pre-attack state to allow continued execution).

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Prior Approaches**: Existing detection tools (e.g., StackGuard, RAD) terminate applications, causing denial of service. Signature generation systems either generate 1-packet signatures (e.g., TaintCheck) or require large pools of malicious network traces and machine learning (e.g., Autograph, Polygraph, N-gram). Existing repair systems often rely on heavyweight checkpointing or OS-specific fork mechanisms.
- **Unified Memory Updates Logging**: DIRA operates as an extension to GCC 3.4.1. It instruments program source code to maintain a runtime circular buffer log recording memory changes, assignments, and standard library functions via proxy wrappers.
- **Multipacket Signature Generation**: DIRA traces dependencies backward through dynamic slicing of the memory log to capture all packets involved in an attack (such as multi-stage authentication sequences in FTP or remote CAD daemons).
- **Attack Recovery without Process Termination**: Rather than aborting the process, DIRA repairs modified memory and restarts execution from a safe earlier state using `setjmp`/`longjmp`.

### Technical Details
- **Log Structure**: Each log record in the circular buffer stores four fields: read address (source), write address (destination), length, and preimage (original value before overwrite). Tags such as function enter and exit are also recorded.
- **Detection**: DIRA adopts a RAD-like return address defense. Function prologues log the return address, and function epilogues compare the current stack value against the logged value.
- **Identification & Signature Construction**: When an attack is flagged, DIRA uses dynamic slicing to trace the corrupted return address back to network receive operations. Using both direct data dependencies and control dependencies (conditional statements like `if` checks governing state flags), DIRA identifies all preceding attack packets. Packet bytes evaluated by program logic (e.g., protocol keywords matched via string comparison) are retained, while uninspected bytes are replaced with wildcards (`?`). A length constraint is calculated to specify the maximum offset where a terminating character (such as null) must appear, effectively creating semantics-aware regular expression signatures from a single attack instance.
- **Repair Mechanism**: DIRA restores overwritten memory using the preimages in the log. To determine the execution resume point, it identifies the least common dynamic ancestor of the function where data was ingested and the function where the attack was detected. Pre-inserted `setjmp` checkpoints enable a `longjmp` back to that function without relying on external operating system snapshots. DIRA proxies manage side effects like socket calls.
- **Evaluation**: Tested against exploits for `ghttpd`, `named` (BIND), and `rcadd` (remote CAD daemon). DIRA successfully produced accurate multi-packet signatures from a single attack instance. The runtime throughput overhead reached up to 70%, which the authors note makes DIRA best suited for deployment on honeypot servers rather than standard client endpoints.

### Takeaways
DIRA demonstrates that fine-grained memory update logging and dynamic slicing can unify attack detection, multi-packet signature generation, and state recovery. Even with a high runtime overhead (~70%), running instrumented servers on honeypots allows defenders to automatically extract context-aware signatures from single attack instances and prevent denial-of-service disruptions by recovering server state.

talks.title: Ian Clarke & Oskar Sandberg, Routing in the Dark
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Ian Clarke & Oskar Sandberg, Routing in the Dark.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Ian Clarke and Oskar Sandberg address a fundamental security and privacy risk in contemporary peer-to-peer (P2P) systems: simply participating in a public network exposes users to monitoring and network harvesting by adversaries or repressive governments. To mitigate this threat, future anonymous networks must shift from promiscuous "light" P2P networks (such as Gnutella or early Freenet), which connect to arbitrary strangers, to "dark" or friend-to-friend (F2F) P2P networks (like WASTE), where nodes exclusively form direct connections with trusted friends. Historically, darknets failed to scale beyond small, isolated clusters of 5 to 10 users. The speakers present a novel routing mechanism that uses small-world network theory to achieve scalable, decentralized greedy routing across a darknet topology without exposing personal user data.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of P2P Architectures**: The transition from centralized indexing (Napster) and semi-centralized architectures (Kazaa) to fully decentralized systems, highlighting the distinction between "light" (vulnerable to harvesting) and "dark" (friend-to-friend, scalable only with appropriate routing) networks.
- **Small-World Networks and Navigability**: The application of Stanley Milgram's sociological experiment (finding targets in five to six steps using local similarity) and John Kleinberg’s mathematical model proving that greedy routing converges in $O(\log^2 n)$ steps if link lengths follow a specific probability distribution with few long links and many short links.
- **Decentralized Position Reverse Engineering**: Constructing an idealized circular address space where participants initially select random numerical positions and iteratively execute a distributed swapping algorithm. Nodes exchange locations if swapping minimizes the product of distance metrics to their immediate friends, naturally embedding the social graph into an easily navigable ring topology without leaking real-world attributes.
- **Empirical Validation**: Simulation on synthetic datasets scaling up to 256,000 nodes, alongside empirical validation using an extracted 2,200-node crawl from Orkut.com.

### Technical Details
Kleinberg's model requires a network to balance frequent local connections with rare long-range chords to allow efficient greedy routing. In human networks, individuals use subjective similarity metrics (geography, professions) as signposts. However, asking an anonymous file-sharing client to collect and evaluate personal attributes is both computationally flawed and counter to privacy goals. 

Instead, Clarke and Sandberg demonstrate that the network topology alone contains sufficient structural information. Under their algorithm:
1. Nodes assign themselves a random coordinate on a unit circle.
2. Pairs of connected nodes contact each other across the network and propose exchanging coordinates.
3. A swap is executed if it reduces the product of distances between the nodes and their respective neighbors, creating localized clusters while preserving occasional long chords.

In simulated networks up to 256,000 nodes, unguided random walks failed entirely within $O(\log^2 n)$ steps, whereas the restored network achieved a 96% success rate, closely matching the mathematically optimal idealized model. When tested on real-world Orkut data exhibiting a power-law degree distribution, the algorithm achieved a 97% routing success rate with an average path length of 7.7 hops (compared to random search requiring ~43 hops across 72% successful queries). Even when node degree was artificially capped at 40 neighbors, greedy routing remained effective. The speakers noted an exception: celebrity/politician accounts (e.g., a fake John Kerry profile) failed to route properly because indiscriminate connections violated the reciprocal clustering properties of organic social networks.

### Practical Concerns & Takeaways
Deploying darknet routing in production Freenet requires overcoming several real-world engineering hurdles:
- **Usability and Peer Introduction**: Users must exchange cryptographic introductions out-of-band (e.g., via email, phone, or third-party introduction helpers) and maintain high uptime.
- **NAT Traversal**: Peer connections behind firewalls require UDP hole punching (as seen in projects like Dijjer or Skype).
- **Adversarial Resilience**: Defending against malicious identity manipulation and fraudulent swap requests (such as through cryptographic commitments in distributed random number generation).
- **Bandwidth Heterogeneity**: Accounting for varying connection speeds by dynamically stratifying connections into faster and slower friend tiers during query dispatch.

talks.title: David Cowan - The Information Security Industry: $3 Billion of Snake Oil
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in David Cowan - The Information Security Industry: $3 Billion of Snake Oil.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, David Cowan, a venture capitalist at Bessemer Venture Partners, evaluates the dynamics of the cybersecurity startup ecosystem and critiques flawed industry investments. Cowan argues that while startups are vital to security innovation, the market frequently pours capital into technologies that fail to deliver practical security. Rather than highlighting successful investments, he analyzes the persistent misalignments between technologies that work and technologies that sell, categorizing industry failures into "bloopers," "blights," and "blunders."

### Key Topics
- **The Security Ecosystem and Startup Dynamics**: Enterprises naturally prefer buying integrated product suites from established vendors (like Symantec, McAfee, and Cisco) for consolidated consoles and vendor viability. However, startups are continually required because networks face constant introduction of new protocols, applications, and platforms. Furthermore, unlike traditional IT infrastructure where systems asymptotically reach stability, security involves adaptive adversaries continually motivated by profit (spamming, extortion, and identity theft).
- **Flawed Purchasing Motivations**: Organizations routinely purchase ineffective tools due to herd mentality, desire to deflect blame, compliance requirements defined by outside parties, bundled software discounts (e.g., antivirus on headless web application servers), or reactive purchasing that only defends against last quarter's specific attack.
- **Taxonomy of Industry Mistakes**:
  - *Bloopers*: Technologies that neither work nor sell, consuming venture capital without harming enterprise customers. Examples include universal management consoles from startups, enterprise digital rights management (DRM), edge-based DDoS mitigation appliances, and general-purpose PKI architectures.
  - *Blights*: Technologies that fail to work effectively yet sell heavily. Examples include Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) that create overwhelming alert fatigue, unmanaged firewalls (often deployed with default configurations), and server-based signature antivirus.
  - *Blunders*: Emerging, heavily hyped technologies that do not work and are poised to become major future liabilities. Key examples include anomaly-based Intrusion Prevention Systems (IPS)—which suffer from high false-positive rates and inevitably get demoted to monitor-only mode—and flawed anti-phishing/authentication defenses.

### Technical Details
- **Deficiencies in Banking and Anti-Phishing Defenses**: Current consumer protection models rely on ineffective heuristics, such as client inbox toolbar lights, simplistic domain checks, and user security warnings that overwhelm end users with incomprehensible information. User awareness training cannot prevent attacks like DNS farming, local browser malware, or rogue search ads. Cowan notes that standard two-factor authentication (smart cards, time-based one-time tokens) and Biometrics cost approximately $20 per user per year yet remain vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks and malware-based session hijacking (slipstreaming) because the endpoint communication channel itself is compromised.
- **Recommended Architectural Shifts**:
  - *Authenticate Transactions, Not Logins*: Instead of securing the low-risk login phase with heavy friction, security should profile session context and apply risk-based step-up authentication exclusively on high-risk operations (e.g., address changes, large fund transfers).
  - *Out-of-Band Multi-Channel Authentication*: Defeating compromised client channels requires out-of-band verification across separate channels (such as an automated phone callback verifying specific transfer parameters and transaction codes) rather than single-channel 2FA tokens.
  - *Reputation and Behavioral Tracking*: Moving away from domain authentication (like Sender ID or DKIM, which spammers readily register) toward sender behavioral reputation monitoring.

### Takeaways
The security industry must critically assess security products on whether they address actual attacker economics and operational realities. Investors, vendors, and CISOs should prioritize zero-false-positive architectures, out-of-band transaction authorization, and automated decision-assistance tools over alert-heavy monitoring appliances, user-education panaceas, and perimeter snake oil.

talks.summary:
Continuing our tradition from previous years, leading experts from different industries, academia and law enforcement will be on stage participating in this panel to discuss the current threats online, hazards inside the Internet, battles between low level cyber criminals all the way to the mafia, special agents, spies, and even information warfare between nation-states.

This panel begins with a short introductory presentation on the latest technologies and operations by the Bad Guys and the Good Guys. We will talk about what's going on with Internet operations, global
routing, botnets, extortion, phishing and the annual revenue the mafia is getting from it. Then we'll move into question and answers from the audience. Panelists will accept questions on any subject related to the concept of Internet warfare, crime, and espionage, and will discuss it openly in regard to what's being done and what we can expect in the future, both from the Bad Guys and the Good Guys.

Discussion will focus on operational issues currently happening on the Internet, not on vulnerabilities or the latest leet hack you might have heard about. The discussion is mostly technical and operational in nature, but in previous years attendees have asked questions directing the discussion to the legal side of things. Participants are people who are involved with battling cyber crime daily, and many are leaders in the security operations community of the Internet.

Audience members bearing six-packs of beer for the panelists will advance to the front of the line.
