talks.title: Ava Latrope - eXercise in Messaging and Presence Pwnage
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Ava Latrope - eXercise in Messaging and Presence Pwnage.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Ava Latrope, a security consultant with iSEC Partners, explores the security landscape of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), formerly known as Jabber. Despite widespread adoption across enterprise workplaces and web applications, XMPP suffers from complex specifications and uneven client and server implementations. Latrope demonstrates how the protocol's design and real-world deployment shortcomings introduce significant opportunities for denial of service (DoS), amplification attacks, and XML parsing issues, while introducing a custom lightweight attack proxy built specifically to evaluate XMPP traffic.

### Key Topics
- **XMPP Architecture and Basics**: XMPP is a decentralized, open-standard protocol operating via XML streams, utilizing TLS for encryption and SASL for authentication. Common stanzas include info-query (`<iq>`), user messages (`<message>`), and presence (`<presence>`). It also supports HTTP binding for inline web clients.
- **Custom XMPP Interception Proxy**: Latrope built a proxy tool extending previous work presented by co-worker Rachel Engel at Black Hat. Designed with a minimal feature set similar to WebScarab or Burp, it adds support for XMPP traffic, multiple concurrent listeners, transparent pass-through logging, manual interception, and modification of stanzas between clients and servers.
- **Extension Exploration (XEPs)**: The talk reviews extensions defined by the community, focusing on Publish-Subscribe (PubSub) and Multi-User Chat (MUC). While official specifications offer blocking and privacy mechanisms, they are frequently neglected in production software.

### Technical Details
- **PubSub & Privacy Deficiencies**: In PubSub, publishers push updates to subscriber leaf nodes with minimal required participation from subscribers. While XEP-0016 specifies privacy lists that would allow users to block nodes or stanzas, it is overly complex and rarely implemented in consumer products. Instead, clients tend to rely on simple user blocking (XEP-0191), leaving users defenseless against unwanted PubSub broadcast spam.
- **HTTP Binding Vulnerabilities**: Web-based inline clients rely on HTTP binding, where the only mandated security mechanism is often a client-generated `request ID`. Latrope notes developers frequently implement these sequentially rather than randomly. Furthermore, recommendations to use HTTP authentication instead of standard SASL expose chat services to traditional web application vulnerabilities.
- **Presence Volume and Amplification DoS**: Group messaging and presence updates generate large volumes of traffic because status changes must be distributed to all participants. Specifications suggest mitigations like rate limiting connection attempts per IP or Jabber ID (JID), stanza size limitations, and denying unauthenticated connections, but Latrope observed that many clients and servers fail to enforce these. This makes MUC and PubSub susceptible to amplification attacks, where manual administrator blocking of individual JIDs is completely inadequate.
- **XML Parsing Failures**: While common XML attacks like entity expansion were mitigated in tested implementations, malformed stanzas regularly crash clients or sever connections. Latrope highlighted an incident where raw ethernet adapter output dumped into a chat room dropped every user running a libpurple-based client due to parsing failures, noting chat clients typically drop connections or crash rather than providing meaningful error feedback.

### Takeaways
XMPP's extensive catalog of community extensions and decentralized architecture have led to implementations that cut corners on security and error resilience. Standard recommendations for rate limiting, connection restrictions, and granular blocking are widely ignored by client and server developers. As a result, critical enterprise communication systems remain vulnerable to disruptive XML parsing crashes, spam, and denial-of-service amplification attacks. Latrope emphasizes the need for better testing tools and intends to release the developed attack proxy to assist researchers in evaluating XMPP implementations.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bosse Eriksson- Runtime Kernel Patching on Mac OS X.
talks.summary:
Runtime kernel patching has been around for almost ten years and is a technique frequently used by various rootkits to subvert the kernel's used in many modern operating systems.

This technique does not require any types of kernel modules or extensions and will allow you to hide various things like processes, files, folders and network connections by modifying the kernel's memory directly. It will also allow you to place various backdoors in the kernel for privilege escalation.

This talk will discuss runtime kernel patching on Apple's operating system Mac OS X and the XNU kernel. We will cover some rootkit basics as well as some Mac OS X specific 'features' which will facilitate our journey into the deepest parts of the darwin operating system and the XNU kernel.

As a bonus we will also show some basic methods for rootkit detection on Mac OS X that will aid you in the process of detecting rootkits that utilize runtime kernel patching to stay hidden.

talks.title: Brandon Dixon - Attacking SMS its no longer your BFF
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Brandon Dixon - Attacking SMS its no longer your BFF.
talks.summary:
It's the year 2009 and spam mail is still taking up a huge percentage of all email sent everyday over the Internet. Could you imagine that same messaging spam making a detour through your favorite cellular provider gateway and right to your SMS inbox? Mobile spam has not reached the same popularity as email spam, but what if it was as easy as submitting a form to spam thousands of people?

Research was done on several messaging services and implementations to identify vulnerabilities to exploit. The end result to the research was that the idea of mobile spam was easily a reality using Jabber/XMPP and some techniques already put in place by multiple vendors. This talk will conclude with a proof-of-concept web application demo that demonstrates the techniques and issues mentioned as well as thoughts for solving the next generation of spam. Expect to walk away with a new look on mobile spam and the damage that could be done just by pressing submit.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at DEF CON titled "Black Ops of PKI", Dan Kaminsky examines the systemic operational and technical fragility of public key infrastructure (PKI) and X.509 certificates. Rather than blaming poor enterprise adoption or "not caring enough," Kaminsky argues that X.509 was fundamentally misengineered for modern cross-organizational authentication. He demonstrates structural flaws in CA trust models, weaknesses in hashing algorithms like MD2 and MD5, and multiple semantic parsing vulnerabilities that enable attackers to bypass domain validation and forge certificates.

### Key Topics
- **X.509 Structural Failures**: Inability to exclude untrusted or weak certificate authorities (CAs) and severe limitations in delegation compared to DNS.
- **The CA Trust Model as a Race to the Bottom**: Because any trusted CA can issue certificates for any domain, the entire system is bounded by its weakest link.
- **Cryptographic Hash Degradation (MD5 & MD2)**: Building on previous chosen-prefix collisions against MD5 (Stevens and Sotirov), Kaminsky details the impending threat of pre-image attacks against legacy MD2 root certificates.
- **Language-Theoretic Security and ASN.1 Parsing**: Semantic parsing exploits in X.509 implementations, including multiple Common Names (CNs), ASN.1 BER encoding quirks, integer overflows in OID parsers, and null-byte injection.
- **Fixing PKI via DNSSEC**: Using DNS's strict hierarchical delegation and exclusivity to anchor and constrain certificates rather than discarding CAs entirely.

### Technical Details
- **Exclusion & Delegation Disparity**: Unlike DNS, where single entities control specific roots/registries and subdomains can be independently delegated, X.509 does not support clean delegation or exclusion without poorly supported mechanisms like name constraints. Companies often resort to sharing wildcard keys or purchasing full intermediate CAs under contractual promises.
- **MD2 Root Collision Risk**: A core VeriSign root certificate in ubiquitous trust stores remains self-signed using MD2-RSA. Because MD2 pre-image complexity has steadily dropped (from 2^104 down to 2^73 and trending toward practical viability), an attacker finding a pre-image could craft a rogue intermediate CA with an identical MD2 hash and reuse the root's self-signature. Furthermore, default configurations (such as Microsoft IIS with client authentication enabled) trust this root to authenticate clients to servers.
- **Semantic Parser Exploitation**:
  - *Multiple CNs*: Different software handles multiple CNs in a single CSR inconsistently (OpenSSL reading the first, IE taking all, Firefox taking the last), allowing attackers to satisfy CA validation on the first name while targeting a bank or wildcard in subsequent names.
  - *ASN.1 OID Encoding*: Object Identifiers (such as 2.5.4.3 for CN) can be manipulated using base-128 leading zeros (e.g., 2.5.4.0003) or 64-bit integer overflows (2.5.4.2^64+3). In clients like Internet Explorer, these evaluate to valid Common Names.
  - *Null-Byte Injection*: As demonstrated independently by Kaminsky and Moxie Marlinspike, inserting a null byte (`\x00`) into a domain string (e.g., `www.target.com\x00.attacker.com`) causes OpenSSL/CAs to validate `attacker.com` using the explicit length, while browsers relying on C-style null-terminated strings terminate early at `www.target.com`, issuing valid rogue certificates. Marlinspike highlighted that this could even compromise Firefox browser updates sent over SSL.

### Takeaways
Kaminsky concludes that Certificate Authorities still serve an important role—specifically in handling human-level semantic collisions (phishing, lookalike domains, brand verification via Extended Validation)—which algorithms cannot resolve alone. However, the underlying trust architecture must be anchored using a signed DNS root (DNSSEC). By publishing certificate hashes into DNSSEC records, organizations can leverage DNS's strict exclusivity to dictate exactly which CAs are authorized to sign for their domains, eliminating the weak-link race to the bottom.

talks.title: Efrain Torres
talks.teaser: Metasploit Goes Web explores Efrain Torres.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Efrain Torres introduces Wmap, a web application assessment tool and plugin designed as an extension of the Metasploit Framework. Torres explains that the project arose from frustration with existing commercial web vulnerability scanners, which often force users to discover vulnerabilities actively while browsing, suffer from detection risks, run strictly on Windows, and rely heavily on arbitrary risk ratings (e.g., high, medium, low) instead of demonstrating real exploitability. Wmap aims to keep web assessment simple, command-line driven, modular, and tightly linked to Metasploit's exploitation capabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Criticisms of Traditional Scanners:** Commercial tools often couple crawling and testing together, are limited by GUI and OS dependencies (such as Internet Explorer controls), and fail to provide reusable data workflows or seamless transitions to exploitation.
- **Decoupled Architecture:** Wmap decouples site crawling/traffic interception from testing. Standard man-in-the-middle proxies (e.g., Fiddler, Burp, or an al-qatab proxy patch) capture HTTP requests and populate a simple Metasploit database schema (tracking path, headers, query, body, and responses).
- **Metasploit Integration:** Instead of building a standalone scanning engine from scratch, Wmap leverages Metasploit auxiliary modules, allowing users to execute assessments and immediately pivot into exploitation.
- **Execution Order and Mixins:** Modules declare specific mixin types so the Wmap plugin can construct a website tree and trigger tests in a structured, logical sequence.

### Technical Details
- **Module Types:** Wmap categorizes assessment tasks using mixins, including `scan_server` (server-wide checks), directory and file scanners, query testers (`scan_query` and `scan_unique_query` to avoid redundant tests on identical parameter sets), body and header analysis, and `generic` modules that evaluate aggregated database results (e.g., the `generic_email_extract` module).
- **Fingerprinting and Signature Matching:** Torres highlights specific modules such as `wmap_ssl`, which extracts virtual host information from SSL certificates across ranges of IP addresses. Additionally, directory detection modules implement signature-based error page matching rather than relying solely on HTTP return status codes, improving accuracy when servers return custom error pages.
- **Workflow Demonstration:** The speaker demonstrates loading the `db_wmap` plugin inside Metasploit, loading targets extracted from captured traffic in the database, configuring module variables (such as target host, domain, and virtual host settings), inspecting the generated website data structure, and executing scans via `wmap_run`.

### Takeaways
Torres emphasizes returning to straightforward, decoupled, command-line tooling that values raw assessment data over bells and whistles. By bridging web application mapping directly into the Metasploit database and module ecosystem, testers gain a flexible, extensible environment capable of shifting directly from vulnerability identification to exploitation.

talks.title: Efstratios Gavas - Asymetric Defense How to fight off the NSA Red Team
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Efstratios Gavas - Asymetric Defense How to fight off the NSA Red Team.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Efstratios Gavas, a professor at the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy (USMMA) and PhD student at Brooklyn Polytechnic, discusses asymmetric defense strategies for securing small, unfunded IT operations. Drawing from his team's participation in the annual Cyber Defense Exercise (CDX)—where academy students defend mock enterprise networks against attacks by the NSA Red Team—Gavas contrasts USMMA's lack of funding and staffing with larger Department of Defense (DoD) academies like West Point and Annapolis. He explains how small teams can succeed by deliberately breaking resource-heavy "best practices" in favor of extreme simplicity, deep system understanding, and low administrative overhead.

### Key Topics
- **Simplicity Over Complexity**: Highlighting that buying complex commercial solutions without understanding them decreases security while increasing cost and confusion.
- **CDX Constraints and Operations**: Defending a mock multi-user enterprise network against live NSA attacks while handling dynamic operational injects, DNS updates, and reporting under strict labor/budget constraints.
- **Consolidated Architecture vs. Distribution**: Deliberately collapsing services onto a single server box to allow solitary students to manage, patch, and monitor systems effectively despite single-point-of-failure risks.
- **GUI Abstractions vs. Native Unix**: Using appliances and GUI management systems for rapid prototyping and learning, followed by transitioning to FreeBSD for fine-grained network control.
- **Practical Administration**: Baseline monitoring, passphrase adoption over complex password rotations, and balanced firewall/antivirus configurations to avoid degrading usability.

### Technical Details
- **Network Architecture**: The USMMA network segregated external DNS and routing from an internal Windows Active Directory domain controller and internal DNS. All core server applications—including a web server, jabber (IM), and database—were consolidated onto a single machine isolated on its own VLAN switch segment, alongside a dedicated monitoring station.
- **Windows Management**: Active Directory Group Policies were utilized to push centralized configurations across Windows XP (primary) and Windows Vista workstations. Sysinternals Process Explorer was emphasized to determine a clean baseline of normal processes and network traffic on trusted machines. Host security tools discussed included internal Windows firewalls and Core Force, with caution regarding excessive AV scans thrashing hard drives.
- **Transition from GUIs to FreeBSD**: The team initially tested and implemented web-managed firewall and gateway tools such as m0n0wall, IPCop, Untangle, and pfSense, alongside eBox (and Webmin) for application hosting. Due to limitations in implementing a segmented split-DNS architecture and NAT with GUI tools, the team migrated both their gateway and core application servers to native FreeBSD. FreeBSD utilized a combination of PF and IPFW for filtering and NAT, while hosting services including web, email, database, and Jabber, relegating eBox to a backup system.

### Takeaways
- For an under-resourced team, simplicity is essential: if you cannot understand or administer a service cleanly, you should not deploy it.
- Understand baseline system behavior on clean builds so anomalies, unfamiliar processes, and sluggishness stand out immediately.
- Passphrases composed of multiple related words offer superior length (20–30 characters) and memorability compared to short, complex passwords with frequent rotation requirements.
- Do not fear non-standard operating systems or native command-line environments; tools like FreeBSD provide granular control, clean routing, and stability once administrators invest time into learning them.

talks.title: Jeff Yestrumskas and Matt Flick - Cross Site Scripting Anonymous Browser 2.0
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Jeff Yestrumskas and Matt Flick - Cross Site Scripting Anonymous Browser 2.0.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Jeff Yestrumskas and Matt Flick introduce XAB 2.0 (Cross-Site Scripting Anonymous Browser), an updated tool and framework designed to tunnel HTTP browsing requests over websites vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS). Inspired by Tor and discussions around cross-site scripting, the creators explored whether anonymous browsing could be achieved without requiring network participants to willingly install client software. Instead, XAB leverages stored or reflected HTML injection to execute JavaScript payloads inside unsuspecting visitors' browsers, turning their browsers into transient proxy nodes.

### Key Topics
- **XAB Concept and Architecture**: Contrasting voluntary anonymization networks like Tor with an involuntary, dynamic network driven by victim web browsers executing injected JavaScript.
- **Component Roles**: The system relies on three core components:
  - `xab attacker`: The core script/tool that coordinates requests, delivers payloads, and processes retrieved data.
  - `HTTP prox AB`: A local HTTP proxy configured in the attacker's browser listening on a designated port (e.g., port 8293 in the demo) to intercept outgoing browsing requests and serve final reconstructed web pages.
  - `CD proxy` (Cross-domain proxy): An external proxy allowing the architecture to bypass browser cross-domain sandboxes that prevent direct `XMLHttpRequest` calls across domains.
- **Data Exfiltration via Image Requests**: Data returned from target sites is transferred by the participant browser using base64-encoded URL parameters embedded in chained image requests, which receive transparent 1x1 GIF responses.
- **HTTP Referer Leakage & Mitigations**: Resolving the security challenge where the `Referer` header sent to the cross-domain proxy reveals the vulnerable site hosting the attacker's payload.
- **Content Handling Improvements**: Upgrades since the initial February release (presented at Black Hat DC) to preserve MIME types directly from the cross-domain proxy rather than relying on file magic.

### Technical Details
1. **Request Queueing**: When the attacker attempts to browse a site (e.g., `target.xab`), the attacker's browser sends the request through `HTTP prox AB`, which enqueues the target URL.
2. **Payload Delivery**: A victim visits a site (`vul site.xab`) containing an injected stored (or reflected) script pointing to `xab attacker`. The attacker script checks its internal queue, pops a pending URL, and instructs the victim's browser to request that URL via the cross-domain proxy (`freehost.xab`).
3. **Chunking and Exfiltration**: The cross-domain proxy fetches the target content and returns it to the victim. Because URL lengths in browsers like Internet Explorer are limited (e.g., ~2,000 characters), the victim's client code splits the base64-encoded response into manageable chunks and issues multiple image requests to `xab attacker`.
4. **Reassembly**: The `xab attacker` script reassembles the segments, base64-decodes the full payload, and saves the asset into a dump directory. `HTTP prox AB` polls this directory and serves the completed webpage, images, and favicon back to the attacker's browser.
5. **Referer Issue Workarounds**: To prevent cross-domain proxy operators from tracing the payload location via the HTTP Referer header, the speakers discuss multiple techniques: hosting payloads on HTTPS/SSL sites (leveraging RFC 2616, where browsers omit the Referer header when moving from HTTPS to HTTP), loading from local files, nesting iframes pointing to reflected XSS parameters to add hops between nodes, or exploiting transient browser bugs.

### Takeaways
XAB 2.0 demonstrates a working proof-of-concept for proxying web traffic through XSS victims, capable of loading full HTML, multi-image pages, and various MIME types. While the concept proves viable, architectural challenges remain—most notably HTTP Referer leaks, transmission speed, and the reliance on transient browser sessions. The speakers noted ongoing development ideas including payload encryption, daisy-chaining multiple participants, and leveraging HTML5 offline storage capabilities for more persistent execution.

talks.title: Johnny Long
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate Johnny Long and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher and author Johnny Long reflects on his personal journey from early hacking, corporate penetration testing, and industry fame to finding purpose through humanitarian work in Uganda. After reaching the peak of his cybersecurity career—writing popular books, speaking at DEF CON, and doing high-profile security assessments—Long felt unfulfilled and self-absorbed. A pivotal mission trip to Uganda transformed his outlook, leading him to establish Hackers for Charity (HFC) to channel the skills and resources of the hacker community toward meaningful global impact.

### Key Topics
- **Early Hacker Journey & Career Peak:** Long details growing up tinkering with basic programming on a TRS-80, TI, and Commodore 64, tapping into BBS communities, scanning 900 MHz cell conversations, intercepting pager data (including White House sysadmin alerts), dropping out of college, and landing a dream penetration testing role at CSC's Strikeforce.
- **Disillusionment with Fame:** Despite publishing in Phrack, speaking at DEF CON 11 ("Watching the Watchers"), and writing best-selling books on Google hacking and "no-tech hacking," Long realized that pursuing personal fame and ego left him deeply dissatisfied.
- **Transition to Humanitarian Work:** Prompted by his Christian faith and his wife Jen's trip to Uganda, Long visited Uganda and set up wireless networking and computer equipment for the organization AOET. Witnessing how simple IT fixes restored operations and allowed hundreds of orphans to receive education, medical care, and food inspired him to start Hackers for Charity.
- **Hackers for Charity Initiatives:** HFC projects expanded from building sponsorship websites (coded by volunteer Paul Madoff) to running food programs in Kenya and Uganda, providing computer classrooms, and supporting local tech enthusiasts like Fred, a self-taught technician repairing laptops.
- **The Power of the Community ("Me to We"):** Long highlights how the hacker community rallies to support humanitarian causes, noting contributions from figures like Simple Nomad, Roelof Temmingh (Maltego), and the BackTrack team via the Informer subscription platform, as well as a community backlash that pressured PayPal to quickly unfreeze HFC's operational funds.

### Technical Details & Observations
- **Classic Exploits & Hardware Modding:** Modifying scanner outputs to capture POCSAG and FLEX pager traffic; writing early Google dorks alongside contributors like "our god" for web application exploits.
- **Field Hacking in Uganda:** Long demonstrates that hacker thinking remains integral to daily life in Uganda. He shares examples of shoulder surfing at local banks (photographing unlocked CSO workstations and guard badges), capturing telecom setup credentials on video, exploiting a menu quirk on the MTN Zone mobile app to lock in a 95% discount, and navigating local informal markets for paper and hardware.

### Takeaways
Long urges the cybersecurity community to pivot from "me" to "we" by pairing technical passion with higher purpose. Rather than focusing solely on ego or commercial gain, hackers can leverage their collective ingenuity, software contributions, hardware donations, and fundraising to create tangible, life-saving impacts for people in need worldwide.

talks.title: Joseph McCray
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Joseph McCray - Advanced SQL Injection.
talks.summary:
Joseph McCray, a network penetration tester, traces his evolution from dismissing web application security to becoming an SQL injection expert. He explains the three classes of SQL injection—in-band (error-based), out-of-band, and inferential (blind)—and emphasizes that automated tools often identify only one or two types, forcing testers to learn manual techniques.

The core methodology involves identifying the injection point, determining whether it's integer or string-based (critical for knowing whether to use quotes), and then attempting attacks in order of preference: error-based first (easiest), then union-based, and finally blind as a last resort.

For error-based injection, McCray shows how to extract data like usernames, database names, and versions directly from error messages. Union-based injection requires determining the correct number of columns and data types, then substituting columns with database queries. Blind injection is tedious—asking the database yes/no questions via time delays or page differences, then using ASCII conversion charts to brute-force character values.

Real-world SQL injection is far harder than training environments. McCray walks through actual challenges: handling unusual error messages, workarounds for BLOB/image data types, and escaping mechanisms. Key tips include using "UNION ALL" (for type flexibility) and "NULL" (when data types are unknown).

IDS signature evasion is straightforward—simple signatures looking for "OR 1=1" can be bypassed with "OR 2=2" or alternative syntax. Hex encoding and uppercase/lowercase UTF variations also work. McCray discusses fingerprinting mod_security, WebKnight, and .NET Defender, then bypassing them with tools like Unicode encoding.

Defenses include prepared statements and parameterized queries, though McCray notes stored procedures can still be vulnerable if input isn't properly validated. For modern applications (AJAX, JSON, web services), manual request manipulation with Burp Suite or similar tools is necessary. The talk emphasizes that real-world security is complex, encoding matters, and proper input validation is essential.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines the operational mechanics, architecture, and security considerations of commercial in-flight Wi-Fi systems. Drawing from personal testing and packet captures gathered over several years across multiple flights and airlines (including flights to Germany and domestic US routes between San Francisco, New York, and Boston), the speaker details the evolution of in-flight connectivity from early satellite offerings to modern air-to-ground EV-DO setups and pico cell implementations.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of In-Flight Services**: The shift from Boeing's early satellite-based Connexion service (launched in 2004 and discontinued around late 2006 due to latency and performance issues) to modern domestic systems like Aircell's Gogo Inflight, LiveTV on JetBlue, and international satellite solutions like OnAir.
- **Air-to-Ground vs. Satellite Architecture**: Contrasting satellite uplinks with domestic US air-to-ground communication utilizing roughly 92 ground base stations, EV-DO cellular-derived frequencies (~3 MHz licensed spectrum inherited from Verizon), and private ground networks.
- **Cabin Wireless Deployments**: Typical access point channel plans (channels 1, 6, and 11 on Boeing 767s with three APs; channels 1 and 11 on Airbus planes with two APs) and standard naming conventions (e.g., cwap1, cwap2).
- **Passenger Privacy and Endpoint Security Risks**: Risks associated with cleartext passenger traffic, laptop shoulder-surfing, leaky preferred wireless network lists, and unpatched operating systems.

### Technical Details
- **Physical and Network Infrastructure**: Modern domestic installations like Gogo on American Airlines and Virgin America utilize wired access points inside the cabin rather than wireless mesh. The external air-to-ground EV-DO antenna is mounted on the belly of the aircraft, whereas satellite systems use top-mounted antennas.
- **Network Routing and Addressing**: Client devices receive private RFC 1918 addresses (such as 172.30.x.x networks) behind NAT, with internal proxy gateways (such as a 10.241.x.x gateway and references to "flamenco proxy"). The public breakout IP assigned to the entire airplane (in Aircell's IP space, e.g., 12.130.106.111) remains persistent and static throughout the flight. Traceroutes show non-responsive layer-2/MPLS characteristics over the ground packet network.
- **Service Controls and Degradation**: Gogo service is administratively enabled only above 10,000 feet; prior to that altitude or during severe turbulence that causes loss of link, traffic is blackholed and redirected to an internal splash landing IP (1.1.1.1). Speeds ranged from roughly 258 Kbps to 1.3 Mbps downlink. Despite terms prohibiting VoIP, basic SIP/Skype calls function in a degraded state.
- **SSID and Beacon Enumeration**: Beyond the public captive portal SSID, spectrum monitoring revealed multiple hidden and encrypted ESSIDs/BSSIDs, attributed to point-of-sale (credit card) terminals and crew networks.
- **Endpoint Information Leakage**: Captures revealed older unpatched Windows clients probing and advertising ad-hoc networks for previously remembered SSIDs (such as airport Wi-Fi like McCarran or corporate SSIDs like 'google-a'), exposing passenger affiliations and movement patterns.

### Takeaways
While the underlying airline networks and in-flight Wi-Fi infrastructure maintain separation from flight avionics and deploy encrypted networks for transactional duties, the passenger Wi-Fi segment functions as an open, unencrypted public hotspot. The primary threats stem from user behaviors, cleartext transmissions, and misconfigured or unpatched client devices leaking sensitive data to nearby passengers in the cabin.

talks.title: Panel - Hardare Black Magic Building Devices with FPGAs
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Panel - Hardare Black Magic Building Devices with FPGAs.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at DEF CON by the Seaborg research group from the University of Delaware, this talk explores digital system design and hardware security using Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). The speakers argue that true security cannot be achieved on unknown or closed-source hardware and encourage security practitioners to understand and build custom hardware using hardware description languages (HDLs). The session introduces core FPGA concepts, open-source and commercial development toolflows, embedded microprocessor implementation, and running Linux on reconfigurable logic.

### Key Topics
- **FPGA Fundamentals & Architecture**: Understanding field programmable gate arrays as reconfigurable semiconductor devices compared to general-purpose CPUs, GPUs (CUDA/OpenCL), and custom ASICs. FPGAs offer massive parallelism, low power, and deterministic timing without operating system scheduler overhead.
- **HDL Toolchains & Simulation**: Contrasting VHDL and Verilog. The presentation highlights open-source simulation options, specifically GHDL (a GNU VHDL simulator based on GCC technology) and GTKWave for viewing waveform timing data, allowing developers to design logic without purchasing physical hardware.
- **Xilinx ISE Workflow**: Walking through the implementation pipeline, including code synthesis, netlist generation, mapping logical ports to physical board traces via user constraint files (.ucf), place-and-route, and programming bitstreams over JTAG.
- **Embedded System Design with Xilinx EDK**: Creating soft-core processor systems using the 32-bit MicroBlaze architecture. The workflow demonstrates integrating peripheral intellectual property (IP) cores, memory-mapped I/O, Fast Simplex Links (FSL) for hardware acceleration, and the Software Development Kit (SDK) for writing C software.
- **Embedded Linux on FPGAs**: Deploying embedded Linux distributions (such as PetaLinux) on a soft-core MicroBlaze processor using low-cost hardware boards.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Platform**: Practical demos were executed using the Xilinx Spartan-3E FPGA development board (XC3S500E), equipped with 232 user I/O pins, 32 KB on-chip block RAM, 64 MB DDR SDRAM, NOR/serial flash, RS-232 serial ports, JTAG/USB interfaces, discrete LEDs, slide switches, and a VGA port.
- **Hardware Acceleration vs. Bus Latency**: The speakers demonstrated how standard bus communication (such as PLB) can introduce latencies of 50 or more clock cycles for peripheral access. By implementing custom accelerators in VHDL connected directly to the processor via FIFO-based Fast Simplex Links (FSL), operations can be dispatched and returned with latency as low as a single clock cycle.
- **Hands-on Demos**:
  - Direct combinational logic mapping slide switches to onboard LEDs.
  - A 50 MHz-to-25 MHz clock divider process in VHDL driving a VGA signal to render test patterns and custom arcade games without external graphics processors.
  - Design and simulation of a multi-cycle 32-bit MIPS CPU core using GHDL and GTKWave.
  - MicroBlaze soft-processor instantiation in EDK communicating over RS-232 to output serial data and stepping through C code with an on-chip hardware debugger.
  - Initial setup and kernel build steps for PetaLinux targeting a MicroBlaze CPU.

### Takeaways
FPGAs eliminate the trade-off between rigid ASIC performance and slow microprocessor execution by enabling custom, parallel hardware accelerators. Beginners can enter FPGA development at low cost or entirely free through command-line simulation suites like GHDL and GTKWave. For embedded systems, combining soft processors (like MicroBlaze) with dedicated HDL modules allows developers to run standard operating systems like Linux while hardware-accelerating performance-critical tasks.

talks.title: Rafael Dominiguez Vega - USB Attacks Fun with Plug and own
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Rafael Dominiguez Vega - USB Attacks Fun with Plug and own.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Rafa (Rafael Dominguez Vega), a security consultant and researcher at MWR InfoSecurity, examines USB attack vectors, USB driver vulnerabilities, and practical exploitation methods using custom hardware. Prompted by a two-week client assessment of a Linux-based hardware device featuring a new USB port, the research investigates how flaws in driver-level handling of USB descriptors can be uncovered and weaponized.

### Key Topics
- **USB Risks and Attack Surfaces**: Contrasting modern USB plug-and-play mechanisms with older serial connections, highlighting corporate exposure ranging from physical social engineering (e.g., rogue keyboard injection) and lost unencrypted drives to malware like Conficker abusing AutoRun.
- **USB Enumeration & Descriptors**: Explaining how the host automatically discovers device identity and selects drivers using descriptors (Device, Configuration, Interface, Endpoint, and String descriptors), noting the vendor ID and product ID as critical selection criteria.
- **USB Driver Fuzzing Approaches**:
  - *Virtualized Fuzzing via QEMU*: Emulating malformed USB devices into a guest Linux virtual machine by recompiling QEMU with predefined test cases. This provides quick setup with minimal overhead, but lacks a dynamic fuzzing engine.
  - *Network Fuzzing via USB over IP*: Utilizing the `usbip` Linux kernel module combined with an existing network fuzzing engine to strip IP headers and inject malformed USB packets into target drivers dynamically.
  - *Hardware Fuzzing*: Conceptualizing physical devices to either inject malformed packets directly or act as a man-in-the-middle device modifying USB packets on the fly.

### Technical Details
- **Vulnerability Discovery**: During a combined fuzzing and source code review of Linux USB drivers, a buffer overflow vulnerability was identified in driver handling of human-readable USB string descriptors (referred to pseudonymously as the "tom dick and harry" function and "vegas girl" device due to disclosure restrictions).
- **Mechanism**: The `usb_string` function copies string descriptor data supplied by the USB device into a driver buffer without adequate bounds checking, overflowing the buffer and overwriting adjacent data structures.
- **Kernel Crash & Live Debugging**: The speaker demonstrated a kernel crash using QEMU emulation. For crash analysis and exploit development, KGDB was connected over a serial port to the target system running the vulnerable Linux driver, allowing live kernel breakpoints in the string-processing routines.
- **Hardware Exploit Implementation**: The exploit payload was implemented using a Microchip PIC18 family microcontroller (specifically a PIC18F14K50) programmed in MPLAB. During enumeration, the device supplies crafted descriptor data containing a static address and a `pop`/`ret` gadget sequence into registers (`ECX` and `EBX`), redirecting control flow toward shellcode.

### Takeaways
Organizations and developers should mitigate USB security risks by:
- Disabling unnecessary USB drivers and disabling unused USB ports via system security policies.
- Conducting rigorous security assessments and source code audits of USB device drivers.
- Implementing corporate security policies regarding USB storage use and employee awareness.

talks.summary:
Beckstrom's Law is a new model or theorem of economics formulated by Rod Beckstrom. It purports to answer 'the decades old question of "how valuable is a network." It is granular and transactions based and can be used to value any network. It applies to any network: social networks, electronic networks, support groups and even the Internet as a whole. To read a white paper explaining the law and mathematics in detail, please see Economics of Networks. This new model values the network by looking from the edge of the network at all of the transactions conducted and the value added to each. It states that one way to contemplate the value the network adds to each transaction is to imagine the network being shut off and what the additional transactions costs or loss would be.

Beckstrom's Law differs from Metcalfe's law, Reed's law and other concepts that proposed that the value of a network was based purely on the size of the network, and in Metcalfe's law, one other variable.

talks.title: Roger Dingledine - Why Tor is Slow and What We Are Doing About It
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Roger Dingledine - Why Tor is Slow and What We Are Doing About It.
talks.summary:
Roger Dingledine from the Tor Project explains why Tor is slow and outlines six priority problems requiring solutions. After briefly reviewing Tor's distributed-trust model—routing through multiple relays so no single relay learns both source and destination—he presents performance measurements: a 50KB file averages ~8 seconds with heavy tails extending to 20–30 seconds, while a 1MB file averages ~50 seconds. The core tension is that Tor was optimized for bandwidth, but different user classes have conflicting priorities: web browsers want low latency while bulk-transfer users (BitTorrent, file sharing) demand capacity.

Dingledine prioritizes six problems:

**1. Congestion and Flow Control**: A single TCP connection between relays means when one user talks fast, everyone gets punished. The solution requires switching to UDP and implementing a secure, portable user-space TCP stack—a challenging research problem lacking consensus among systems experts.

**2. Bulk Transfer Users**: Simulations show 20 BitTorrent users can ruin performance for 10,000 web browsers. Current round-robin scheduling lets fast circuits dominate bandwidth; the top 10% of circuits send ~2.5MB while the slowest send 1–2 cells.

**3. Insufficient Capacity**: More relays help but don't solve root congestion problems. When relays spiked from 1,500 to 1,900 during the Iran election crisis, median 50KB latency improved from ~9 to ~7–8 seconds—but improvements disproportionately benefited file-sharing users. Adding capacity alone without fixing congestion won't help web browsers.

**4. Load Balancing**: Bandwidth measurement doesn't work correctly; relays advertising higher bandwidth get overused, creating high variability. Active measurement could improve this but introduces anonymity attack vectors (e.g., intersection attacks on incentive mechanisms).

**5. High Variability**: Token bucket rate limiting forces burst-silent-burst traffic patterns, creating artificial one-second delays at each relay hop and forcing a minimum three-second circuit build time. Circuit build times range from 1–30 seconds; using slow circuits hurts subsequent performance. Solutions include adaptive timeouts based on observed performance.

**6. Directory Overhead**: Clients fetch ~150KB every couple hours plus ~3MB daily, prohibitive for modem users in developing countries. Proposed fix: micro descriptors and consensus optimization.

Key challenges include reconciling anonymity/performance trade-offs (e.g., incentive mechanisms enable intersection attacks), the lack of a good network simulator for testing optimizations, and conflicting latency tolerances across user classes. Real-world impact is demonstrated through Iran election data (surge to ~8,000 daily users) and China's Gmail blocking (triggered Tor usage spike).

talks.title: Christopher Soghoian - Your ISP and the Government: Best Friends Forever
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Christopher Soghoian - Your ISP and the Government: Best Friends Forever.
talks.summary:
Your Internet, phone and web application providers are all, for the most part, in bed with the government. They all routinely disclose their customers' communications and other private data to law enforcement and intelligence agencies. Worse, firms like Google and Microsoft specifically log data in order to assist the government, while AT&T and Verizon are paid $1.8 million per year in order to provide real time access to customer communications records to the FBI. How many government requests does your ISP get for its customers' communications each year? How many do they comply with? How many do they fight? How much do they charge for the surveillance assistance they provide? Who knows. Most companies have a strict policy of not discussing such topics.

You might assume that the law gives companies very little wiggle room - when they are required to provide data, they must do so. This is true. However, companies have a huge amount of flexibility in the way they design their networks, in the amount of data they retain by default, the emergency circumstances in which they share data without a court order, and the degree to which they fight unreasonable requests.

The differences in the privacy practices of the major players in the telecommunications and Internet applications market are significant: Some firms retain identifying data for years, while others retain no data at all; some voluntarily provide the government access to user data - Verizon even argued in court that it has a 1st amendment right to give the NSA access to calling records, while other companies refuse to voluntarily disclose data without a court order; some companies charge the government when it requests user data, while others disclose it for free. For an individual later investigated by the government, the data retention practices adopted by their phone company or email provider can significantly impact their freedom.

Unfortunately, although many companies claim to care about end-user privacy, and some even that they compete on their privacy features, none seem to be willing to compete on the extent to which they assist or resist the government in its surveillance activities. Because information about each firmís practices is not publicly known, consumers cannot vote with their dollars, and pick service providers that best protect their privacy.

This talk will pierce the veil of secrecy surrounding these practices. Based upon a combination of Freedom of Information Act requests, off the record conversations with industry lawyers, and investigative journalism, the practices of many of these firms will be revealed.

talks.title: Craig Heffner - How to Hack Millions of Routers
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Craig Heffner - How to Hack Millions of Routers.
talks.summary:
This talk will demonstrate how many consumer routers can be exploited via DNS rebinding to gain interactive access to the router's internal-facing administrative interface. Unlike other DNS rebinding techniques, this attack does not require prior knowledge of the target router or the router's configuration settings such as make, model, internal IP address, host name, etc, and does not rely on any anti-DNS pinning techniques, thus circumventing existing DNS rebinding protections.

A tool release will accompany the presentation that completely automates the described attack and allows an external attacker to browse the Web-based interface of a victim's router in real time, just as if the attacker were sitting on the victim's LAN. This can be used to exploit vulnerabilities in the router, or to simply log in with the router's default credentials. A live demonstration will show how to pop a remote root shell on Verizon FIOS routers (ActionTec MI424-WR).

Confirmed affected routers include models manufactured by Linksys, Belkin, ActionTec, Thompson, Asus and Dell, as well as those running third-party firmware such as OpenWRT, DD-WRT and PFSense.

talks.title: Dan Kaminsky - Black Ops Of Fundamental Defense: Web Edition
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Dan Kaminsky - Black Ops Of Fundamental Defense: Web Edition.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At DEF CON, Dan Kaminsky discusses the signing of the DNS root and presents a pragmatic approach to deploying and utilizing DNSSEC. Contrary to common perceptions that DNSSEC is too complex, expensive, and low-benefit, Kaminsky argues that it provides a foundational mechanism for scalable cross-domain authentication and federation, introducing the concept of Domain Key Infrastructure (DKI) as an effective evolution of Public Key Infrastructure (PKI).

### Key Topics
- **Target Audiences:** Addressing the security community through four perspectives—users (who deserve transparent security without blame), buyers (investing in working authentication), builders (who must deliver scalable, usable security products), and breakers (security researchers invited to audit code).
- **Transparency and Auditing:** Announcement that Kaminsky's company, Recursion Ventures, is backing an open audit of the ldns library conducted by Justin Ferguson, with the report released publicly.
- **Operational Realism vs. Rigidity:** Prioritizing operational stability, deployment speed, and practical compatibility over protocol purism or bureaucratic compliance.
- **Federation and Governance:** Using DNSSEC and the neutrally governed ICANN root hierarchy to resolve long-standing federation problems (such as end-to-end complexity, single 'kingmaker' entities, and certificate authority key bleed).

### Technical Details
- **Freebird (Dynamic / Online Key Signing):** Instead of burdensome offline pre-signing pipelines that create massive operational friction, Freebird acts as a proxy in front of existing DNS servers. It signs records dynamically on the fly, caches cryptographic signatures, and enables rapid DNSSEC deployment (demonstrated via registrar configuration in under a minute).
- **End-to-End Validation Strategies:** Standard DNSSEC models relying on the resolver-set Authenticated Data (AD) bit require trusting local network resolvers (e.g., untrusted hotel networks). To achieve true client-side verification, Kaminsky explores:
  - *Chasing and Superchase:* Walking up the chain from domain to root; 'superchase' optimizes this by returning the full chain back to root in a single query.
  - *Tracing:* Applications embedding recursive resolution using libunbound.
  - *DNS over HTTP:* Tunneling DNS lookups over HTTP/TCP to bypass restrictive middleboxes.
  - *Wrapping:* Embedding DNSSEC trust chains directly into X.509 SSL certificates, tested in an experimental build of Chrome.
- **Client Integration and Hooking Tooling:**
  - *FreeShell:* Authenticating SSH sessions via DNSSEC-published public keys tied to user identities (e.g., email addresses) rather than hardcoded server keyrings.
  - *Freeload:* An `LD_PRELOAD` shared library hooking OpenSSL's `X509_verify_cert` function to transparently enforce certificate fingerprint matching against DNSSEC records across OpenSSL-based utilities (such as curl, wget, Apache, and Postfix).
  - *Foxy:* An HTTPS/SSL proxy designed to provide DNSSEC validation feedback into desktop browsers without altering OS crypto stacks.
  - *FreeCAPI:* Injecting API hooks into Windows CryptoAPI (`CertGetCertificateChain`) via tools like remoteDLL to validate S/MIME signatures in Microsoft Outlook against fingerprints secured by DNSSEC.
- **Exclusionary Property for CAs:** Rather than replacing Certificate Authorities, DKI allows domain owners to pin authorized Extended Validation (EV) certificates directly in signed DNS records, blocking unauthorized or compromised CAs from issuing conflicting valid certificates.

### Takeaways
Kaminsky concludes that DNSSEC and DKI make end-to-end authenticated federation, scalable TLS pinning, and trusted email identity achievable with existing software frameworks. By coupling accessible tools with runtime hooks and online signing, security practitioners can build high-assurance systems without breaking usability.

talks.title: Dave King - Hardware Hacking for Software Guys
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Dave King - Hardware Hacking for Software Guys.
talks.summary:
Hardware hacking is cool, but it can be daunting to software guys. Microcontrollers mix hardware and software basically allowing software guys to do hardware in software. Lately several products have emerged that make it even easier for software guys to get hardware up and working.

Arduinos are relatively cheap, open source, all-in-one prototyping boards with a strong community behind them. All you need is a USB cable and the Arduino IDE (which is also open source). The Arduino language is easy to learn for anyone with even a basic knowledge of coding. Arduinos can be made into many different security devices including keyboard emulators, RFID readers/writers, combination lock brute forcing robots, magnetic stripe card emulators, and automated cell phone dialers. In a way, an Arduino is kind of like the hardware equivalent of scripting languages. They make development quick and are a good fit for many projects.

In this talk you'll see examples of projects built with Arduinos and information on how they were done. You'll also see some limitations of Arduinos and some alternatives to typical Arduinos. In the end you'll see that anyone can make really cool hardware, even without a degree in electrical engineering.

This presentation will explore the various hacks, both hardware and software, that people tried against a system they had little-to-no prior knowledge about, and both the failures and successes that resulted. It will also discuss the decisions made to make the firmware hackable in a way that was accessible to as many people as possible, but not entirely trivial. talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Toool - The Search for Perfect Handcuffs... and the Perfect Handcuff Key.
talks.summary:
The few handcuff talks which have appeared at conferences in the past have focused mostly on how these restraints function and how to open them without a key. While this talk is no exception (going into great detail about the specialized anti-pick protections used by many brands) we will also reveal the product of ongoing, precision research that TOOOL members have conducted.

Did you know that although there is a ?standard? size and shape for basic handcuff keys, every manufacturer has variations, special features, and sizing issues that make creating a single, universal key quite difficult? In our talk, we will explain how to create this type of "ultimate" key that opens all major brands of handcuff, both in the United States and elsewhere around the world. The über key is verified as working with...

Smith & Wesson (USA)

Peerless (USA)

ASP (USA)

Chicago (USA)

Winchester (USA)

Hiatt-Thompson (UK)

RBS (UK)

Kyoung Chang (Korea)

Yuil (Korea)

Republic Arms (South Africa)

... and more!

We have the math, we have the means, and will demonstrate to everyone how to obtain the best handcuff key you might ever own!

TOOOL

The Open Organization of Lockpickers is a non-profit sportpicking group dedicated to the advancement of the general public knowledge about locks and lockpicking. By examining locks, safes, and other such hardware and by publicly discussing our findings we hope to strip away the mystery with which so many of these products are imbued.

The more that people know about lock technology, the better they are capable of understanding how and where certain weaknesses are present. This makes them well-equipped to participate in sportpicking endeavors and also helps them simply be better consumers in the marketplace, making decisions based on sound fact and research.

talks.title: Dondi West - An Examination of the Adequacy of the Laws Related to Cyber Warfare
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Dondi West - An Examination of the Adequacy of the Laws Related to Cyber Warfare.
talks.summary:
This paper argues that the current rules of war are adequate for addressing the unique issues that are encountered as a result of conducting and defending against cyber warfare. The author begins by giving a survey of the laws that have the biggest impact on cyber warfare. Next, the author describes several paradigms that have come about as a result of cyber warfare, followed by a direct rebuttal. The author then asserts five reasons for why the U.S. should not enter into an international treaty for cyber warfare: (1) combatant commanders already have proper guidelines for conducting warfare; even in the information age; (2) fields of law are seldom demarcated by technology; (3) an unintended consequence of a cyber warfare law is that it may pose an undue limitation on a primarily non-lethal strategic deterrence; (4) our adversaries are unlikely to comply; and (5) the rate of technology growth will outpace the ability for an international cyber regime to produce responsive policy, while the flexibility allotted by the UN Charter and laws of war are able to absorb technological advances. The author concludes that the current UN Charter and Laws of War should continue to govern cyber warfare and that creating an international treaty or law for cyber warfare would do more harm than good and seriously cripple our ability to conduct war.

WebSphere Application Server (WAS), IBM's Java Enterprise Edition (JEE) application server, is one of the leading application servers and is the predominate application server in the financial and insurance sectors. It is also embedded in several of IBM's other products including WebSphere Portal, WebSphere Process Server and WebSphere Message Broker.

In March 2009, IBM released PK81387 which patches a "Possible application source file exposure" in WAS. Detailed explanation of this vulnerability and it's exploitation will be provided including how implementation details such as character encoding and multiple vulnerabilities, some still unpatched, can be orchestrated to provide file and directory exposure inside a applications Web Archive (WAR). In some cases, with common libraries or WAS feature use, these vulnerabilities can be extended to achieve arbitrary code execution resulting in full compromise of the application server.

Exploitation details will be described and use of this vulnerability and others to execute a remote operating system shell will be demonstrated. Source code to the exploit and other tools will be provided.

talks.title: frank^2 - Trolling Reverse-Engineers with Math: Ness... It hurts...
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in frank^2 - Trolling Reverse-Engineers with Math: Ness... It hurts....
talks.summary: y = mx+b? f(x) = sin(x/freq)*amp?! SIN X = (A+BX+CX^2)/(P+QX+RX^2)?! None of these formulas as they stand alone really mean much of anything-- except maybe a headache for some. Isolating the variables, however, will eventually open the door for us to manipulate our code in creative and exciting ways. This isn't necessarily a ground-breaking technique in obfuscation, but who cares if it's fun? Given an arbitrary formula, we can place our code anywhere we like. It doesn't even need to be a traditional f(x) formula like a sinewave, either-- all we need is a number and some constants. Draw your code in circles? Sure! Sexually harass a reverse-engineer by the shape and girth of your code in memory? Hell yes! This talk will attempt to teach a functional method that allows for the random placement, concatenation and manipulation of assembly instructions for the attempt of filling up a reverser's swear jar. You don't need to write any assembly-- but you better come knowing its mechanics.

talks.title: Fyodor & David Fifield - Mastering the Nmap Scripting Engine
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Fyodor & David Fifield - Mastering the Nmap Scripting Engine.
talks.summary:
Most hackers can use Nmap for simple port scanning and OS detection, but the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) takes scanning to a whole new level. Nmap's high-speed networking engine can now spider web sites for SQL injection vulnerabilities, brute-force crack and query MSRPC services, find open proxies, and more. Nmap includes more than 125 NSE scripts for network discovery, vulnerability detection, exploitation, and authentication cracking.

Rather than give a dry overview of NSE, Fyodor and Nmap co-maintainer David Fifield demonstrate practical solutions to common problems. They have scanned millions of hosts with NSE and will discuss vulnerabilities found on enterprise networks and how Nmap can be used to quickly detect those problems on your own systems. Then they demonstrate how easy it is to write custom NSE scripts to meet the needs of your network. Finally they take a quick look at recent Nmap developments and provide a preview of what is soon to come. This presentation does not require any NSE experience, but it wouldn't hurt to read http://nmap.org/book/nse.html.

talks.title: Greg Conti - Our Instrumented Lives: Sensors, Sensors, Everywhere...
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Greg Conti - Our Instrumented Lives: Sensors, Sensors, Everywhere....
talks.summary: Make no mistake, your analog life is under siege. Virtually every facet of your day to day existence is being sampled, digitized, aggregated, collated, shared, and reality mined. Whether the reason is to support your friendly neighborhood targeted advertiser or to help win a war on terror, a thickening web of sensors tracks our day to day existence in the physical world. Sensors are everywhere: our sneakers, cell phones, appliances, game consoles, power meters, automobiles, highways, bridges, airports, shopping malls and night clubs, among many others. At the same time, technologies that uniquely identify us from a sea of others are on the rise. Financial and other incentives motivate many to start sampling our lives and the law does little to protect us. Convergence of the resultant islands of data is occurring now. More important however is the next step. Because sampling is occurring on a scale never before imaginable, our uniqueness and individuality are giving way to previously impossible models of collective and individual human behavior. How these models will be used is up for debate, but you can be certain they will be abused by some. This talk examines the problem of our impending instrumented existence, studies where it is all going, and provides you with ways to defend yourself, your family, and friends.

talks.title: Honey - Ripping Media Off Of the Wire
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Honey - Ripping Media Off Of the Wire.
talks.summary:
The proprietary protocol developed by Adobe Systems for streaming audio, video and data over the Internet, the ëReal Time Messaging Protocol- (RTMP) and the proprietary protocol created by Macromedia used for streaming video and DRM, -Encrypted Real Time Messaging Protocol- (RTMPE) implementations for MySpace use security through obscurity and actually provide zero security.

This talk will describe methods and demonstrate how to download media from MySpace directly and convert the media into MP3s, breaking the DRM by manipulating the RTMP/RTMPE protocol implementation.

talks.title: Jimi Fiekert - The Anatomy of Drug Testing
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Jimi Fiekert - The Anatomy of Drug Testing.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, hospital laboratory worker Jim (Jimi Fiekert) explains the operational, legal, and biochemical foundations of drug testing. He details federal drug scheduling, mandatory testing standards, laboratory testing methodologies, biological specimen types, commonly tested versus rarely tested compounds, and mechanisms used to detect adulteration and sample tampering.

### Key Topics
- **Legal Framework and Testing Protocols:** Fiekert outlines legal drug scheduling, noting that Schedule 1 covers drugs deemed highly addictive with no accepted medical use, whereas Schedule 2 includes medically applicable substances like cocaine (used as a surgical anesthetic). He highlights Department of Transportation (DOT) testing regulations as the strictest standard, requiring a minimum five-panel screen (typically THC, amphetamines, cocaine, opiates, and barbiturates), strict chain of custody forms, and secured collection rooms (taped dispensers, blued toilet water, disabled running water). Under specific conditions like reasonable suspicion or accidents, DOT rules mandate directly observed collections.
- **Testing Methodologies:** The speaker covers five core analytical methods:
  - *EIA and ELISA:* Immunoassays using antibody-enzyme reactions to produce a qualitative color line (similar to a home pregnancy test).
  - *Spectrophotometry:* A quantitative technique using enzymatic dry slides that measure drug concentration via color change, heavily used for alcohol in emergency rooms.
  - *Chemiluminescence:* Uses antibodies and cuvettes exposed to acids, bases, and light flashes, measuring light absorption and re-emission for quantitative results.
  - *Breath Alcohol Testing (BAT):* Breathalyzers measure deep-lung air at the end of an extended exhalation to avoid surface saturation and false positives from food or mints.
  - *Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrophotometry (GC-MS):* The analytical gold standard. GC separates vaporized chemicals through a coated coil by transit time, while MS fragments molecules on a charged detector plate. Combining retention time with atomic fragmentation provides definitive identification and quantitative measurements down to at least 5 micrograms per deciliter.
- **Specimens and Detection Windows:** 
  - *Hair:* Standard tests capture metabolites up to 9 months and require metabolic processing (passive exposure does not trigger a positive).
  - *Urine:* The most common testing matrix, evaluating excreted metabolites.
  - *Blood:* Utilizes gray-top tubes containing anticoagulants and anti-metabolites to test directly for active drugs or metabolites.
  - *Meconium:* The first stool of an infant, useful because it lacks bacterial contamination and provides legally binding evidence of maternal drug transmission.
  - *Saliva, Sweat, and Tissues:* Less common formats; adipose (fat) tissue stores fat-soluble drugs like THC.
- **Common vs. Uncommon Drugs:** Common screens target amphetamines, tricyclic antidepressants, oxycodone, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and illicit drugs like cocaine, heroin, PCP, and THC. Uncommon drugs include LSD, psilocybin, DMT, mescaline, and peyote; these are rarely tested because they clear the body rapidly, are not fat-soluble, or require cost-prohibitive specialized panels.

### Technical Details
Fiekert clarifies how adulteration and manipulation are detected in urine:
- **Dilution and Specific Gravity:** Normal urine specific gravity ranges from 1.010 to 1.025. Samples falling below thresholds like 1.005 are classified as dilute. While not an automatic failure, it requires retesting.
- **Creatinine and Nitrates:** Creatinine is measured to confirm authentic renal excretion rather than plain or salted water dilution. Nitrates are evaluated to detect chemical oxidizing adulterants added in vitro or taken in vivo.
- **Physical Adulterants:** Bleach or soap alters specific gravity, creates odor, and triggers immediate observed recollects sent concurrently for lab analysis.
- **Medical Review Officer (MRO):** An MRO verifies legitimate prescriptions (e.g., hydrocodone) to prevent confirmed legitimate medications from resulting in an unexcused failure.

### Takeaways
Drug detection windows are primarily driven by metabolic rates and whether a substance is fat-soluble (such as THC, which can persist for months in chronic users) versus rapidly cleared water-soluble drugs. Diluting specimens or taking unproven supplements like high-dose niacin carries health risks (such as liver strain) without bypassing multi-factor laboratory validation checks like creatinine, specific gravity, and GC-MS confirmation.

In this session, John Curran, CEO of the American Registry for Internet Numbers (ARIN), will describe the key considerations for and benefits of IPv6 adoption and the steps all network operators and engineers should be taking to prepare for IPv4 depletion challenges.

talks.title: John McNabb - Cyberterrorism and the Security of the National Drinking Water
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding John McNabb - Cyberterrorism and the Security of the National Drinking Water.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, John McNabb, an IT professional and former water commissioner with 13 years of service in Massachusetts, provides a realistic assessment of kinetic and cyber threats against the United States national drinking water infrastructure. While drinking water has historically been an attractive target during warfare and terrorism—and supports virtually all other critical infrastructure sectors—McNabb evaluates the feasibility and likelihood of large-scale contamination versus disruption. He concludes that while massive nationwide contamination is hindered by extreme system fragmentation and dilution, serious vulnerabilities remain in the distribution system and increasingly interconnected SCADA networks.

### Key Topics
- **Critical Infrastructure Interdependencies**: Drinking water underpins agriculture, public health, food production, and firefighting. Cascading failures stemming from power grid outages can directly trigger water system breakdowns.
- **Threat History & Perceptions**: Historical precedent stretches from Vlad the Impaler poisoning wells to domestic extremist groups (e.g., Order of the Rising Sun, Covenant, Sword, and the Arm of the Lord) and Al Qaeda training documents referencing water poisoning. However, authorities like Dorothy Denning note that while adversaries possess IT capabilities for communication, propaganda, and cybercrime, evidence of direct cyberterrorism causing real-world kinetic harm remains absent.
- **Fragmentation vs. Centralization**: The US has approximately 155,000 public water systems, each custom-designed for local water characteristics and demand. This fragmentation makes nationwide attacks practically impossible, contrasting with the interconnected power grid. However, private conglomerates like American Water (serving 15 million people across 35 states) introduce potential centralized networking exposures. Additionally, the supply chain for treatment chemicals—specifically chlorine gas, with 38% produced in Louisiana and transported by rail—represents a critical single point of failure.
- **Cyber Incidents in Water Systems**: Incidents documented by RISI and other bodies show an upward trend, though numbers remain small. Notable historical cases include the Maroochy water breach in Australia (an insider consultant using wireless to dump untreated sewage), a modem breach at Salt River Project, an employee introducing spyware via laptop at Harrisburg, and unauthorized software installation at the Tehama Colusa Canal Authority.

### Technical Details
McNabb examines attack feasibility across distinct water system components using the operational framework of PSA (Pressure, Safe to drink, Availability):
- **Water Sources (Reservoirs and Well Fields)**: Contaminating surface reservoirs like the Dillon Reservoir requires massive quantities of toxic agents (such as tanker trucks), making intentional poisoning impractical due to dilution. Confined aquifers and well fields are more vulnerable to long-term contamination (e.g., Superfund sites or leaking tanks), though still slow and difficult to weaponize quickly. Instrumentation such as remote SCADA or radio-controlled dam floodgates present potential sabotage vectors.
- **Water Treatment Plants**: Plants process raw water via coagulation, flocculation, chemical dosing, filtration, and chlorination before entering the clearwell. Kinetic sabotage of custom, long-lead-time components like high-lift pumps (which took 18 months to replace in the speaker's plant) poses high disruption risk. Cyber tampering with SCADA dosing controls could alter chemical concentrations (e.g., dangerous over-chlorination or under-chlorination leading to fatal bacterial proliferation).
- **Distribution Networks & Hydrants**: Identified as the most vulnerable vector because it lies post-treatment. With an estimated 1.8 million miles of pipes and 6 to 12 million fire hydrants lacking backflow check valves or continuous monitoring, back-pumping chemical, biological, or radiological (CBR) agents into a hydrant could poison localized targets within minutes. Contaminants must be weaponized, toxic/infectious, stable, and chlorine-resistant.
- **SCADA & Control Evolution**: Transitioning from electromechanical relays and pen recorders to Windows-based SCADA HMIs has dramatically increased IP exposure. A McAfee survey highlighted that 76% of critical infrastructure SCADA systems connected to IP networks or the Internet. The emergence of the Stuxnet worm—specifically targeting Siemens Simatic WinCC and PCS 7 systems commonly found across industrial and water sectors—marks a critical shift where malware seeks direct administrative and process control.

### Takeaways
- Routine "noise"—such as aging infrastructure (earning a D- rating nationally with an estimated $350 billion shortfall), water main breaks, valve failures, and accidental contamination (e.g., the Boston MWRA pipe break and bird contamination in Woburn)—often eclipses terrorism concerns for local operators.
- The Public Health Security and Bioterrorism Preparedness and Response Act of 2002 mandated vulnerability assessments and emergency response plans, but lacked ongoing enforcement or uniform minimum standards.
- An estimated $1 to $1.6 billion is needed nationally to implement recommended security measures.
- The primary technical countermeasure needed is 24/7 real-time water quality monitoring in the distribution system.
- The EPA should use its statutory authority to mandate universal cybersecurity baselines (such as the 21 steps to improve SCADA security) across all municipal and private water providers.

talks.title: Lineberry, Richardson, and Wyatt - These Aren't the Permissions You're Looking For
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Lineberry, Richardson, and Wyatt - These Aren't the Permissions You're Looking For.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researchers from Lookout Mobile Security examine the security boundaries of the Android operating system, focusing on its permission model and sandboxing mechanisms. The speakers demonstrate how malicious applications can bypass expected restrictions by abusing zero-permission techniques, leveraging the single `READ_LOGS` permission to extract sensitive user data, and exploiting root vulnerabilities on unpatched carrier devices.

### Key Topics
- **Android Architecture and Sandboxing**: The session begins with an explanation of core Android components—such as the Android Manifest, activities, intents, broadcast receivers, and background services. The speakers clarify that Android's sandbox relies on standard Linux/Unix UID/GID process separation rather than the Dalvik Virtual Machine itself.
- **Zero-Permission Attacks**: Analysis of capabilities accessible to an application without requesting any permissions, including device rebooting, auto-starting on boot or installation, UI hijacking, and covert data exfiltration.
- **Abusing System Logging (`READ_LOGS`)**: How a single permission can act as a master key to capture sensitive data, including GPS coordinates, SMS messages, browser bookmarks, search history, authentication tokens, and contacts.
- **Root Exploitation and Patch Fragmentation**: Discussion of rooting vulnerabilities—notably a netlink uevent validation bug similar to CVE-2009-1185—and the broader security risks posed by slow carrier patch cycles and user reluctance to apply updates.

### Technical Details
- **Rebooting and Auto-Starting Without Permissions**: While the `REBOOT` permission requires system or signature privileges, an app without permissions can trigger a device reboot by spamming toast notifications inside a `while (true)` loop. Each toast creates a weak JNI global reference in the Android system server; reaching 2,001 references causes the system server to throw a `SIGSEGV` and crash. Furthermore, the researchers noted that `RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED` permission checks could be bypassed in Android versions at the time simply by omitting the permission declaration while registering the receiver. Apps could also execute immediately on installation by registering a broadcast receiver for market referral intents, which Android 2.2 (Froyo) automatically generates.
- **UI Hijacking ('Circle of Death')**: By overriding `onKeyDown` to consume all keypress events (except the home button) and bouncing execution between an activity's `onDestroy` hook and a lightweight service, an app can lock the user interface. Escaping this state requires pulling the battery or booting into safe mode by holding the trackball.
- **Covert Two-Way Exfiltration**: An application lacking internet permissions can communicate with an external server by launching the browser to a target URL while the screen is off (querying `PowerManager`). To receive incoming commands, the app can register a custom URI scheme (such as `nethack://`) mapped to a transparent activity that immediately finishes itself, enabling covert two-way command and control.
- **Log Scraping Framework**: Using a client service requesting only `READ_LOGS` (with internet for demonstration) connected to a Ruby on Rails backend, the researchers monitored log devices (`/dev/log/main`, `/dev/log/events`, and `/dev/log/radio`). They showed that third-party apps, OEM additions, and framework components leak SQLite queries (first 64 characters), incoming/outgoing SMS contents and phone numbers, visited URLs, screenshots with auth tokens, and location data (GSM cell ID, LAC, CDMA base station coordinates, and GPS coordinates from weather widgets and system libraries).
- **Local Privilege Escalation**: A vulnerability in Android's handling of netlink uevent messages—conceptually matching the `libudev` vulnerability CVE-2009-1185 discovered by Sebastian Krahmer—failed to verify message provenance. Packaged into a JNI-based APK, this exploit allowed local root and a reverse root shell on nearly every flagship US carrier phone prior to Android 2.2.

### Takeaways
Users should not assume an application is benign simply because it requests few or no permissions, and must apply OS updates promptly. Developers must strictly avoid logging sensitive user or authentication data, parameterize SQL queries, and enforce component permissions on activities and broadcast receivers. Finally, OEMs and carriers must accelerate testing and update deployment to prevent widespread vulnerabilities across device fleets.
